title: Travelling
questions: What transport do you often use when travelling?
Do you often ride a bicycle?
Do you prefer to sit by the window when travelling?
Did you have a long journey with your family as a child?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 1 示范答案】
1) What transport do you often use when travelling?
Whenever I travel, the metro and high-speed rail are my go-to options. They are quick, they run to the minute, and I can just sit back and get some work done on the way.

2) Do you often ride a bicycle?
Not as often as I would like, to be honest. I cycle to the nearest metro station when the weather is decent, but the moment it turns cold and rainy I switch straight back to public transport.

3) Do you prefer to sit by the window when travelling?
Absolutely - a window seat makes the whole journey far more interesting. I like watching the scenery flash past, and it gives me a bit of privacy, so I can either doze off or daydream without being disturbed.

4) Did you have a long journey with your family as a child?
I did, actually. We used to take an overnight train to my grandparents place every summer, and it took something like fourteen hours. Looking back, those trips were a huge part of my childhood - we would play cards, eat snacks, and by the end of the night the whole carriage felt like one big family.

title: Rubbish and recycling
questions: Did you recycle when you were a kid?
Is waste sorting common in your country?
How do you recycle things like paper and plastic?
What do you do when you see rubbish on the street?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 1 示范答案】
1) Did you recycle when you were a kid?
Not really, and I am a bit embarrassed about it now. When I was little, everything went into one bin, and it was only at secondary school that I started separating paper from plastic.

2) Is waste sorting common in your country?
It is becoming far more common, especially in big cities. Most residential compounds now have colour-coded bins, and there are usually volunteers standing by to remind you what goes where.

3) How do you recycle things like paper and plastic?
I keep it simple: I rinse out bottles and cartons, flatten the boxes, and drop everything into the recycling bins downstairs. Anything I am unsure about, I check on my phone rather than guess.

4) What do you do when you see rubbish on the street?
If it is right next to me and there is a bin within reach, I will pick it up - it takes two seconds. But I would not lecture a stranger about it; I would rather set a good example than pick a fight.
advancedWords: rinse out bottles（把瓶子冲洗干净）
go into one bin（全丢进一个桶）
set a good example（以身作则）

title: Tiredness
questions: What do you do when you feel tired?
When would you feel tired?
Do you often feel tired?
When you feel tired, do you still go out with your friends?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 1 示范答案】
1) What do you do when you feel tired?
If I can, I take a quick power nap - twenty minutes and I am a different person. Otherwise a hot shower and a cup of tea do the trick, and if I am really knackered I switch off my phone and turn in early.

2) When would you feel tired?
Usually mid-afternoon, right after lunch - that is when I hit a wall. Long meetings or a day of staring at screens also drain me pretty quickly.

3) Do you often feel tired?
More often than I would like, mainly because I stay up too late. It is a bit of a vicious circle: I am tired during the day, so I work slowly, and then I stay up to catch up.

4) When you feel tired, do you still go out with your friends?
It depends on the plan. If it is a close friend and a low-key dinner, I will drag myself out, because seeing people usually perks me up. But if it is a loud party and I am running on empty, I will give it a miss and sleep instead.
advancedWords: do the trick（管用、解决问题）
perk me up（让我精神起来）

title: Shoes
questions: Which do you prefer, fashionable shoes or comfortable shoes?
How much money do you usually spend on shoes?
Have you ever bought shoes online?
Do you like buying shoes? How often?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 1 示范答案】
1) Which do you prefer, fashionable shoes or comfortable shoes?
Comfort wins hands down for me - I am on my feet a lot, so if a pair pinches my toes it is a deal-breaker. That said, I do like shoes that look sharp without sacrificing comfort.

2) How much money do you usually spend on shoes?
Not a huge amount, maybe a few hundred yuan a pair. I would rather buy one decent pair that lasts a couple of years than four cheap ones that fall apart in a season.

3) Have you ever bought shoes online?
Plenty of times, although it is a bit of a gamble. Sizing varies from brand to brand, so I have had to send a couple of pairs back, but the return process is usually painless.

4) Do you like buying shoes? How often?
I would not call myself a shoe person, but I do enjoy it when I stumble on a good bargain. I probably buy two or three pairs a year, usually once the old ones are worn out.

title: Politeness
questions: What did you do to show your politeness as a child?
On what occasions should we be polite?
Do you think being polite is very important?
How did you learn to be polite as a child?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 1 示范答案】
1) What did you do to show your politeness as a child?
The usual things - greeting my elders, offering my seat on the bus, and thanking a neighbour when they held the door open. My parents drilled those habits into me early.

2) On what occasions should we be polite?
Pretty much all the time, but especially when you are dealing with people who are serving you - waiters, drivers, nurses. And when there is a disagreement, being polite stops things from escalating.

3) Do you think being polite is very important?
I would say so. Politeness is essentially a way of showing respect, and it costs you nothing. Nine times out of ten it makes people far more willing to help you.

4) How did you learn to be polite as a child?
Mostly by copying my parents, and partly by being corrected. If I forgot to greet a relative, my mum would give me a look, and I would know straight away what I had done wrong.

title: Fruit and vegetables
questions: Do people in your country like planting vegetables?
Were there any kind of fruits and vegetables you disliked as a child?
What kind of fruits and vegetables do you dislike?
Where do you usually buy fruit and vegetables?
How often do you eat fruit and vegetables?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 1 示范答案】
1) Do people in your country like planting vegetables?
A fair number do - my grandparents grow tomatoes and cucumbers on their balcony, and in the countryside it is simply part of daily life. For city dwellers, though, it is more of a hobby than a necessity.

2) Were there any kind of fruits and vegetables you disliked as a child?
I could not stand bitter melon or celery; the taste was far too strong for me. I have come round to celery since then, but bitter melon and I are still not on speaking terms.

3) What kind of fruits and vegetables do you dislike?
Durian is the one thing I have never been able to get on board with - the smell alone puts me off. Apart from that, I eat pretty much everything.

4) Where do you usually buy fruit and vegetables?
Mostly at the wet market near my place, because it is fresher and cheaper than the supermarket. I also order through a grocery app when I am short on time.

5) How often do you eat fruit and vegetables?
Every day, without fail - I have fruit with breakfast and vegetables with at least two meals. If I skipped them for a couple of days I would feel sluggish.

title: Advertisement

ninePointAnswer:
【Part 1 示范答案】
1) Do you often see advertisements when you are on your phone or computer?
Constantly - I would say a couple of hundred times a day, mostly on social feeds and short videos. They are so well targeted now that they are almost impossible to ignore.

2) What kind of advertising do you like?
I quite like ads that tell a story or make me laugh, especially the ones with a clever twist at the end. What I cannot stand are those loud, in-your-face ones that interrupt a video every thirty seconds.

3) Do you like advertisements?
On the whole I am fairly neutral about them - they pay for the free content I use, so I accept they are part of the deal. Having said that, I would happily pay a bit extra to watch something ad-free.

4) Do you see a lot of advertising on trains or other transport?
Plenty. The metro is basically a moving billboard: every wall and screen is covered, and even the tickets have logos on them. It works, too, because you have nothing else to look at.

5) Is there an advertisement that made an impression on you when you were a child?
There is one I still remember - a milk advert with a talking cow that ended on a joke. I must have been about seven, and my friends and I would repeat the punchline at school for weeks.

6) Have you ever bought something because of an advertisement?
More often than I care to admit. I once bought a pair of running shoes after seeing an ad about a marathon, and to be fair they turned out to be excellent, so no regrets.

Not as much as I used to - my phone does everything these days. I do keep a slim notebook in my bag for meetings, because scribbling things down by hand helps me remember them.

2) Do people still keep handwritten letters today?
Some do, mainly for sentimental reasons. I know people who keep birthday cards and love letters in a shoebox, whereas an email tends to be deleted without a second thought.

Very rarely - maybe a card at New Year. It feels like a bit of an effort now, which is a shame, because there is something special about receiving something handwritten.

I was obsessed with paper planes and origami frogs. My desk was covered in scraps, and at break time we would fold them and see whose plane flew the furthest.

A few, mostly around festivals - paper lanterns and, more recently, some hand-made cards. I am not particularly gifted at it, but it is a lovely way to switch off.

I miss the easy routine, and the fact that my friends were in the same building all day. There was no commute, no bills to pay, and lunch break came with guaranteed company.

2) What was your favourite subject at secondary school?
History, without a doubt - my teacher was a brilliant storyteller and made the past feel like a drama series. It was the only subject where I looked forward to the homework.

3) Were there any subjects that you found difficult at secondary school?
Physics, definitely. I could memorise the formulas all right, but the moment the questions changed shape I was completely lost, and I never quite caught up.

4) Do you remember your first day at secondary school?
I do, quite vividly. I got lost looking for the science block, turned up late to my first lesson, and sat next to a boy who ended up being my best friend for years - so it worked out fine.

Far too often, and it is mortifying when they remember mine perfectly. I am much better with faces than with names, which I suspect is a fairly common problem.

2) How do you feel when people can't remember your name?
I try not to take it personally, because I am just as bad. It only stings a little when it is someone I have met three or four times.

I repeat it back when we are introduced, then link it to something - a place, a hobby, a rhyme. Writing it down in my phone afterwards makes a big difference too.

Not really, especially with names from other languages. It might take two or three meetings before it sticks, and even then I sometimes second-guess myself.

title: Describe a time you made an important decision and were happy with the result
titleZh: 对结果开心的重要决定
questions: 【Part 2】
Describe a time you made an important decision and were happy with the result
You should say: What the decision was / Why you made the decision / How easy it was for you to make the decision / And explain why you were happy with the result
【Part 3】
1. Which is better, to make a decision quickly or slowly?
2. Do you think most people's decisions are made in their 20s?
3. What if people in a group have different opinions on a decision?
4. What little decisions do people make every day?
5. Do you think it is a good idea to make a small decision every day?
6. How can we tell the difference between an important and an easy decision?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 2 示范答案】
So, the decision I want to talk about is one I made about two years ago - I turned down a place on a master's programme and took a job instead. Sounds straightforward, but at the time it felt like a proper fork in the road.

The offer came from a company I'd wanted to work for for ages, and the timing was awful - I'd already paid a deposit for the course, and my parents were very much in the "more education" camp. So I wasn't choosing between two good options; I was choosing between a plan and an opportunity.

How easy was it? Honestly, not easy at all. I talked it through with a tutor and a couple of friends who'd gone straight into work, and what swung it for me was that the job would actually pay me to learn the things I wanted to learn. I also told myself I could always go back to study later, but that team might not be hiring again.

And then the first three months were terrifying - I felt completely out of my depth and kept thinking I'd made a huge mistake. But the work suited me, my manager put real time into me, and about eighteen months later I was running a small project of my own. Looking back, I'm really glad I trusted my gut instead of taking the safer path.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 快 vs 慢：小事可以快，大事值得慢。Big calls deserve a night sleep before you commit.
2) 20 多岁是否定型：很多决定确实发生在那时候，但人生随时可以转向。People are not locked in by one choice made at twenty-two.
3) 组内意见不合：先对齐目标，再比较方案。If the goals match, the disagreement is usually about details rather than direction.
4) 每天的小决定：吃什么、几点睡、回不回消息。Most everyday choices are about habits rather than strategy.
5) 每天做小决定好不好：好，但别耗尽精力，重要的事要留出注意力。
6) 重要 vs 容易的决定：看代价和可逆性。If a decision is hard to undo and costs a lot, it is important by definition.

【Part 3 全文】
1) Which is better, to make a decision quickly or slowly?

It depends entirely on the size of the decision. I would say big calls deserve a night sleep before you commit, because you rarely get the money or the time back. Small ones are better made quickly, though — agonising over which brand of coffee to buy just wastes the attention you need for the important stuff. So: slow on the irreversible ones, fast on everything else.

2) Do you think most people's decisions are made in their 20s?

A lot of the big ones, yes — your first job, the city you settle in, probably the person you build a life with. But people are not locked in by one choice made at twenty-two, and I think that stereotype frightens younger people more than it should. I know plenty of people who retrained at forty and were far happier for it.

3) What if people in a group have different opinions on a decision?

First, align on the goal, then compare the options — because if the goals match, the disagreement is usually about details rather than direction. After that, it helps to agree in advance on how the decision will actually be made: a vote, or letting the person who owns the problem decide. What ruins groups is deciding twice: once in the meeting and again in the corridor afterwards.

4) What little decisions do people make every day?

What to eat, when to go to bed, whether to reply to a message now or later, which route to take, what to wear. Most of them are really about habits rather than strategy — we are not weighing options, we are repeating what we did yesterday. That is probably a good thing, because nobody could cope with a hundred real decisions before lunch.

5) Do you think it is a good idea to make a small decision every day?

As a habit, sure, but I would not turn it into a ritual. The risk is decision fatigue: if you spend your willpower on breakfast and wardrobe choices, you have less left for the things that actually matter. I would rather automate the trivial decisions and deliberately slow down for the important ones. Quality of attention beats quantity of choosing.

6) How can we tell the difference between an important and an easy decision?

Two tests: how much it costs, and how hard it is to undo. If a decision is hard to reverse and expensive to get wrong, it is important by definition — buying a flat, quitting a job, moving abroad. An easy decision is usually one where you can change your mind next week at very little cost. Notice that importance and difficulty are not the same thing; a decision can be easy to make and still be important.

title: Describe a person you know who did something difficult and was successful
titleZh: 做困难事情并成功的人
questions: 【Part 2】
Describe a person you know who did something difficult and was successful
You should say: Who this person is / What difficult thing this person did / Why this person was successful / And explain how you feel about this person
【Part 3】
1. In which sectors are companies more likely to succeed in China?
2. Is it easy to start up a company?
3. Other than making money, what is more important for a company?
4. Does money equal success?
5. How can companies help protect the environment?
6. Is it difficult to do business in today's world?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 2 示范答案】
The person I want to talk about is my aunt. She runs a small bakery in a town where three supermarkets opened within two years.

And when her old customers started buying sliced bread instead, she did something I still think was really brave. She closed for a month, sold her old equipment, and reopened as a shop that only does sourdough and celebration cakes.

It was a gamble, honestly. She'd never baked sourdough in her life, so she spent that month learning from videos, burning dozens of loaves and taking notes like a student. At first the shop was almost empty, and she had to borrow money just to cover the rent. What saved her was persistence, plus a bit of cleverness - she started inviting people in for free tastings, and taking orders for birthdays.

Two years on, she's got a queue on Saturday mornings and a small online business. And I really admire her for it, because she didn't sit around waiting for sympathy or for things to improve. She rebuilt the whole business on a skill she taught herself at fifty.

So whenever I feel like giving up on something, I think about her flour-covered apron and get back to work.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 哪些行业容易成功：刚需和新兴科技相关行业更稳，风口会变。Sectors that solve everyday problems tend to weather downturns better than fads.
2) 创业容易吗：开始容易，活下来难。Starting up is easy; staying afloat past years  is the real test.
3) 除了赚钱什么更重要：信誉与员工。Reputation is the one asset you cannot buy back once it is gone.
4) 钱等于成功吗：不等于，但缺钱很难谈理想。Money is a measure of some kinds of success, not the whole scoreboard.
5) 公司如何环保：从包装和供应链入手，最容易见效。Cutting waste in packaging is the quickest win for most firms.
6) 现在做生意难吗：竞争更激烈，但工具和渠道也更多。Small businesses have more competition but also cheaper access to customers.

【Part 3 全文】
1) In which sectors are companies more likely to succeed in China?

Right now I would put my money on healthcare, green energy and anything to do with AI. They all sit on problems that are not going away — an ageing population, pollution, and businesses trying to cut costs. Sectors that solve everyday problems tend to weather downturns better than fads, so a company selling medical devices is safer than one selling bubble tea.

2) Is it easy to start up a company?

Starting up is easy; staying afloat past years is the real test. Registration takes a morning and a modest deposit, and there is plenty of cheap software to get you going. What is brutal is the second year, when the savings run out, staff need paying and nobody knows your name yet. Plenty of founders underestimate that part completely.

3) Other than making money, what is more important for a company?

Its reputation, without a doubt. Reputation is the one asset you cannot buy back once it is gone — customers forgive a delay, but they rarely forgive being cheated. Looking after your staff matters just as much, because the way a company treats its own people is exactly how it will eventually treat its customers.

4) Does money equal success?

Not in my book, though it is a decent scoreboard for some kinds of success. Money tells you that you solved a problem people were willing to pay for, which is real. But a founder who burnt out his team to get there has bought himself a very expensive kind of failure. I would rather run a smaller company that people are proud to work for.

5) How can companies help protect the environment?

By starting with the boring things: packaging, logistics and energy bills. Cutting waste in packaging is the quickest win for most firms, and rerouting deliveries saves fuel and money at the same time. The clever part is that the green option is often the cheaper option, so it survives even when nobody is watching. Big pledges are nice; a smaller van fleet is better.

6) Is it difficult to do business in today's world?

Yes, but not for the reason people expect. Small businesses have more competition but also cheaper access to customers, so the tools have never been better. The hard part is standing out when everyone can reach the same audience and copy you within a month. Attention, rather than capital, is the scarce thing now.

title: Describe a happy person you know
questions: 【Part 2】
Describe a happy person you know

【Part 3】

5. What would make a student happy at school?
6. Do you think doing a job that you like is more important than other things?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 2 示范答案】
The person I want to talk about is a colleague of mine - a woman in her forties who works in our finance team.

On paper, her life doesn't exactly sound glamorous. She's got an hour's commute each way, and two teenagers waiting for her at home. And yet she's easily the happiest person I know.

What really strikes me about her is her temperament. She's never in a rush, she's almost impossible to ruffle, and she's got this knack for seeing the funny side of things everybody else finds annoying - even a system crash ten minutes before a deadline. And she doesn't show her happiness in big dramatic ways. It's all small stuff: she brings in fruit for the whole office, she remembers everyone's birthday, and honestly, she just hums while she works.

I think the reason she's so happy is that she's stopped comparing herself to other people. She told me once that she spent her whole thirties chasing a promotion, and when she didn't get it, it turned out to be a blessing in disguise - because it freed her up to actually enjoy the job she already had.

That really stuck with me. So I'd say her happiness isn't luck. It's a set of choices.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 人什么时候最快乐：被需要、有盼头的时候。People tend to be happiest when they are working towards something with other people.
2) 艺术如何传播积极情绪：音乐和戏剧能共情，让人不孤单。Music and theatre let people feel understood without having to explain themselves.
3) 老师能看出不开心的孩子吗：通常能，但需要时间和信任。
4) 老师该时刻掌握孩子在做什么吗：不该，过度监控反而让孩子隐瞒。Constant supervision teaches children to hide things rather than share them.
5) 什么让学生在学校开心：被公平对待、有朋友、有成就感。
6) 喜欢的工作比其他更重要吗：很大程度是，因为工作占据了一天中最好的时间。Since work fills the best hours of the day, enjoying it matters more than the salary on its own.

【Part 3 全文】
1) When do you think people are happiest?

People tend to be happiest when they are working towards something with other people. It sounds a bit worthy, but you can see it in everyday life — a team finishing a project, a family cooking together, a running club on a Sunday morning. Pure relaxation is lovely for a weekend and slightly depressing by the third day. I think we need a bit of momentum to feel good about ourselves.

2) How can the arts spread positive emotions in society?

Music and theatre let people feel understood without having to explain themselves, and that is surprisingly powerful. A song about homesickness tells thousands of strangers that they are not the only ones feeling it. Public art does something similar for a whole city: a mural or a festival gives people something to share that is not a problem. That shared feeling is where the positivity comes from.

3) Do you think teachers are able to spot the unhappy children?

Usually, yes — but it takes time and trust rather than a special skill. A teacher who sees the same thirty faces every day notices when somebody goes quiet, stops answering, or stops eating lunch with friends. That said, the quiet child is easy to miss, because quiet children do not cause trouble. So the teacher has to be looking for it, which is a lot to ask on top of everything else.

4) Should teachers know what children are doing all the time?

No, I think that crosses a line. Constant supervision teaches children to hide things rather than share them, and it kills the small mistakes they need to make in order to grow. Teachers should know how a child is doing, not what they are doing every minute. There is a difference between being watchful and being a camera.

5) What would make a student happy at school?

Being treated fairly, having a friend or two, and the feeling that they are getting better at something. You can see it in a classroom: the same lesson feels completely different to a child who has just been praised for trying. Schools cannot hand out happiness, but they can make sure nobody is invisible, and that does most of the work.

6) Do you think doing a job that you like is more important than other things?

To a large extent, yes. Since work fills the best hours of the day, enjoying it matters more than the salary on its own. If you dread Monday, no weekend is long enough to fix it. Obviously pay and security count — I am not suggesting everyone should quit for a passion project — but a job you actively like is worth a lot more than a slightly bigger number.

So, the interview I want to talk about is one I watched last year with Eileen Gu, the freestyle skier. It was recorded in a studio in front of a small live audience.

I came across it on a video platform late one night, and I ended up watching the whole thing without touching my phone once - which, for me, says a lot.

What made it memorable was how unguarded she was. She talked about the pressure of competing for China while growing up in America, she talked about how she handles the hate she gets online, and she explained why she chose to go to Stanford instead of turning professional straight away.

And the interviewer was good too - short, sharp questions, and then he just stayed quiet, which is rare. Gu's answers felt rehearsed but still honest. She's clearly been media-trained, but she didn't hide behind talking points.

Afterwards I felt this strange mixture of admiration and unease. Admiration, because she's achieved more at twenty than most people do in a lifetime. Unease, because she's had to grow up in public and defend her identity to strangers. And hearing someone that young talk about burnout so calmly - that's sobering.

I actually went to bed thinking about how I handle pressure, rather than about her medals.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 面试该穿什么：看行业，干净整洁比昂贵重要。Smart and clean beats expensive in almost every sector.
2) 为什么需要面试：简历看不到沟通和临场反应。A CV shows what you have done; an interview shows how you think on your feet.
3) 面试怎么准备：研究公司、准备三个具体例子。Rehearsing three concrete stories is worth more than memorising answers.
4) 为什么有人觉得面试浪费时间：一小时判断一个人确实粗糙。An hour is a crude way to judge a person, and everyone knows it.
5) 为什么有人不喜欢被面试：被审视的感觉让人紧张。Being evaluated makes even confident people self-conscious.
6) 谁常被采访：名人、专家和经历特殊的人。People with something rare to say or a name that draws an audience.

【Part 3 全文】
1) What should people wear to a job interview?

It depends on the sector, but the safe rule is that smart and clean beats expensive in almost every industry. A well-fitted shirt and polished shoes will take you further than a designer suit that does not sit right. The aim is to look like you made an effort without looking like you are trying too hard. When in doubt, I would check what people at that company wear on a normal day and go one notch smarter.

2) Why do we need to attend interviews when applying for jobs?

Because a CV only shows what you have done — it cannot show how you think on your feet, how you handle pressure, or whether you would be good to work with. An interview gives the employer a sense of your personality and your communication skills, which matter just as much as qualifications. In a way it is a two-way test: you are also finding out whether you would actually want to work there.

3) What should people do to prepare for a job interview?

Research the company properly, then prepare three concrete stories rather than memorising answers. Rehearsing three examples — a problem you solved, a mistake you fixed, a time you worked in a team — is worth more than fifty rehearsed phrases, because you can bend them to almost any question. I would also prepare two questions of my own, since asking nothing looks like you do not care.

4) Why do some people think interviews are a waste of time?

Mainly because an hour is a crude way to judge a person, and everyone knows it. Somebody charming can talk their way past a weak CV, and somebody brilliant can freeze up in a strange room. Companies also repeat the same questions, so candidates simply rehearse. I would not scrap interviews, but I would treat them as one signal rather than the whole verdict.

5) Why do some people dislike being interviewed?

Because being evaluated makes even confident people self-conscious. You are sitting in an unfamiliar room, being judged on a few minutes of speech, and every pause feels enormous. Introverts find it especially draining, since the format rewards people who can perform rather than people who can think. That is why I think a trial task tells you more than an interview sometimes.

6) What kinds of people are usually interviewed?

People with something rare to say or a name that draws an audience — actors, athletes, politicians, and increasingly ordinary people who went through something unusual. Journalists love anyone with a story attached to a big event. The odd thing is that the people who get interviewed most are usually the ones who are most used to it, which is exactly why the answers start to sound the same.

【Part 2 示范答案】
The most organized person I know is my flatmate. He's a project manager, which probably explains a lot, but his habits go well beyond work - he plans his weekends as carefully as his meetings.

His routine is almost comically systematic. Everything he owns has a place. He keeps a shared calendar for the flat, with the cleaning schedule on it, and he does a short review every Sunday evening to plan the week ahead. And he writes things down immediately instead of trusting his memory - which, I think, is the real secret.

I first noticed it when we moved in together. He produced a spreadsheet of bills before I'd even unpacked a box. And later, when I was ill for a week, he just took over my share of everything without being asked, and he didn't make a fuss about it.

Which, for me, is what being organized is really for. I think it matters to him because his childhood was quite chaotic, so structure gives him a sense of control.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 管理者需要有组织性吗：需要，团队靠他的节奏运行。A disorganised manager transmits anxiety to the whole team.
2) 父母该教孩子整理吗：该，从小处开始。Children learn tidiness from routines rather than reminders.
3) 怎么变得更自律：列清单、固定位置、每周复盘。
4) 有条理的人更容易成功吗：效率上占优势，但创意有时来自混乱。Organised people get more done, though some creative work thrives on mess.
5) 孩子该从小学习条理吗：越早越自然，习惯比意志力可靠。Habits outlast willpower.
6) 为什么有条理重要：省时间、少焦虑、别人更信任你。Being reliable is what makes people trust you with bigger things.

三、Part 3 全文
1) Do managers need to be organized?
Yes, absolutely. A disorganised manager transmits anxiety to the whole team — people never know what's expected of them or when things are due. A good manager doesn't have to be the most organised person in the room, but they do need to set a clear rhythm that everyone else can follow.

2) Should parents teach children to be tidy?
Yes, and it's best to start small. Children learn tidiness from routines rather than reminders — if there's a place for everything and a fixed time to tidy up, it becomes second nature. Nagging, on the other hand, usually just creates resistance.

3) How can people become more self-disciplined?
A few things help. Making lists, giving everything a fixed home, and doing a short weekly review are all simple but effective. It also helps to start ridiculously small — one habit at a time — because trying to overhaul your entire life overnight almost never works.

4) Are organized people more likely to succeed?
They do have an edge when it comes to efficiency — organised people get more done, and they're less likely to drop the ball. That said, some creative work actually thrives on mess, so I wouldn't say organisation is the only path to success. It's more of a foundation than a guarantee.

5) Should children learn to be organized from an early age?
Yes, the earlier the better, because it feels natural rather than forced. Habits outlast willpower — a child who grows up putting things away without thinking about it will carry that into adulthood. Waiting until they're teenagers usually means a lot more friction.

6) Why is being organized important?
It saves time, reduces anxiety, and makes other people trust you. Being reliable is what makes people trust you with bigger things — whether that's a project at work or a responsibility at home. In a way, being organised is a form of respect for other people's time as well as your own.

ninePointAnswer:
【Part 2 示范答案】
The noisiest place I've ever been to is a wholesale electronics market in my city - a six-storey building packed with hundreds of tiny stalls.

I went there last summer to buy a replacement laptop charger, which tells you how badly I'd underestimated the place. From the moment I stepped inside, it was just overwhelming. Every stall owner was competing to be heard, people were testing speakers at full volume, and somewhere on the ground floor a man was shouting prices into a microphone. And then there was the noise of the building itself: escalators, shutters, fans, and this permanent hum you could actually feel in your teeth.

But here's what I remember most clearly - how quickly I adjusted. After about twenty minutes I stopped noticing the din, and I found myself haggling back without raising my voice at all, because in there the quietest person tends to be taken seriously.

I left with my charger and a headache, and, honestly, a new respect for people like my uncle who spent years working in that market.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 公共场合聊天如何顾及他人：降低音量、缩短时间。Keeping your voice low in a shared space is basic manners, not weakness.
2) 我们国家的人通常如何回应噪音：多数人忍，少数人直接说。
3) 城市还是乡村噪音更大：城市更严重，夜里尤其。Cities never fully quieten down, especially near main roads.
4) 生活中有哪些噪音：交通、施工、邻居装修、手机提示音。Most of it comes from machines we chose to buy.
5) 孩子该完全不许出声吗：不该，但要有场合概念。Children should learn when noise is acceptable, not be silenced altogether.
6) 孩子吵闹有好处吗：有，是表达和玩耍的一部分。Noise is often how young children explore the world.
【Part 3 全文】
1) How should people be considerate of others when chatting in public?

Mainly by keeping their volume down and keeping it short. Keeping your voice low in a shared space is basic manners, not weakness — it shows you're aware that other people are there too. If it's a really important conversation, stepping outside or finding a quieter corner is the considerate thing to do.

2) How do people in your country usually respond to noise?

It depends on the person. Most people just put up with it — they'll sigh, maybe give a dirty look, but they won't say anything. A minority are more direct and will politely ask the person to turn it down. On the whole, I'd say we're fairly tolerant, sometimes to a fault.

3) Is there more noise in the city or the countryside?

The city, without a doubt. Cities never fully quieten down, especially near main roads — there's always traffic, construction, or somebody's air conditioning unit. The countryside has its own sounds, like birds and insects, but they're natural and far less intrusive. The main difference is that city noise never really stops, even at night.

4) What kinds of noise are there in daily life?

Traffic, construction, neighbours doing renovations, phone notifications, and household appliances. Interestingly, most of it comes from machines we chose to buy — so in a way, we've engineered a lot of the noise ourselves. The rest is just the price of living in a busy city.

5) Should children be forbidden from making any noise at all?

No, that would be unrealistic and probably unhealthy. Children should learn when noise is acceptable, not be silenced altogether — there's a big difference between running around in a park and screaming in a restaurant. The goal is to teach context, not to suppress them.

6) Is there anything good about children being noisy?
Yes, definitely. Noise is often how young children explore the world — they shout, sing, and make silly sounds as a way of testing boundaries and expressing themselves. It can be annoying, but it's also a sign of healthy development. A completely silent child would actually be more worrying.

title: Describe a natural place in your city that you enjoy visiting

Describe a natural place in your city that you enjoy visiting

5. Do you think people should spend more time in nature?

ninePointAnswer:
【Part 2 示范答案】
The place I'd like to talk about is a wetland park by the river, on the eastern edge of my city - about forty minutes from where I live.

It's basically a strip of land behind a water treatment plant that used to be wasteland, and about five years ago the city turned it into a proper park with wooden walkways and reed beds. No rides, no loudspeakers, just boardwalks, a couple of bird hides and some benches facing the water. In autumn the reeds go golden and you can hear fish jumping, which feels bizarre in a city of eight million people.

I probably go once a month, usually with a friend of mine who's obsessed with photography, or on my own when I need to think something through.

And the reason I like it so much is the contrast. Twenty minutes earlier I was sitting in traffic, and then suddenly the loudest thing around me is wind in the reeds. I always come home feeling like I've slept better than I actually have.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 环保 vs 经济发展：短期冲突，长期是一回事。You cannot grow an economy on a poisoned river.
2) 自然环境能改变心情吗：能，而且效果很快。Even twenty minutes among trees lowers the volume in your head.
3) 城市里该有很多自然空间吗：该，是城市的基础设施。Green space is infrastructure, not decoration.
4) 政府如何鼓励人们亲近自然：步道、免费公园、公共交通。Free access and safe paths get people out more than campaigns do.
5) 人们该多花时间在自然里吗：应该，尤其常看屏幕的人。
6) 什么样的人喜欢自然：压力大的人、老人、有孩子的家庭。Anyone who spends all day under artificial light tends to crave it.

【Part 3 全文】
1) Which is more important, protecting the environment or developing the economy?

In the short term they can clash, but over the long run they are the same project. You cannot grow an economy on a poisoned river, and cleaning up afterwards always costs more than protecting it in the first place. The interesting part is that green industries now create real jobs — solar, batteries, public transport. So I would stop treating it as a trade-off and start treating pollution as money we have already lost.

2) Do you think staying in a natural place would help change people's mood?

Yes, and the effect is surprisingly fast. Even twenty minutes among trees lowers the volume in your head — your breathing slows down and the endless mental to-do list goes quiet for a while. It is not magic; it is just that nature does not demand anything from you. That is exactly why hospitals put gardens in them and why I would rather walk home through a park than along a main road.

3) Do you think there should be many natural places in cities?

Definitely — green space is infrastructure, not decoration. Trees cool the streets, soil absorbs the rain that would otherwise flood the metro, and people who can walk somewhere green are simply healthier. The cost is tiny compared to what we spend on roads. I would rather have ten small parks scattered around than one showcase park on the edge of town that nobody can reach.

4) What can governments do to encourage people to spend more time in nature?

Make it easy and free: safe walking paths, clean toilets, shade, and a bus route that actually gets you there. Free access and safe paths get people out more than campaigns do. I would also stop selling off small patches of green space for car parks, because that quietly removes the park that a family could actually walk to on a Sunday.

5) Do you think people should spend more time in nature?

Yes, especially people whose whole day happens under artificial light — office workers, students, anyone glued to a screen. That said, I am wary of turning it into another thing to feel guilty about, since not everyone has a car or spare hours. The realistic advice is small and regular: a walk at lunchtime, a park on the way home, a weekend outdoors when you can.

6) What kind of people do you think enjoy being in nature?

Anyone who spends all day under artificial light tends to crave it, so a lot of city office workers are secretly the keenest. Older people often value it because they grew up closer to it, and families with small children use parks as a free playground. Then there are the serious ones — hikers and birdwatchers — who plan whole weekends around it.

title: Describe a time when you saved money to buy something special

5. Should parents teach their children to spend money freely or to save money?
6. Should schools teach children how to manage money from a young age?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 2 示范答案】
The thing I saved up for was a second-hand camera, when I was about nineteen. It doesn't sound like much now, but for a student on a small allowance it took me the best part of a year.

I wanted it for two reasons: I'd joined the photography club at university, and borrowing the club camera every single week had started to feel embarrassing. So I worked out I needed about four thousand yuan, and I gave myself one simple rule - a quarter of my monthly allowance went into a box the day it arrived, and no more coffee on campus.

The real sacrifice was food. I ate in the canteen instead of the little places across the road, and I said no to a couple of trips with friends, which felt like a big deal at the time.

And when I finally bought it? I was almost scared to use it, and my first photos were honestly terrible. But the thing I actually took away from it wasn't the camera - it was the saving habit. That stayed with me long after I sold the camera.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 慈善该花时间还是钱：都行，时间往往更稀缺。Money is easier to give, but time is what people remember.
2) 人们一般为什么存钱：房子、婚礼、应急。Most savings are for things you cannot postpone for ever.
3) 花钱容易还是存钱容易：花钱容易得多。Spending is frictionless; saving requires a decision every single day.
4) 教 16-17 岁孩子理财容易吗：相对容易，他们有真实需求。Teenagers learn money quickly once it is their own money.
5) 父母该教花还是存：先存后花，比例固定。Teach the habit of putting something aside before you spend the rest.
6) 学校该教理财吗：该，很多成年人都在为这件事头疼。Most adults learn personal finance the hard and expensive way.

【Part 3 全文】
1) Should people spend time on charity, or just money?

Both are useful, but they are not interchangeable. Money is easier to give, but time is what people remember, and it is also scarcer for most of us. I would say the best version combines them: give cash to organisations that know what to do with it, and give your own hours to something you can actually do well, like teaching or translating. What does not help is giving either one purely for the photo.

2) What kind of things do people usually save money for?

Most savings are for things you cannot postpone for ever: a house deposit, a wedding, a car, education, and an emergency fund. I would put emergencies at the top, because that is the money that stops a bad month from turning into a disaster. Saving for something enjoyable is fine too — I just think you should be clear about which of the two you are doing, or you spend the emergency money on a holiday.

3) Is it easier to spend money or save money?

Spending is frictionless and saving requires a decision every single day, so spending wins by default. That is why the trick is to make saving automatic: move a fixed amount the moment your salary lands, so the money you see is the money you are allowed to spend. Basically, decide once instead of arguing with yourself twenty times a month. Willpower is a terrible long-term strategy.

4) Do you think it is easier to teach teenagers how to manage money when they are around 16 or 17 years old?

Yes, I think that is close to the ideal age, because teenagers learn money quickly once it is their own money. At that age they have real costs — clothes, going out, a phone plan — and they care about being independent. A part-time job teaches budgeting faster than any lecture. The remaining risk is impulse buying, so I would still keep an eye on the big purchases.

5) Should parents teach their children to spend money freely or to save money?

I would teach the habit of putting something aside before you spend the rest, with a fixed proportion like a third. But I would not make saving feel like punishment — children who are never allowed to spend develop a strange relationship with money and end up splurging the moment they get the chance. Modelling matters most: children copy what their parents do with a card, not what they say about it.

6) Should schools teach children how to manage money from a young age?

Yes, because most adults learn personal finance the hard and expensive way, and a lot of that pain is avoidable. Basic things would already help: how interest works, what a budget is, how buy-now-pay-later traps and scams are worded. I would keep it practical rather than mathematical. Honestly, I learned more from one failed online purchase in my twenties than from any lesson.

1) Is it important for everyone to have a specialized skill?

2) Can a child learn skills from another child?

Absolutely, and often faster than from an adult, because children copy other children far more readily than they copy adults. It is less intimidating to watch someone your own size get it wrong and then get it right. That is why siblings and older cousins are so influential. Adults can explain the theory, but a slightly older child shows you that it is actually possible.

3) Do you think it is easier for children to learn new skills than for adults?

For physical things, yes — pronunciation, swimming, handwriting, anything involving muscle memory. Young brains absorb faster and children are much less embarrassed about being bad at something. But adults decide better what is worth learning, and they are better at grinding through boredom. So children win the first month and adults often win the first year.

4) What are the differences between the way adults learn and the way children learn?

Children learn by imitation and play: they copy, repeat and are not really aware that they are learning. Adults want an explanation, a goal and a reason why this matters, and they tend to be held back by the fear of looking silly. Children need to be shown, adults need to be convinced. The good news is that adults can borrow the child's method — just copy first and worry about the theory later.

5) What are the differences between learning in a group and learning by yourself?

In a group you get feedback, and a bit of social pressure that makes you show up, which is exactly what most self-learners lack. On your own you get to set the pace and skip the parts you already know. For me the ideal is a mix: a group for structure and correction, and solo practice for the boring repetitions. Nobody improves much from watching a class.

6) What skills should children learn before they go to school?

Mostly social and practical things: how to ask for help, how to share, how to wait their turn, how to put on their own coat and use a toilet without drama. Learning to ask for help is worth more than early reading, in my opinion, because it protects them on the days when things go wrong. The alphabet can wait a year; confidence cannot.

【Part 2 示范答案】
The person I want to describe is a friend of mine from university who is genuinely obsessed with photography. We met in the photography club - he turned up with a battered old film camera while the rest of us were using our phones - and he's been dragging me to interesting places ever since.

He takes photos basically everywhere: old alleys, riverside steps, markets at dawn. He's especially good at finding the corners of the city everybody walks past. He gets up at four in the morning for the light, walks twenty kilometres on a Sunday, and develops black-and-white film in his bathroom, which I find both impressive and slightly mad.

How do I feel about him? A mixture, honestly - admiration and amusement. Admiration, because photography has given him a way of actually noticing things, and amusement, because dinner with him always involves waiting while he photographs the food from three different angles.

Still, it's rubbed off on me. I carry a camera far more often than I used to.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 有人不介意别人入镜：人多的地方很难避免，宽容一点。In a crowded square you either accept strangers in the frame or give up.
2) 游客为什么爱拍照：记录证据和情绪。Photos are partly proof that you were really there.
3) 什么地方都适合拍照吗：涉及隐私和宗教场所要谨慎。Some places deserve consent rather than a lens.
4) 人们常拍什么：食物、风景、家人和朋友。Food and family make up most of the photos on any phone.
5) 为什么有人热衷摄影：留住瞬间、表达自己。It gives people a reason to look more carefully at ordinary things.
6) 人们什么时候爱拍照：旅行、节日、聚会。Anything that breaks the routine invites a camera.

【Part 3 全文】
1) Some people don't mind others walking into their shot when they're taking photos.

In a crowded square you either accept strangers in the frame or give up on the photo entirely, so I would say being relaxed about it is the practical choice. I know a lot of people who deliberately wait for the crowd to thin out instead, but that can take twenty minutes and everyone else is waiting for you. Where I would not accept it is in quiet or formal places — there, the polite thing is to reshoot rather than push someone out of the way.

2) Why do tourists like taking photos while they are travelling?

Partly as proof that you were really there, and partly to capture the feeling while it is still fresh, because memory is far less reliable than we like to think. Photos also give you something to share when you get home, which is when the trip actually becomes a story. I would add a third reason: looking for the shot changes how you notice a place, so taking pictures is a way of paying attention.

3) Do you think it's ok to take photos everywhere?

No, and the exceptions matter more than the rule: places of worship, somebody's home, hospitals, and anywhere children are the subject. Some places deserve consent rather than a lens. Even in public, if it is clearly a personal moment — somebody crying, an argument, a funeral — I would not photograph it, or at least not post it. The existence of a camera in my pocket should not change what is decent.

4) What kind of photos do people often take?

Food and family make up most of the photos on any phone, along with scenery and friends, and increasingly themselves. Phones have made everything worth documenting, which is charming and slightly exhausting at the same time. I notice people take far more pictures of a view than of the people they are looking at it with, which always strikes me as the wrong way round.

5) Why are some people keen on taking photos?

It gives people a reason to look more carefully at ordinary things, which is quietly satisfying. There is also the creative outlet of it, and the fact that it has a visible result — unlike a lot of hobbies, you can see the progress on a screen. And the social side matters: photos are how people tell their friends what their life looks like.
【Part 3 全文】
6) When do people like taking photos?

Mainly when something breaks the routine: travel, festivals, birthdays, graduation, meeting up with friends you rarely see. Ordinary Tuesdays almost never get photographed, which is why photo albums are misleading — they make life look like a series of events. I would say the recent habit of photographing everyday things, like a nice breakfast, is actually an attempt to make the ordinary count too.

ninePointAnswer:
【Part 2 示范答案】
The person I want to describe is my grandfather. He's eighty-four, and he's still the most curious man I know.

He was a primary-school teacher for nearly forty years, so I've known him all my life - though I've only really appreciated him since I got old enough to ask him proper questions.

These days we do simple things together. We walk along the river near his house, we play Chinese chess, and he gets me to help him with his phone, which is a running joke between us. He also tells me stories about the town in the sixties, and about how he met my grandmother at a bus stop in the rain - which he tells slightly differently every time, I should say.

And the reason I admire him is that he's kept his interest in the world without becoming cynical. He learned to use a tablet at seventy-nine just so he could follow a documentary series, and last year he started growing orchids.

So whenever I catch myself saying I'm too old to learn something, I think of him. He's living proof that curiosity is a choice, not an age.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 老人长期记得什么：童年的气味、艰难的日子。People keep the hard years and the songs, not the paperwork.
2) 老年人流行什么运动：太极、广场舞、快走。Tai chi and walking groups are the backbone of it.
3) 老人日常做什么：买菜、带孙辈、下棋、锻炼。Their days are routine but rarely empty.
4) 为什么有代沟：经历不同、技术不同、表达感情的方式不同。Different technologies create different habits of talking.
5) 老年人生活质量提高了吗：医疗和养老金改善了，孤独是新的问题。Better healthcare has not solved loneliness.
6) 彼此能学到什么：年轻人学从容和经验，老人学新工具和开放。Older people teach patience; younger ones teach curiosity about change.

【Part 3 全文】
1) What kinds of things do the elderly remember for a long time?

Mostly the emotional things: songs, the smell of a childhood kitchen, and the genuinely hard years. People keep the hard years and the songs, not the paperwork. My grandmother can sing a tune from 1965 word for word but cannot remember what she ate yesterday, which tells you how memory actually works. I take that as a hint to make more of the days worth keeping.

2) What sports are popular among older people?

Tai chi and walking groups are the backbone of it, along with square dancing in the evenings and swimming if there is a pool nearby. The common thread is that they are low-impact, cheap and social, so you can chat while doing them. Badminton is also popular in parks, played at a pace that would surprise you. Nobody there is training for a medal.

3) What do old people usually do in their daily life?

In my city they shop for food in the morning, look after grandchildren in the afternoon, and then meet friends to play cards or walk. Their days are routine but rarely empty, which is something I envy a bit from my chaotic week. The happiest ones I know have at least one fixed appointment with other people every single day; that seems to be the key.

4) Why is there a generation gap between the young and the old?

Different technologies create different habits of talking, and that shows up as a gap. My grandfather considers a phone call the polite way to reach somebody; I consider it almost confrontational. Add different childhoods, different prices, different ideas about saving, and small differences look enormous. It is less about values being opposed and more about the tools being different.

5) Has old people's life quality improved compared to the past?

In material terms, enormously: pensions, heating, better food and far better medicine. But better healthcare has not solved loneliness, and that is now the biggest problem for a lot of people who live alone. So I would say the body has been taken care of and the social side has been left behind. The next improvement will not be medical.

6) What can young and old people learn from each other?

Older people teach patience and perspective, mainly by proving that disasters pass. Younger ones teach curiosity about change, which is a real skill when the world keeps updating. The trick is that neither side can lecture the other into it; it only works through actually spending time together. I learned more from my uncle over cooking than from any book on patience.

ninePointAnswer:
【Part 2 示范答案】
So, the shop I want to talk about is a tiny shoe repair place near my old flat. I went there last spring with a pair of boots I was basically ready to throw away.

It's the kind of place you walk past for years without noticing: one room, a wall of tools, and an old man who's clearly been doing this for decades.

What struck me was how seriously he took a job that was worth almost nothing. He examined the soles, told me honestly that the boots would last another winter at most - and then repaired them anyway. And when I came back the next morning, he'd cleaned the leather and replaced a broken eyelet, and he didn't charge me for the eyelet. He said he'd had the part lying in a drawer for years.

I left feeling oddly cheerful, because it's rare to be treated as a person rather than a transaction. I've taken two more pairs to him since, and I recommend him to everyone.

That's why I think good service isn't about being polite. It's about caring when there's nothing in it for you.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 消费能拉动经济吗：能，但靠消费撑起来的经济很脆弱。Spending drives growth until the debt behind it catches up.
2) 网购的优缺点：方便便宜，但退换和冲动购物是代价。
3) 网购 vs 实体店：网购比价方便，实体店能试能感受。
4) 为什么有人不喜欢小店：选择少、担心售后。Small shops live and die by trust, and not everyone trusts them yet.
5) 在小店购物的优缺点：有人情味和议价空间，但价格不透明。
6) 为什么商场在中国流行：一站式、有空调、适合家庭出行。Malls are popular because they are comfortable places to spend an afternoon, not just to buy things.

【Part 3 全文】
1) Can consumption drive economic growth?

Yes, up to a point, but a growth model built on it is fragile. Spending drives growth until the debt behind it catches up, and you can see that in economies where household debt is now bigger than the whole output. What I would rather see is spending backed by real wages and by people buying things that last. Consumption is an effect of prosperity as much as a cause of it.

2) What are the advantages and disadvantages of shopping online?

The advantages are obvious: cheaper prices, endless choice, no queues, and it arrives at your door. The price is that you cannot touch the thing before buying it, returns can be a headache, and the 'buy now' button is far too easy to press at eleven at night. I would say I save money on prices and then lose it again on impulse purchases.

3) What are the differences between online shopping and in-store shopping?

Online wins on comparing prices, on choice and on time; in-store wins on actually seeing, trying and feeling the product. For clothes and shoes I still prefer a real shop, because sizing online is a lottery, whereas for books and electronics the website is simply better. In-store also has the advantage that you can ask a human a question — which is what good service is built on.

4) Why do some people not like shopping in small shops?

Mainly the fear that there is no real after-sales protection, plus a suspicion that the prices are made up on the spot. Small shops live and die by trust, and not everyone trusts them yet. Add limited choice and a feeling of being watched while you browse, and I understand why some people just go to a chain store instead — even when the small shop is nicer.

5) What are the advantages and disadvantages of shopping in small shops?

You get real people, advice, and often a bit of room to negotiate, which is genuinely pleasant. The disadvantages are narrower choice, less certainty about returns, and prices that are not always displayed. With food, fruit and vegetables, the small shop wins easily on freshness. I would say the trade-off is personality against predictability, and it depends what you are buying that day.

6) Why are shopping malls so popular in China?

Malls are popular because they are comfortable places to spend an afternoon, not just to buy things — air conditioning, a food court, a cinema, a children's play area. They also suit families, since grandparents, parents and children can each do their own thing and meet for dinner afterwards. In a hot or a very cold city, that is genuinely useful. So partly shopping, partly a public living room.

ninePointAnswer:
【Part 2 示范答案】
The person I want to describe is a neighbour of my parents - a retired carpenter in his sixties who everyone in the building just calls Uncle Zhou. I've known him since I was a child, and he's made half the furniture in his own flat.

He works mostly with wood, walnut and elm, using hand planes, chisels and sandpaper instead of power tools, because he says machines take the character out of a piece. Over the years he's made stools, a shoe rack, picture frames, and for my parents a small bookcase that's survived two moves. And he repairs things for free - a wobbly chair or a broken drawer is never a problem in our building.

I think he's so good at it because he's patient in a way my generation finds hard to imagine. He'll spend an entire evening shaping one joint, and he keeps a notebook of his mistakes, which he shows people proudly.

Watching him work makes me realise that craftsmanship is less about talent than about refusing to rush.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 艺术对社会有影响吗：有，音乐和戏剧能把陌生人聚在一起。Art gives a community shared memories.
2) 团队里有创意的人好吗：好，但要有人负责落地。Creativity needs someone to turn ideas into schedules.
3) 有艺术感的建筑对社会的影响：让人愿意停留和拍照，成为城市名片。
4) 现在孩子还喜欢做手工吗：喜欢，只是材料变了，从黏土到模型套件。
5) 为什么孩子爱手工：能亲手做出东西并获得成就感。Making something with your own hands is proof that you can.
6) 美术课对孩子重要吗：重要，锻炼耐心和空间感。Art classes teach patience as much as technique.

【Part 3 全文】
1) Does art, like music or theatre, have an impact on society?

Yes, and a bigger one than it usually gets credit for: art gives a community shared memories. When a song or a play belongs to a place, strangers have something in common to talk about and to be proud of. It also gives people a way to process things that are hard to discuss directly. A city with a theatre scene feels different to live in, even for people who never go.

2) Is it good to have creative people in a team?

Definitely, as long as somebody is there to make it happen. Creativity needs someone to turn ideas into schedules, otherwise you get an inspiring meeting and nothing else. The best teams I have seen pair a person who asks 'what if' with a person who asks 'by when'. Where it goes wrong is when the creative person is expected to also be the organiser.

3) What impact can artistic buildings have on society?

They become a landmark and a meeting point, and they quietly raise the standard people expect from new buildings. A striking library or museum gets photographed, which brings visitors and money, so cities copy the effect. The risk is that governments chase the look and forget the function — a beautiful building nobody can actually use is just a sculpture. The test is whether locals use it on a normal Tuesday.

4) Do children these days still like doing arts and crafts?

Yes, they seem to enjoy it just as much, only the materials have changed: less clay, more model kits, resin charms, and video tutorials. Screens have actually made it easier, because a child can copy a technique step by step from a video. What has not changed is the pride on their face when they finish something. My cousin's bedroom is basically a small workshop now.

5) Why do some children enjoy making things by hand?

Because making something with your own hands is proof that you can do things, and that confidence is worth a lot to a child. There is also an obvious reward: the thing exists at the end, unlike a bad mark at school. And it is usually quiet and absorbing, which some children badly need. I would say the messy children are the keenest ones.

6) Do you think art classes are important for children?

Yes, and not mainly for artistic reasons: art classes teach patience as much as technique. You have to sit with something unfinished, try again when it looks wrong, and accept that the result depends on how much effort you put in. Those are life skills that show up later in maths homework. Cutting the art budget is a false economy, in my opinion.

4. What are the differences between young people’s leisure time activities and those of old people?

ninePointAnswer:
【Part 2 示范答案】
The evening I want to talk about was last October, and it turned out far better than anyone expected. It started as a birthday dinner for a friend at a tiny Sichuan restaurant near the river, and it ended at two in the morning on a bench looking at the water.

There were six of us, all from university, and we hadn't been together for over a year because two of them had moved to other cities. We did the usual things - ordered far too much food, argued about who should pay, told the same stories we always tell. But what made it special was that nobody was in a hurry. Nobody was checking their phone, and nobody had to leave early for a train.

And what I remember most is the walk afterwards. It was cold, so we bought hot drinks and walked along the river while one friend tried to teach us a card trick.

It was enjoyable because it felt effortless - no planning, no performance, just people who know each other well enough to be boring together. Which I've come to think is the highest form of friendship.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 人为什么需要朋友：分担情绪、提供反馈、抵消孤独。
2) 老人更愿意陪家人还是朋友：多数偏家人，朋友在减少。Old friends shrink in number but matter more.
3) 年轻人更愿意陪家人还是朋友：平时偏朋友，节日偏家人。
4) 年轻人与老人休闲方式的差别：年轻人爱外出和刺激，老人爱固定和熟悉。Young people seek novelty; older people seek comfort.
5) 怎么让家人更亲近：一起吃饭、一起做点事，而不是只靠问候。
6) 大家庭怎么相处：靠明确的边界和有人情味的妥协。Big families work when someone is willing to compromise and everyone keeps boundaries.

【Part 3 全文】
1) Why do people need friends?

Because friends do three things that family cannot always do: they share the load, they tell you the truth, and they make the week less lonely. A friend can say 'that plan is a bad idea' without it turning into an argument about your whole life. I also think friends keep you interesting, since you hear about lives that are nothing like your own. Loneliness is dangerous in a very practical way.

2) Do older people prefer spending time with family or with friends?

Mostly family, and the number of friends tends to shrink with age — though the ones that remain matter more. Old friends shrink in number but matter more. A lot of that is practical: retirement moves you closer to grandchildren and further from the people you used to work with. I have noticed my parents' social life is now mostly family plus two or three people they have known since school.

3) Do young people prefer spending time with family or friends?

On an ordinary weekend, friends — you are building your own identity and your friends are the ones doing the same thing at the same time. But on festivals and holidays, family takes over almost completely, because those days are defined by it. So I would say young people do not choose between them; they just split the calendar differently. The drift back towards family happens much later than people expect.

4) What are the differences between young people's leisure activities and those of old people?

Young people seek novelty: new bars, new cities, loud music, staying out late. Older people seek comfort and familiarity, so the same park, the same group, the same restaurant for twenty years. Young people seek novelty; older people seek comfort. Neither is better, and the interesting thing is that most people slowly slide from one to the other without noticing when it happened.

5) What can we do to bring family members closer together?

Eat together regularly and do something side by side, rather than only exchanging greetings. Cooking a meal as a group works much better than a formal dinner where everyone behaves politely. Shared tasks are how people actually talk. I would also say stop waiting for the perfect holiday: a Tuesday evening supper is worth more than a big trip that happens once a year.

6) How do people get along in a big family?

It works when boundaries are clear and somebody is willing to compromise — usually one patient person holding the whole thing together. Big families work when someone is willing to compromise and everyone keeps boundaries. Without both, the same argument reappears at every single meal. In my experience the families that look peaceful have simply agreed not to discuss certain topics, and that agreement is a form of respect.

So why do I keep doing it? Because the alternative is lying in the dark with my own thoughts, and when I'm exhausted that feels harder. Which, I suppose, is exactly how the app hooks people like me.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 为什么有人不守规矩：觉得不公平、图方便、或者根本没被解释过。Most rule-breaking starts with the belief that the rules are unfair.
2) 什么让人有压力：比较、期限、以及无法掌控的局面。Comparison is the quietest source of pressure.
3) 明知浪费时间你还会继续做吗：会，但要设个界限。
4) 如何平衡生活和工作：把休息写进计划，而不是等崩溃再休息。
5) 有日常作息好吗：好，规律能省下大量决策精力。A routine protects your energy for the things that matter.
6) 压力重要吗：适度有用，长期有害。A little stress sharpens you; chronic stress hollows you out.

【Part 3 全文】
1) Why do some people refuse to abide by rules?

Usually one of three things: they think the rule is unfair, it is inconvenient, or nobody ever explained why it exists. Most rule-breaking starts with the belief that the rules are unfair. Where the penalty is serious the behaviour disappears quickly, which tells you it was a calculation rather than a character flaw. That is why explaining the reason behind a rule works better than adding another one.

2) What kinds of things make people feel pressured?

Comparison, deadlines, and situations where you have no control over the outcome. Comparison is the quietest source of pressure, because nobody announces it — you just notice that a classmate bought a flat. The worst combination is a high-stakes deadline with no authority to change anything. Sleeping badly makes all of it feel about twice as heavy as it really is.

3) Will you continue doing something when you are aware that it's a waste of time?

Sometimes, yes — scrolling at midnight being the obvious example, or watching one more episode of something I do not even like. But I try to set a limit rather than fight it, because telling myself 'never again' lasts about two days. Awareness helps a little; rules help more. I would say the honest answer is that I keep doing it and feel slightly guilty.

4) How do you balance life and work?

By putting rest in the plan instead of waiting until I collapse, and by keeping one fixed appointment with friends each week. The other thing that works is a hard stop at a reasonable hour, because work expands to fill whatever time you give it. My rule is that if a task is genuinely urgent, it is allowed to break the plan; if everything is urgent, then nothing is.

5) Is it good to have a daily routine?

Yes — a routine protects your energy for the things that matter, because it removes dozens of tiny decisions from your day. Once breakfast, exercise and the commute run themselves, you have attention left over for actual work and people. The failure mode is when the routine becomes the point and you get rigid. So: a routine in the boring parts, freedom in the interesting ones.

6) Do you think stress is important in people's lives?

A little stress sharpens you, and the fact that a deadline improves most people's work is proof of it. Long-term stress is a different animal: it hollows you out, damages sleep, and makes good decisions impossible. So I would not say stress is important in itself, but having something that matters enough to worry about is. The problem is never one hard week; it is eleven of them.

title: Describe a crowded place you went to
questions: 【Part 2】
Describe a crowded place you went to
You should say: Where it was / When you went there / Who you went there with / What you did there
【Part 3】
1. Do you think it is a good trend to have more big cities?
2. Do you think there are some people who enjoy crowded places?
3. Why do people go to crowded places?
4. Will people use bikes more or less in cities in the future?
5. Will there be more or less green space in cities in the future?
6. Which cities are overcrowded in your country?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 2 示范答案】
The place I want to talk about is a lantern festival I went to with my cousin on the last day of the spring holiday. It was in a park in the old part of the city, and I'd say the organisers had clearly not expected how many people would turn up.

Getting there was already an experience. The metro station was closed because it was too full, so we ended up walking the last two kilometres in a slow-moving crowd.

And inside? Honestly, shoulder to shoulder. We could only move at walking pace, my cousin lost a glove, and at one point I was basically carried along by the crowd rather than walking. We still managed to see two of the big lantern displays, and we ate skewers standing up against a wall.

What I took away from it was a strange mixture of irritation and enjoyment. I wouldn't go again on the busiest night. But there was something impressive about several thousand people all being cheerful in the same place at the same time - the crush was part of the occasion, in a way that's hard to explain unless you were actually there.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 大城市越来越多是好趋势吗：便利与工作机会多，但通勤和房租成问题。
2) 有人喜欢拥挤的地方吗：有，热闹本身是吸引力。Some people go for the crowd, not for the event.
3) 人们为什么去人多的地方：气氛、免费、和他人同步的仪式感。
4) 未来城市骑车会更多还是更少：电动自行车会更多，政策决定上限。
5) 未来城市绿地会更多还是更少：长期看会更多，短期常被开发挤压。Green space tends to increase once a city is rich enough to afford it.
6) 哪些城市过度拥挤：一线城市和热门旅游城市最明显。Holiday crowds turn tourist towns into obstacle courses.

【Part 3 全文】
1) Do you think it is a good trend to have more big cities?

Partly. Big cities create jobs, better hospitals, and a social life you cannot find in a small town, which is genuinely a good thing for the people who move there. The problems are the side effects: long commutes, unaffordable rent, and a feeling of being anonymous when something goes wrong. I would rather see a few smaller cities strengthened than one capital absorbing everything.

2) Do you think there are some people who enjoy crowded places?

Oh, definitely. Some people go for the crowd itself, not for the event — the noise and the jostling are the point, because it makes the city feel alive. Others like the anonymity: you can be surrounded by thousands of people and nobody is watching you, which is strangely relaxing. I enjoy it for about two hours and then I want a quiet room.

3) Why do people go to crowded places?

For the atmosphere mainly, and often because a crowd is itself the event — a festival, a market, a firework display. Some of it is free entertainment, and some is the ritual of doing the same thing on the same day as everybody else. I also think people like the reassurance of shared enthusiasm. A stadium is not really about the game; it is about forty thousand people agreeing on something.

4) Will people use bikes more or less in cities in the future?

More, I think, and mostly electric ones. E-bikes solve the two objections to cycling — hills and sweat — so they work for commuters who would never consider a normal bike. Whether that happens quickly depends on policy: safe lanes and parking will decide it. Weather still wins on rainy days, but for two-wheeled trips under five kilometres, the e-bike is hard to beat.

5) Will there be more or less green space in cities in the future?

Over the long run, more: green space tends to increase once a city is rich enough to afford it. In the short run it keeps losing to development, which is why the parks appear late and usually on land nobody wanted. I am optimistic though — the floods and the heatwaves have made the argument for trees in a very practical way. Once it becomes cheaper to plant than to air-condition, the politics change.

6) Which cities are overcrowded in your country?

The obvious ones are the biggest: Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou and Shenzhen, where the metro at eight in the morning is a physical experience. Holiday towns are overcrowded in a different, seasonal way — places like Suzhou or the old towns of Lijiang, where the streets become an obstacle course in early October. The pattern is that the crowd follows the reputation, so the solution is usually spreading the same attractions across more places.
