title: Describe a person who learns history and loves history
questions: 【Part 2】
Describe a person who learns history and loves history
You should say: Who this person is / How he/she learns history / Why he/she loves history / And explain how you feel about him/her
【Part 3】
1. Besides big historical events, what else is important when learning history?
2. Do you think people should learn ancient history before learning modern history?
3. Is it important to learn how people in the past lived their lives?
4. How do children learn history before they attend school?
5. At what age do you think people should begin to learn history?
6. Do you think children should begin learning history from an early age?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 2 示范答案】
The person I want to describe is a former classmate of mine who's turned history into a hobby that borders on an obsession. We were at university together, and while the rest of us were revising for exams, he was reading about the Ming dynasty for pleasure.

He learns in a pretty systematic way. He reads academic books and old newspapers, watches lectures, and keeps a notebook full of timelines and maps. He also travels specifically to see old buildings - sometimes dragging friends to tiny museums nobody else visits - and he argues politely with tour guides when they get their dates wrong.

I admire him, although his enthusiasm can be exhausting. What I like most is that his interest isn't decorative: he actually understands why institutions changed, and it makes him unusually thoughtful about the present.

Talking to him is a reminder that history isn't a list of dates, it's a long argument about how people behave. And I always leave our conversations wanting to go and read something.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 除大事件外还有什么重要：普通人的日常、物价、衣食住行。The price of bread tells you more about daily life than a treaty does.
2) 该先学古代史再学近代史吗：不必，先后不如联系重要。
3) 了解过去人的生活方式重要吗：重要，能打破对过去的想象。
4) 上学前孩子怎么学历史：听故事、看节日习俗。
5) 几岁开始学历史合适：六七岁起通过故事接触，十岁后写系统。
6) 孩子该从小学历史吗：该，但要讲故事而不是背年表。Children remember people and stories, not dynasties and dates.

【Part 3 全文】
1) Besides big historical events, what else is important when learning history?

The everyday details: what things cost, what people ate, how they kept warm, when they married. The price of bread tells you more about daily life than a treaty does. Big events explain the outline, but the small stuff is what makes the past feel like a place real people lived in rather than a list of dates. I would also add the histories of ordinary people, women, and working families.

2) Do you think people should learn ancient history before learning modern history?

Not necessarily — sequence matters less than connection. If you start with modern history, you have things you can see around you today, which makes the ancient stuff easier to understand when you get to it. What actually works is following a thread: money, disease, or technology, all the way through. I would say teach whatever makes the period feel relevant, then move sideways from there.

3) Is it important to learn how people in the past lived their lives?

Yes, because it breaks the lazy assumption that everyone before us was primitive and gloomy. People two hundred years ago had jokes, music, complicated friendships and opinions about their neighbours; they simply had worse plumbing. Once you see that, the past stops being a costume drama and becomes a set of people making choices under different constraints. That is what makes history useful rather than decorative.

4) How do children learn history before they attend school?

Through stories and through festivals: grandparents talking about when they were young, a mid-autumn lantern, a dragon boat race, and the questions children ask at a family grave. It is all anecdote and ritual at that age, which is exactly right, because they are learning that time has depth. My nephew knows a lot about the past and believes it all happened to one specific uncle.

5) At what age do you think people should begin to learn history?

Around six or seven through stories and pictures, then move to something more systematic around ten, when they can handle cause and effect. Children remember people and stories, not dynasties and dates, so an early start works as long as it stays narrative. What ruins it is turning history into memorisation too early, which puts children off a subject they were naturally curious about. Better late and interested than early and bored.

6) Do you think children should begin learning history from an early age?

Yes, as long as the method suits the age. History at primary level builds a sense of where you come from and how change works, which is a genuinely useful way of thinking. It also teaches that the world was not always like this, which is the antidote to assuming nothing can change. Just do not test them on dates; the dates can come later.

title: Describe a person who taught you a new skill
questions: 【Part 2】
Describe a person who taught you a new skill
You should say: Who this person was / What the skill was / How you learned it / And explain how you felt about this person
【Part 3】
1. Why is self-discipline important when learning a new skill?
2. What are the differences between learning from a teacher and learning by oneself?
3. How do adults learn a new skill?
4. How can parents and teachers teach children new skills?
5. Where can children learn new skills?
6. Why should children learn new skills?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 2 示范答案】
The person I want to describe is an older colleague who taught me how to use a spreadsheet properly - which sounds dull until you realise it changed the way I work.

It happened during my first internship. I'd been given a task that should have taken an hour, and it took me a whole day. She watched me struggle for about ten minutes, then sat down next to me and taught me pivot tables, keyboard shortcuts, and, most importantly, how to structure the data before touching any formulas.

The skill itself is modest, but she taught it in a way I still copy: explain the principle once, then let the person do it badly for a while.

And how did I feel? A mixture of embarrassment and gratitude. Gratitude, because she never once made me feel stupid. Embarrassment, because I'd been pretending to know more than I did.

What I really learned from her wasn't the spreadsheet. It was that the best teachers don't rescue you immediately - they let you fail for ten minutes first. I use that with juniors now.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 自律为什么重要：没人能替你练，重复是唯一的办法。Skill is built in the boring repetitions nobody sees.
2) 跟老师学 vs 自学：老师省时间、纠错快，自学更贴合自己的节奏。
3) 成人怎么学新技能：目标驱动，碎片时间，边用边学。
4) 父母老师如何教孩子：示范、拆小步、及时反馈。Show it, break it down, then let them try.
5) 孩子在哪学技能：学校、兴趣班、家里、和同伴一起。Most skills are picked up from other children.
6) 孩子为什么要学新技能：建立自信和耐挫力，而不只是技能本身。The real lesson is that effort pays off.

【Part 3 全文】
1) Why is self-discipline important when learning a new skill?

Because nobody can practise on your behalf; skill is built in the boring repetitions nobody sees. Motivation gets you to the first lesson and then disappears exactly when the beginner's excitement wears off. Self-discipline is what carries you through the middle period, when you are too good to feel the early thrill and far too bad to feel confident. Everyone who is now good at something passed through a stretch where they were visibly mediocre.

2) What are the differences between learning from a teacher and learning by oneself?

With a teacher you save time, because they correct the mistake in week one instead of letting you spend three years polishing a bad habit. On your own, you can go at your own pace and focus on the parts you actually care about. The catch is that self-teaching requires you to judge your own work, which is the hardest part. I would use a teacher for the foundations and then teach myself.

3) How do adults learn a new skill?

Usually in a goal-driven, slightly opportunistic way: a fixed target, fragmented time, and learning by doing rather than studying theory first. Adults want to see that it works within a week, otherwise they drop it. They also learn much faster from a problem they need to solve than from an abstract course. The best adult learners I know simply use the skill in real life from the second week.

4) How can parents and teachers teach children new skills?

Show it, break it into small steps, then let them try and fail with feedback. Demonstration first matters enormously, because children copy what they see far more readily than what they hear. Then the key detail is letting them struggle a little before helping, since that is where the skill actually gets built. Praise the effort rather than the talent, or they will avoid anything difficult.

5) Where can children learn new skills?

School and after-school classes, but honestly most of them are picked up from other children — in the playground, at a friend's flat, or from a cousin two years older. Screens have added a new place too: watching a tutorial and copying it step by step. The common factor is that they need access to someone slightly better, plus enough free time. Hobbies learned from a friend tend to stick for life.

6) Why should children learn new skills?

The real lesson is that effort pays off, which is more valuable than the skill itself. Watching yourself improve at something genuinely hard teaches patience, and it gives you proof that you are not fixed at whatever you are today. It also gives a child a place to be competent when school is going badly. I would say the confidence is the product and the skill is the bonus.

title: Describe a movie/film you don’t like
questions: 【Part 2】
Describe a movie/film you don’t like
You should say: When you watched it / Where you watched it / What it was about / And explain why don’t like it
【Part 3】
1. Do people’s movie preferences change as they get older?
2. Should documentary films be completely truthful?
3. Can movies help people better understand the cultural background of a country?
4. Are movies more likely to help people become more creative than books?
5. What are the differences between watching movies at home and in a cinema?
6. What kinds of movies are the most popular in China?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 2 示范答案】
The film I want to talk about is a very expensive science-fiction sequel I watched at the cinema about two years ago. I went with two friends on a Friday night, with high expectations, because the first one had been genuinely clever.

Unfortunately, it was a mess. The plot was almost impossible to follow, the characters spent most of the film shouting at each other about a device nobody explained, and the dialogue was so dramatic that my friends were laughing out loud. It looked spectacular, but after about forty minutes I was checking my watch, and I only stayed because we'd all paid for the tickets.

What annoyed me most was the wasted potential. The premise - a city where memories can be traded - was interesting enough to make a brilliant film, and it ended up as noise and special effects.

So I felt irritated rather than disappointed, which is worse, I think. Two hours and a lot of money, and the only thing I remember is my friends laughing at a line that was supposed to be serious.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 年龄会改变电影口味吗：会，年轻时爱刺激，之后更看重故事。Taste moves from spectacle to character as you get older.
2) 纪录片该完全真实吗：应尽量真实，但剪辑本身就是选择。
3) 电影能帮助理解他国文化吗：能，但常是简化版。Films open a door, but you should not take them for the whole house.
4) 电影比书更能激发创造力吗：书更能，电影更直观。
5) 在家 vs 影院看电影：影院专注、氛围强，家里自由、能暂停。
6) 中国最流行的电影类型：喜剧、科幻和情感片最卖座。Family-friendly comedy still fills the cinemas here.

【Part 3 全文】
1) Do people's movie preferences change as they get older?

Yes, quite predictably. Taste moves from spectacle to character as you get older — at twenty I wanted explosions and fast cuts, and now I want two people talking in a kitchen for an hour. I think it is partly patience and partly having seen the tricks once before. The films that survive the change are the ones with real characters rather than a clever plot.

2) Should documentary films be completely truthful?

They should aim for it, but everyone should understand that editing is itself a form of choice. Choosing which hour of footage to keep already shapes the argument. So I want documentaries to be honest about their point of view rather than pretending to have none. Where it becomes a problem is when a film quietly invents a scene and the audience never finds out.

3) Can movies help people better understand the cultural background of a country?

They can open a door, but you should not take them for the whole house. A film gives you the sound of a family dinner and the way people argue, which a textbook never can. What it gives you is a version chosen for dramatic reasons, so the families are more dramatic and the cities are prettier than reality. Use it as a starting point and read something afterwards.

4) Are movies more likely to help people become more creative than books?

Books probably do more, because you have to build the whole world in your head and the images are yours. Film hands you a finished vision, which is inspiring but leaves less room to invent. That said, a really inventive film can teach you techniques you would never have imagined — how to cut time, how to tell a story backwards. So: books for imagination, films for craft.

5) What are the differences between watching movies at home and in a cinema?

The cinema gives you focus and atmosphere: big screen, dark room, no notifications, and a shared reaction with strangers. At home you have freedom — pause it, make tea, watch it in bed across three evenings — but you also have your phone, which is the real enemy. I would say the cinema is better for films you care about, and my sofa is better for everything else.

6) What kinds of movies are the most popular in China?

Family-friendly comedy still fills the cinemas here, especially around the Spring Festival, along with big science-fiction productions and emotional dramas about families and ordinary lives. Comedies travel best because grandparents and grandchildren can watch them together. The holiday release date matters as much as the film itself, which is why the box office figures look strange in February.

title: Describe a short trip you often take but do not like
questions: 【Part 2】
Describe a short trip you often take but do not like
You should say: Where you go / When you go there / Why you go there / And explain why you do not like the trip
【Part 3】
1. What problems does it cause for transportation when everyone commutes at the same time?
2. What are the benefits of travelling abroad?
3. Which is better for knowing more about a country? Travelling or reading books about it?
4. How much time do you think people should spend on a trip abroad?
5. Who prefers travelling abroad? The young or the old?
6. Do Chinese people like travelling abroad?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 2 示范答案】
The trip I want to talk about is the ninety-minute journey I make several times a month to visit my parents. In theory it should be pleasant - a train along the coast, then a bus from the station to their door.

I go because they're getting older and I want to see them regularly, and honestly because it's easier for me to travel than for them. The problem is the journey itself. The train is usually packed, so I stand for an hour with a backpack, and the bus only runs every forty minutes, which means if the train is late I wait on a windy platform. In summer the air conditioning fails, and in winter the bus is cold and damp.

I wouldn't say I hate it - my parents are worth far more than ninety minutes of discomfort. But the trip has come to represent a kind of routine exhaustion. I arrive tired, eat too much, sleep badly, and then do it all again on Sunday.

So I keep going, and I keep complaining about the bus. Both things at once, which I think is quite normal for family.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 大家同时通勤带来什么交通问题：拥堵、车次挤爆、准点率下降。
2) 出国旅行的好处：开阔视野、练语言、被迫适应陌生环境。
3) 了解一个国家：旅行还是读书？旅行给直觉，读书给背景，最好结合。
4) 出国旅行该花多长时间：两周起步，太短只够倒时差。
5) 谁更喜欢出国旅行：年轻人更多，但退休人群时间更充裕。Retired travellers have the time that young workers lack.
6) 中国人喜欢出国旅行吗：喜欢，短途周边国家尤其热门。Short-haul destinations dominate because of visas and holiday length.

【Part 3 全文】
1) What problems does it cause for transportation when everyone commutes at the same time?

It creates a spike that no system can afford to build for — congestion, packed trains, and delays that spread like a cold. Everybody arrives at work already tired, which is a hidden cost to the employer. The odd thing is that the problem is only about two hours a day, so building enough capacity for that peak means expensive infrastructure that sits empty the rest of the time. Flexible hours would be cheaper than more tunnels.

2) What are the benefits of travelling abroad?

You are forced to handle ordinary life in a language and a system that are not yours, and that is genuinely educational in a way a classroom is not. It makes you more patient with people who are confused, because you have been that person. And you come home with a sense of proportion about your own country. I would rate the confidence it builds higher than the sightseeing.

3) Which is better for knowing more about a country, travelling or reading books about it?

They do different jobs: travelling gives you the texture and the instincts, and reading gives you the background that makes sense of them. Books tell you why the food is like that and what the argument in the newspaper is actually about. So the strongest version is to read a little first, travel, and then read again — the second reading is where it clicks. Only travelling gets you the smell of the place.

4) How much time do you think people should spend on a trip abroad?

Two weeks is about the minimum for a long-haul destination, because the first three days are jet lag and orientation, and the last day is packing. Anything shorter and you spend more time in airports than in the country. That said, ten short trips beat one three-week trip if the point is to see variety. I would rather do one place properly than five cities in a coach.

5) Who prefers travelling abroad, the young or the old?

Young people travel more, because they have the energy and fewer responsibilities. But retired travellers have the time that young workers lack, and they often go for longer and slower trips — three weeks in one region rather than a weekend in five capitals. So the young dominate the numbers and the retired get the better trips. I have watched my parents do exactly that.

6) Do Chinese people like travelling abroad?

Very much, and short-haul destinations dominate because of visas and holiday length: Japan, Korea, Thailand, Singapore and Malaysia. Long-haul trips to Europe or America tend to be once-in-a-lifetime journeys planned for months. Group tours are still common, especially for parents, while younger travellers book everything themselves. The travel bug is definitely there; the limits are visas and annual leave.

The popular person I want to describe is our team leader at work, who I see almost every day. She's in her early thirties, quite quiet in meetings, and she has no obvious desire to be liked - which makes it slightly funny that everyone in the office adores her.

What makes her popular isn't charm, it's reliability. She remembers what people are working on, she defends her team when a project slips, and she never takes credit for something she didn't do.

She's also genuinely curious about people, and the questions she asks are the sort that make you realise she was actually listening. In meetings she's the one who notices that somebody hasn't spoken, and quietly asks for their view.

So I think she's popular precisely because she doesn't chase popularity. She does small decent things consistently, which in an office is rarer than talent, and people respond to that by trusting her with the jobs nobody else wants. That's a much better kind of popular than being funny, in my opinion.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 人为什么想受欢迎：归属感、机会、以及被认可的需求。Being liked opens doors, but wanting it too much closes them.
2) 现在更容易受欢迎吗：曝光更容易，但名声也更容易崩塌。
3) 好老师的品质：讲得清楚、公平、对学生有期待。A good teacher is fair before being funny.
4) 好老师一定受欢迎吗：不一定，严格的老师常先被抱怨后被感谢。
5) 老师受欢迎重要吗：不太重要，被尊重更重要。
6) 为什么有些学生在学校受欢迎：运动、幽默、或者天生外向。Playground popularity is mostly confidence and timing.

【Part 3 全文】
1) Why do people want to be popular?

Mainly for belonging, and for the practical doors it opens — being liked gets you invited, recommended and forgiven. There is also the simple human need for recognition. The catch is that being liked opens doors, but wanting it too much closes them, because you start shaping yourself around other people's reactions. I would rather be respected by fifteen people than liked by a thousand strangers.

2) Is it easier to become popular nowadays?

It is much easier to be seen and much easier to be destroyed, and both happen faster than before. One good clip can reach a million people in a day, and one bad week can end the same story. So I would say visibility is easier and popularity is more fragile. The people who last are usually the ones with something to do beyond being watched.

3) What are the qualities of being a good teacher?

Explaining clearly, treating everybody the same, and expecting something of you. A good teacher is fair before being funny, and they remember what it felt like not to understand the thing they now teach. The best ones I had could tell the difference between a student who was lazy and one who was lost, and they responded differently. That takes attention, which is why it is rare.

4) Do you think good teachers are always popular among students?

No — the strict ones are often complained about first and thanked ten years later. Students are not always the best judges of what is good for them, and a teacher who lets everybody coast will be loved and useless. The teachers I now admire most were the ones I found irritating at fourteen, because they refused to accept my excuses. Popularity and quality overlap, but they are not the same thing.

5) Is it important for a teacher to be popular?

Not really; being respected matters far more, and respect survives a bad grade. Popularity based on easy marking disappears the moment you ask for any real work. What a teacher genuinely needs is enough trust that students will ask a question when they are lost — that is the useful version of being liked. Beyond that, they can be as unpopular as they like.

6) Why are some students popular in school?

Mostly confidence and timing: being good at something the others value, having a sense of humour, and not appearing anxious about it. Playground popularity is mostly confidence and timing. Sport, jokes and being a bit older all help, and sadly a nice phone or nice shoes helps too. What is interesting is how completely that hierarchy disappears five years after graduation.

title: Describe a successful sportsperson you admire
questions: 【Part 2】
Describe a successful sportsperson you admire
You should say: Who he/she is / What you know about him/her / What he/she is like in real life / What achievement he/she has made
【Part 3】
1. Why are there so few top athletes?
2. What is the most popular sport in your country?
3. Is it easy to identify children’s talents?
4. Is talent important in sports?
5. What qualities should an athlete have?
6. Should students have physical education and do sports at school?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 2 示范答案】
The sportsperson I admire most is a badminton player who dominated the international circuit for the better part of a decade. I've followed her since I was a teenager, partly because I played badly at school, and partly because my father watched every final she was in.

What I know about her goes beyond the medals. She came from a small city, trained in a hall with no air conditioning, and lost three major finals before she won her first title - which is the part of her story I find most useful.

And in interviews she's unfailingly modest. She credits her coaches, talks about her opponents generously, and refuses to make excuses when she loses.

What impresses me is her consistency rather than her talent. She kept her weight, her sleep and her training routine for more than ten years, which is a kind of discipline that's almost invisible.

So whenever I'm tempted to skip something because I'm tired, I think about that. Talent gets you into the room, but turning up for ten years is the actual achievement.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 为什么顶尖运动员那么少：天赋只是入场券，剩下靠十几年枯燥训练。Talent gets you in the door; boredom tolerance keeps you there.
2) 你们国家最流行的运动：羽毛球和乒乓球场地最多，足球观众最多。
3) 容易看出孩子的天赋吗：不容易，早期表现常被发育差异掩盖。
4) 天赋在运动里重要吗：重要，但心态和训练决定上限。
5) 运动员该有什么品质：自律、抗压、尊重对手。Discipline over decades beats talent over months.
6) 学生该上体育课吗：该，身体和情绪都受益。Sport teaches losing in public, which is a useful skill.

【Part 3 全文】
1) Why are there so few top athletes?

Because talent only gets you through the door — after that it is a decade of boring work that most people quietly quit. Talent gets you in the door; boredom tolerance keeps you there. There is also the lottery of injuries, coaching and family support, none of which the athlete controls. When you see someone at the top, you are seeing the survivor of a very long filter.

2) What is the most popular sport in your country?

In terms of people actually playing, badminton and table tennis, because they are cheap, need little space and can be played in a park or a school hall. In terms of watching, football has the biggest audience, especially European leagues at weekends. Basketball is somewhere in between, huge among students. So the sport people play and the sport people watch are not the same one.

3) Is it easy to identify children's talents?

No, and the biggest reason is that children develop at wildly different ages, so early strength is often just an earlier birthday. A child who looks ordinary at nine can be several years behind physically and perfectly normal. That is why good coaches look at coordination, attitude and how quickly a child learns rather than at results. Plenty of talent is discarded by selection at the wrong age.

4) Is talent important in sports?

It helps, and at the very top it is probably the entry requirement. But the ceiling is set by attitude and training: how you respond to a bad season, whether you keep the boring drills going, and whether you can be coached. I would put it this way — talent decides how fast you improve in year one, and discipline decides whether you are still improving in year ten.

5) What qualities should an athlete have?

Self-discipline, the ability to cope with pressure, and respect for opponents. Discipline over decades beats talent over months. They also need a certain tolerance for boredom, because most of the job is repetition, and the ability to lose in public without falling apart. The ones who last tend to be quite calm people, which is not the image most of them are sold with.

6) Should students have physical education and do sports at school?

Yes, for the body and just as much for the mind. Sport teaches losing in public, which is a genuinely useful skill, and it is one of the few subjects where effort and outcome are honestly connected. It also gives the children who struggle academically a place to be good at something. Cutting PE to make room for exams is a false economy.

title: Describe a public building you enjoy visiting (e.g. a library, a shopping mall, a sports hall, etc.)
questions: 【Part 2】
Describe a public building you enjoy visiting (e.g. a library, a shopping mall, a sports hall, etc.)
You should say: Where it is / How you knew it / What it looks like / And explain why you enjoy visiting it
【Part 3】
1. Why do people visit historic buildings?
2. Should modern buildings replace traditional buildings?
3. Is it better to live in an apartment than in a house?
4. Is it important to protect historic buildings? Why?
5. Why is it hard to protect historic buildings?
6. Why do some people prefer to live in the countryside?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 2 示范答案】
The building I want to talk about is the municipal library in my city. It sits at the end of a quiet avenue near the river, and I found it almost by accident in my first year of university. It's been my favourite place to work ever since.

It's a long, low building from the fifties, with a stone facade, tall windows, and a reading room with a glass roof, so the light falls straight onto the desks. It isn't fashionable architecture, but the proportions are lovely, and the silence inside is the kind that makes people whisper without being asked. There's also a small courtyard with two trees where everyone goes to eat lunch.

The reason I enjoy it is that it's one of the few places in the city where you can sit for hours without spending money or being asked what you want to order. The staff are patient, nobody hurries you, and there are always students asleep on the sofas.

So I'd say it's a public building that actually behaves like public space. In a city where everything else wants something from you, that's a rare and generous thing.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 人们为什么参观历史建筑：好奇、审美、以及与过去建立联系。
2) 现代建筑该取代传统建筑吗：不该盲目取代，可以共存与改造。
3) 住公寓比住房子好吗：城市里公寓更实用，房子适合有家庭和耐心打理的人。
4) 保护历史建筑重要吗：重要，它是城市的记忆和身份。Old buildings give a city a face that new towers cannot.
5) 为什么保护历史建筑很难：维护昂贵、产权复杂、开发压力大。
6) 为什么有人更想住乡下：空间、安静、以及生活成本更低。People move out for space, not necessarily for quiet.

【Part 3 全文】
1) Why do people visit historic buildings?

A mixture of curiosity, aesthetics and a wish to feel connected to something older than themselves. You can read about a period, but standing in a room where people actually lived makes it real in a different way. Some of it is also simple pleasure — old buildings are often just more beautiful than new ones. And they make good photographs, which is not a cynical point as often as people think.

2) Should modern buildings replace traditional buildings?

Not blindly, no — cities need new buildings, but the answer is usually coexistence and careful renovation rather than demolition. Keeping a historic facade and rebuilding behind it gives you both, and plenty of cities do this well. What I object to is the pattern of losing an entire district in a decade, because you cannot get that back. Growth does not require erasing everything in its path.

3) Is it better to live in an apartment than in a house?

In a city, an apartment is more practical: less to maintain, better transport, and you are not paying for a garden you never use. A house is better for a family with children and someone who genuinely enjoys DIY, because you get space and a private patch of outdoor. So it depends on the stage of life. I would also say apartments are sociable only if the neighbours are.

4) Is it important to protect historic buildings?

Yes — old buildings give a city a face that new towers cannot, and once they are gone the identity goes with them. They also hold the memories of ordinary people: the school, the theatre, the street where everyone bought breakfast. I would not protect every old wall, but I would be very careful about losing something irreplaceable to build something that could have gone anywhere. That is a decision you cannot undo.

5) Why is it hard to protect historic buildings?

Money, ownership and development pressure, usually all three at once. Maintenance is expensive and constant, the ownership is often split between dozens of families or a state body, and the land is worth more as a tower. So the incentives point the wrong way and nobody is rewarded for keeping something standing. That is exactly why it takes a law rather than goodwill.

6) Why do some people prefer to live in the countryside?

Space, lower costs, and calmer surroundings. People move out for space, not necessarily for quiet — the main driver is usually wanting a bigger home or a garden for the same money. Some go for health reasons or to be near ageing parents. What they often discover is that the quiet is lovely and the driving is not, so the decision is a trade rather than a win.

ninePointAnswer:
【Part 2 示范答案】
The party I want to talk about was my grandmother's eightieth birthday, held in a restaurant last winter. It wasn't a huge event - about thirty people, one long table - but it impressed me far more than any wedding I've been to.

What made it special was how carefully it had been planned by people who definitely aren't party planners. My cousins had collected old photographs from relatives all over the country, and there was a slide show of my grandmother's life, from a village childhood to her grandchildren. The food was ordinary and the music came from someone's phone, but three generations stood up and said something about her, including my uncle, who never speaks in public.

So I was impressed because it was a party with a purpose. Nobody was performing, nobody was trying to impress a client, and everyone there actually had a reason to be there.

It also made me realise something about my own life: the best gatherings I've been to were never the expensive ones. They were the ones where everyone had a reason to show up.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 人们什么时候喜欢办聚会：生日、毕业、节假日和久别重逢。
2) 现在更喜欢大聚会还是小聚：小聚更受欢迎，人少才聊得深。
3) 年轻人和老人庆祝方式的差别：年轻人爱外出喝酒拍照，老人爱在家吃饭叙旧。
4) 你们国家庆祝什么特殊事件：春节、中秋、婚礼、满月宴。Family milestones matter more than national ones for most people.
5) 政府花钱庆祝国家节日是浪费吗：看效果，公共庆典能凝聚认同但要量力而行。
6) 最重要的节日：春节无疑，因为它是唯一能让全家聚齐的理由。It is the only holiday that pulls the whole family into one room.

【Part 3 全文】
1) When do people like to hold a party?

Birthdays, graduations, weddings, holidays, and reunions with people you have not seen for years. The common factor is a reason to mark time together, because most people will not gather just for the pleasure of it. I have noticed that reunions are the ones people remember most, since the emotion is already there. Anything with a photograph opportunity also helps.

2) Do people nowadays prefer big parties or small gatherings with close friends?

Small gatherings, I think, and it has become more obvious since everyone got tired of being online. With six people you can actually talk to everyone; with sixty you spend the evening greeting and leaving. Big events are good for celebration and photographs, but the real conversation happens at the small table afterwards. So the trend is many small dinners instead of one grand party.

3) Are there differences between how young people and older people celebrate events?

Quite big ones. Young people like going out, loud music, drinks, and lots of photographs; older people prefer eating at home or in a familiar restaurant and talking about the past. Young celebrations are about the moment, and older ones are about the people. The funny part is that by forty most people have quietly switched sides without admitting it.

4) What special events are celebrated in your country?

Spring Festival, the Mid-Autumn Festival, weddings, and the first-month celebration for a new baby, along with birthdays and graduations. Family milestones matter more than national ones for most people, in the sense that they change your week. The scale matters too: weddings are enormous, involving several hundred guests and months of planning. Festivals here are usually about food and going home.

5) Do you think it's a waste of money for governments to celebrate national events?

It depends on what the money buys. A public celebration that brings people together and gives small businesses work is money well spent; a parade nobody wanted is just expensive. What I would object to is the spending being invisible — if the same money could fix the pavements, people resent the fireworks. So I am not against public celebration, I am against unaccountable celebration.

6) What festivals are the most important for people in your country?

Spring Festival, without any real competition — it is the only holiday that pulls the whole family into one room, and everything else is arranged around it. Mid-Autumn is second, partly because the visit is shorter and sweeter. National Day is important but it is more about travel than tradition. The reason Spring Festival matters is that it is the one appointment nobody is allowed to miss.

title: Describe a person you know who has healthy habits and a healthy daily routine

questions: 【Part 2】
Describe a person you know who has healthy habits and a healthy daily routine
You should say: Who this person is / How you got to know each other / What he/she does to keep this lifestyle / And explain how you feel about him/her
【Part 3】
1. Does the government play an important role in promoting healthy lifestyles in a community?
2. Do you think it is important to live in a community where people have healthy lifestyles?
3. How can people relieve stress in daily life?
4. What effect does stress have on health?
5. Which group pays more attention to health, young people or old people?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 2 示范答案】
The person I want to talk about is a colleague of mine who's famous in the office for her routine. We met three years ago when we were put on the same project, and at first I found her slightly alarming, because she leaves at six sharp and never eats at her desk.

Her habits are simple, but unusually consistent. She runs three times a week, cooks her own lunch from vegetables she buys on Sundays, goes to bed before eleven, and doesn't drink during the working week. And she's stopped talking about all of it. It took me a year to notice that she's never once commented on anyone else's diet, which is probably why nobody resents her.

I really respect her for that, mainly because her version of healthy living is realistic. She eats cake at office birthdays and takes the lift when she's tired, so it's a routine rather than a religion.

Since I started copying just two of her habits, I've been sleeping better. Which tells me the boring version of health is the one that actually works.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 政府在推广健康生活方式上重要吗：重要，公园、步道、禁烟政策都在起作用。
2) 住在健康习惯的社区重要吗：有影响，环境比意志力更有力。Your environment shapes your habits more than your intentions do.
3) 日常怎么缓解压力：运动、睡眠、和人说说话、减少刷手机。
4) 压力对健康的影响：睡眠差、免疫下降、容易情绪化。
5) 年轻人和老人谁更关注健康：老人更注意身体，年轻人更注意体型和饮食潮流。Older people manage illness; younger people manage appearance.

【Part 3 全文】
1) Does the government play an important role in promoting healthy lifestyles in a community?

A big one, because it controls the things individuals cannot fix alone: parks, cycling lanes, food labelling and smoking policy. It is very hard to walk every day if there is no pavement and no lighting in the evening. So while nobody wants a lecture from the state, the state can make the healthy choice the easy one. That works better than any campaign poster.

2) Do you think it is important to live in a community where people have healthy lifestyles?

Yes, and I would put it above individual willpower. Your environment shapes your habits more than your intentions do. If your neighbours walk in the evening and the shops sell fresh food, those things become normal and unremarkable, and you barely notice yourself copying them. In a place where nobody moves and everything comes fried, the same person finds it twice as hard.

3) How can people relieve stress in daily life?

Exercise first, even a walk, because the body deals with stress much faster than the mind does. Then decent sleep, and talking to somebody about it instead of rehearsing it alone. I would also add cutting down on the phone at night, since scrolling keeps the stress awake. The trick is having two or three things ready before you need them, because in a bad week nobody invents a new habit.

4) What effect does stress have on health?

It ruins sleep first, and everything else follows from there: a weaker immune system, digestive problems, headaches, and a much shorter temper. Long-term stress makes people irritable with the people they love, which then creates more stress, so it becomes a loop. I would say the psychological effect is underestimated — you can recover from one hard week, but not from eleven of them.

5) Which group pays more attention to health, young people or old people?

They pay attention to different things. Older people manage illness: blood pressure, joints, medication, regular check-ups, because their body sends them signals. Younger people manage appearance, so they focus on weight, diet trends and the gym, and they ignore sleep. The irony is that the group with the most to gain by prevention is the least interested in hearing about it.

title: Describe a book you enjoyed reading and that made you happy
questions: 【Part 2】

4. Do you think people today read less than before? Why?
5. Why do some people prefer watching movies to reading books?
6. How can parents help children develop a love of reading?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 2 示范答案】
The book I want to talk about is a short collection of essays about ordinary life in a small town, which I read during a difficult month last year. It's not a famous book, and there's no plot to speak of - just twenty or so pieces about kitchens, buses, neighbours and the weather.

I read it because a friend left it on my desk with a note saying it had made her feel better. And she was right. The writing is extremely plain, but the author notices things most people ignore, like the way a bus driver waits for a woman running with shopping bags. There's very little drama in it, and that turned out to be exactly what I needed at a moment when everything felt urgent.

It made me happy in a quiet, steady way rather than an exciting one. I ended up reading one essay each night instead of scrolling, and I started noticing small things on my own street.

So I'd say it's the only book I've finished this year that actually changed my evening routine. That's a strange thing for a book to do.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 中国流行什么书：实用类、网络小说和悬疑小说最畅销。Practical books and thrillers dominate the bestseller lists.
2) 该先读原著再看电影吗：不一定，但原著通常更完整。
3) 成功类书籍对所有人有用吗：不是，很多只是幸存者故事。Most success books are survivor stories dressed up as method.
4) 现在的人读书更少了吗：碎片阅读更多，完整读书更少。
5) 为什么有人更爱看电影：更省力，两小时就有一个完整故事。
6) 父母如何培养读书爱好：自己先读书，家里有书，别逼。Children copy readers, they do not obey them.

【Part 3 全文】
1) What kinds of books are popular in China?

Practical books and thrillers dominate the bestseller lists, along with web novels that people read in short chapters on their phones, and a lot of popular psychology and self-improvement. Non-fiction about money and careers sells strongly, probably because people feel they need to keep up. Literature sells less, but it sells for decades rather than months. So the bestseller list and the shelf people keep at home are two different things.

2) Do you think people should read the original book before watching the movie?

Not necessarily, but I do think the book tells you more, simply because it has room to. A two-hour film has to cut entire characters and reorder events, so what you lose is usually the inner life of the characters. If you watch the film first you will enjoy the book anyway, since you already know why everyone matters. The only rule I would keep is: do not judge the book by the film.

3) Are success books useful to everyone?

Far from it. Most success books are survivor stories dressed up as method, and the people who failed with the same method do not write books. So you are reading a very selective sample and mistaking luck for technique. They can be motivating, and a little motivation is not useless, but I would treat them as entertainment with a to-do list rather than as instructions. Read one and then go and do something.

4) Do you think people today read less than before?

They read more words and fewer books, if that makes sense. Screens have filled our days with short text — messages, articles, captions — while the habit of sitting with one long book has weakened. Deep reading takes an hour of uninterrupted quiet, and quiet is now the scarce thing. So I would say reading has not disappeared; concentration has.

5) Why do some people prefer watching movies to reading books?

Because it is easier: two hours, finished, no effort required to build the world, and you can do it when you are tired. A book demands attention and a lot of it pays off later rather than immediately, which suits some moods and not others. Films are also social — you can watch one with friends in the evening. There is nothing wrong with it, as long as films are not the only thing you ever consume.

6) How can parents help children develop a love of reading?

By being readers themselves, by keeping books around the house, and by not turning reading into a chore with a reward attached. Children copy readers, they do not obey them. Let them choose comics or whatever grabs them, since the habit matters more than the title. And reading aloud at bedtime does more than any reading list — it makes books part of feeling safe.

【Part 2 示范答案】
So, the time I want to talk about is an evening in my building last summer, when I helped an elderly neighbour who'd locked herself out of her flat. I was coming home at about ten, and she was standing in the corridor in her slippers with a bag of vegetables - she'd gone out to throw away rubbish and left her keys inside.

The first thing I did was stay calm and try not to make her feel silly about it, because she was quite embarrassed. Then I took her down to my flat, made her tea, and called her son, who lives in another city and had a spare key but no way to get it to us that night. In the end I found a locksmith on my phone, negotiated the price in advance, and stayed with her while he worked, which took nearly an hour.

And how did I feel afterwards? Honestly, better than I expected. It cost me a whole evening I'd planned to use for work, and yet walking her back to her door felt like the most useful thing I'd done all week.

So that's why I remember it. Not because it was dramatic, but because it was so easy to do and it mattered so much to her.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 该教孩子善待他人吗：该，从日常小事和示范开始。Children learn kindness by watching it, not by hearing about it.
2) 帮人时要特别热心吗：适度就好，过度热心会让人有负担。Help should leave people with dignity, not gratitude debt.
3) 孩子能帮父母做什么：家务、照顾弟妹、提醒事情。Small chores build a sense of belonging.
4) 父母该给孩子建议吗：该，但要在被问的时候。
5) 该给什么建议：具体、可执行、不替他人做决定。
6) 父母该帮孩子做作业吗：可以陪，不应代做。Helping with homework should end when the child can explain the answer.

【Part 3 全文】
1) Should children be taught to be kind to others?

Yes, but not by lecturing them about it. Children learn kindness by watching it, not by hearing about it, so the most useful thing a parent can do is be visibly kind in ordinary situations — holding a door, helping a neighbour carry shopping. Then it becomes normal rather than a lesson. I would also praise them when they notice somebody needs help without being told.

2) Should people be very kind when they help others?

Help should leave people with dignity, not gratitude debt, so I would say be generous but not overwhelming. If you insist on solving everything, the other person can end up feeling useless or obliged to you. The best help is usually specific and finite: I will do this one thing on Thursday. Anything more persistent starts to feel like an inspection.

3) Can kids provide any help to parents?

Plenty, and small chores build a sense of belonging — carrying bags, setting the table, watching a younger sibling for ten minutes. It also changes the child's self-image from guest to member of the household. I would not pay them for basic jobs, because the point is that everyone contributes. My nephew became noticeably more responsible once he had two fixed tasks.

4) Should parents give children advice? Why?

Yes, but the timing matters far more than the advice: the moment you are asked, your opinion is worth ten times what it is worth when you volunteer it. Unsolicited advice sounds like criticism, especially to a teenager. So I would stay available and answer honestly when they come to me, and bite my tongue the rest of the time. Harder than it sounds.

5) What kind of advice should parents give to their children?

Specific, practical, and stopping short of making the decision for them: what you did in a similar situation, what to watch out for, who to talk to. If it is vague — 'work harder' — they cannot use it. And it should leave the choice with the child, otherwise they learn to wait for instructions. The best advice I got from my parents was a story, not a command.

6) Should parents help their kids with their homework?

They can sit with them, ask questions and keep them company, but they should not do the work. Helping with homework should end when the child can explain the answer back to you. Otherwise you are teaching them that a correct page matters more than understanding it, and the teacher gets a completely false picture of the class. Assistance, not authorship.

【Part 2 示范答案】
The building I want to talk about is a ninety-storey tower in the centre of my city. And I have to say, I have very mixed feelings about it.

It's a mixed-use skyscraper - offices in the lower half, a hotel above, a viewing platform at the top, and a shopping centre underneath.

In photographs it looks impressive. Close up, though, it's a piece of glass and steel that could have been built anywhere in the world, and it stands at the edge of an old neighbourhood where it looks like a visitor from another planet.

What I dislike most is what it does to the street. It generates so much traffic that the little lanes around it are permanently jammed, and the shadow it casts falls on the courtyard where the elderly residents used to sit.

I don't hate tall buildings as a principle - they're part of how a crowded city works, and I'd rather build up than spread out. But this one feels like a monument to money rather than a place built for people. Which is a shame, because the view from the top is genuinely beautiful.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 你们国家高楼多吗：多，一线城市尤其密集。Almost every mid-sized city now has a cluster of towers.
2) 这些高楼有什么差别：高度相近，用途和设计差别很大。
3) 为什么不同地方的布局设计不同：气候、历史、人口密度和规划政策。
4) 住高楼的优点：视野好、采光足、离地铁近。The view and the light are the real luxuries.
5) 为什么有人喜欢自己装修：省钱、有成就感、想要自己的痕迹。Doing it yourself leaves your own fingerprints on the place.

【Part 3 全文】
1) Are there many tall buildings in your country?

Yes, a lot, and not only in the biggest cities — almost every mid-sized city now has a cluster of towers, usually with a shopping centre underneath. They went up extremely fast over the last twenty years. The result is that the skyline has become similar everywhere, which is why people say all Chinese cities look alike from a distance.

2) What are the differences between those tall buildings in your country?

Mostly in use and design rather than height: residential towers, office blocks, hotels, and mixed-use complexes where the first five floors are shops. Older ones look boxy with tiled facades, newer ones are all glass and curves. Some are landmark buildings with interesting shapes, and the rest are very functional. So the variety is in purpose, not silhouette.

3) Why are different places laid out and designed differently?

Climate, history, population density and planning rules all push in different directions. A hot city builds deep shade and narrow streets; a place with expensive land builds upwards; an old town has to build around what already exists. Planning policy matters enormously, because a single rule about how far a building must sit from the road changes the whole city. So it is never only about taste.

4) What are the advantages of living in tall buildings?

The view and the light are the real luxuries, along with less noise from the street and usually a short walk to the metro. In a hot, crowded city, a high flat catches the breeze and stays cooler. And you get facilities you could not afford yourself — a gym, a pool, security at the door. The trade-off is lifts, service charges and not knowing your neighbours.

5) Why do some people like to remodel and decorate their homes themselves?

Partly to save money, partly for the satisfaction of doing it themselves, and partly because they want their own fingerprints on the place. Renting for years makes people desperate to have one room that is entirely theirs. Doing it yourself leaves your own fingerprints on the place, literally — the wonky shelf nobody else would build. I understand the appeal, though I would still hire an electrician.

6) What kind of interior design style do most people like?

Simple modern interiors with warm wood still dominate, with a lot of white and grey, and one accent colour. People want calm and light rather than decorative clutter, partly because flats are small and partly because it is easy to keep clean. Storage is the real design decision — where do the shoes go. Anything that looks expensive but is easy to maintain wins.

【Part 2 示范答案】
The video I want to talk about is a twenty-minute documentary I watched on my phone last month, sitting on a bus on the way home.

It was made by a young filmmaker who spent a year following a night-shift baker in a small town, filming from two in the morning until the shop opened.

And what made it interesting was how much happened without any commentary. The man kneads dough, complains about his back, argues with his wife about whether to sell the shop, and then at dawn the regular customers start arriving with their own troubles. No music, no narrator - just small decisions and the sound of the oven. Which, honestly, was more gripping than most dramatic television I've watched.

I felt quietly moved by it, and slightly embarrassed about how rarely I think about the people who work while I'm asleep.

And it made me think about my own routine, which is probably the sign of a good documentary. You sit down to watch somebody else and end up examining yourself.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 你们国家的人爱看什么视频：短视频、美食、搞笑和知识类最受欢迎。
2) 看视频和读书哪个更有用：学操作看视频，理解概念读书。

4) 年轻人和老人视频口味差异：年轻人要快和刺激，老人要实用和熟悉。Older viewers prefer instructions; younger ones prefer company.
5) 年轻男女视频口味差异：差异存在但被算法放大了。
6) 视频为什么会走红：情绪强、前几秒抓人、可模仿。Viral videos are easy to imitate and quick to feel.

【Part 3 全文】
1) What kind of videos do people in your country like to watch?

Short videos dominate: food, comedy, pets, and a growing amount of educational content — someone explaining how to fix a tap in ninety seconds. Practical videos do very well because they are searchable and endlessly repeatable. Then there is a huge appetite for life-style content: cooking, travel, and shopping reviews. Most of what people watch is short, useful or funny, often all three.

2) Which is more helpful, watching videos or reading books?

For learning a physical procedure, video wins easily, because you can see the hand movement and copy it. For understanding a concept, a book is better, since you set the pace and you cannot accidentally skip the hard paragraph. I would use them in that order: watch to get started, read to actually understand. Video gives you the shape; reading gives you the structure.

3) What skills can people learn from watching videos?

Cooking, repairing things, playing an instrument, drawing, and fairly quickly, spoken languages — especially pronunciation, because you can copy a real mouth rather than a phonetic symbol. People also learn software, exercise routines and gardening. The limit is that watching is far easier than doing, so it is very common to be an expert viewer and a total beginner in practice. You still have to get your hands dirty.

4) Are there any differences between the videos that young people and old people like to watch?

Quite clear ones. Older viewers prefer instructions and familiar genres — news, cooking, health, traditional music — and they watch for longer. Younger viewers want speed, humour and novelty, and they switch constantly. Older viewers prefer instructions; younger ones prefer company. My parents put on a cooking video as background company, while my cousins use video the way people once used the radio.

5) Are there any differences between the videos that young men and young women like to watch?

There are differences, but the algorithm exaggerates them: watch one car video and you get a hundred, so the gap looks wider than it is. Broadly, gaming, sport and tech skew male; beauty, lifestyle and true-crime skew female. Comedy and music are shared by everyone. I would be careful about drawing conclusions, because your feed is a mirror, not a survey.

6) What makes a video go viral online?

An emotion you can feel in the first three seconds, a format that is easy to copy, and a length that fits in a gap in the day. Viral videos are easy to imitate and quick to feel, which is why dance clips and short reactions spread so fast. Comedy, outrage and heart-warming moments travel best. What almost never works is something genuinely complicated, however good it is.

6) 明星新闻无聊吗：多数人觉得无聊，但看的人依然不少。It is dull by design, which is why it is easy to consume.

【Part 3 全文】
1) Why do most children think education is boring?

Because they cannot see what the knowledge is for, and because they have no choice in the matter. Children find lessons boring when they cannot see what the knowledge is for — algebra at twelve looks like a rule invented to annoy you. Add sitting still for hours and being tested on things you did not choose, and boredom is almost rational. The fix is usually showing them a use, even a small one.

2) Why aren't young people willing to listen to the experiences of older people?

Partly because the advice arrives as a lecture rather than a conversation, and partly because the conditions have genuinely changed. A parent's story about starting work in 1995 does not map onto a graduate job market with three hundred applications per post. Older people often lead with 'when I was your age', which closes the door immediately. Listening happens when the older person asks a question first.

3) What can people do when they feel bored?

Doing something with your hands is the quickest cure — cooking, cleaning, fixing, drawing, anything with a visible result. Exercise works too, especially outdoors, and so does seeing another human being, even briefly. I would add learning one small skill, because boredom is often the absence of a challenge rather than the absence of entertainment. The worst response is scrolling, which fills time and leaves you flatter than before.

4) Why are some teachers' classes boring? Are there any solutions?

Usually because the teacher reads the textbook aloud without adding anything — no examples, no questions, no stories from their own experience. That happens when there is too much material to cover and no time to prepare, which is a system problem rather than a personal one. The solutions are known: ask questions, use one concrete example per idea, and let students explain something to each other. Interaction is cheap and it works.

5) Why do some young people feel bored when talking with old people?

Because the conversation repeats, the questions are personal, and there is little shared experience to build on. Being asked about salary and marriage every single visit gets tiring very fast. Young people also dislike being evaluated rather than talked to. It improves a lot when the older person tells a story instead of asking a question — then both sides have something to say.

6) Do most people think news about celebrities is boring?

Most people say it is boring and then read it anyway, which tells you it works on a different level. It is dull by design, which is why it is easy to consume — nothing is at stake and you can stop at any moment. It is also safe to discuss with anyone, which makes it useful social filler. I would call it low-value rather than boring; it is deliberately undemanding.

title: Describe a time when you got up early
questions: 【Part 2】
Describe a time when you got up early
You should say: When it was / What you did / Why you got up early / And how you felt about it
【Part 3】
1. Do you know anyone who likes to get up early?
2. Why do people get up early?
3. What kinds of occasions need people to arrive early?
4. Why do some people like to stay up late?
5. Is it good to arrive early in any situation?
6. What kind of people like getting up early?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 2 示范答案】
The time I want to talk about is a morning last September, when I got up at half past four to climb a mountain with two friends and watch the sunrise from the top.

It was a plan we'd made three weeks in advance, and I nearly cancelled the night before because of the weather forecast.

Why so early? Because the walk takes about two hours, and we wanted to be above the clouds before six. And I have to say, the hardest part was the preparation: I laid my clothes out the night before, made a flask of tea, and went to bed ridiculously early, which meant I woke up every hour worrying about my alarm.

On the way up we barely spoke. And at the summit it was freezing and windy, and the sky went from grey to orange in about twenty minutes.

How did I feel? A mixture of exhaustion and delight. My legs hurt for two days and my photos were useless, but there was something about standing up there at six in the morning knowing that everyone else was asleep.

So I'd do it again, though I'd check the forecast more carefully next time.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 认识爱早起的人吗：认识，多是跑步和做饭的人。
2) 人们为什么早起：赶路、锻炼、安静地工作。
3) 什么场合需要早到：面试、考试、婚礼和看医生。Being early is a form of respect in most cultures.
4) 为什么有人爱熬夜：夜里没人打扰，安静让人上瘾。Late hours feel private in a way mornings do not.
5) 早到总是好吗：不总是，太早到别人家里会尴尬。
6) 什么人爱早起：习惯成自然的人和需要照顾家庭的人。Once it becomes a habit, it stops feeling like a sacrifice.

【Part 3 全文】
1) Do you know anyone who likes to get up early?

Yes, several — mostly people who run in the morning or cook properly for their families. The ones who like it tend to describe the same thing: the day belongs to them before anyone else wakes up. My uncle gets up at five to swim and has done for twenty years; he says it is the only part of the day nobody can take from him. So it is a habit, but a chosen one.

2) Why do people get up early?

Three main reasons: the commute, exercise, and quiet time to work or study before the noise starts. A lot of people also get up early simply because they went to bed early, which is the least glamorous and most common explanation. And parents with small children get up when they get up, whether they like it or not. Nobody is choosing to be a morning person at six with a toddler.

3) What kinds of occasions need people to arrive early?

Interviews, exams, flights, weddings, and medical appointments, basically anything where being late affects other people. Being early is a form of respect in most cultures, and it also protects you from the thing you cannot control, like traffic. I give myself thirty minutes of buffer for anything important. It is cheaper than a taxi apology.

4) Why do some people like to stay up late?

Because the night is quiet and unclaimed — no messages, no demands, and nobody expecting anything. Late hours feel private in a way mornings do not, which is why so many people do their best thinking at midnight. There is also a small rebellion in it: staying up is the one decision of the day nobody can overrule. The cost, of course, arrives at seven in the morning.

5) Is it good to arrive early in any situation?

Not always. Being very early for a dinner party is awkward, because your host is still cooking and now feels rushed. The rule I use is: early for anything formal or timed, on time for a social invitation, and never more than five minutes early to somebody's home. Being twelve minutes early is basically an accusation that they were not ready.

6) What kind of people like getting up early?

People with children, people with serious hobbies, and people whose bodies have simply adjusted — the ones who have done it for years, so it stops feeling like a sacrifice. Once it becomes a habit, it is no harder than staying up late is for the rest of us. I would also include anyone whose job starts before the traffic, like bakers and market traders.

title: Describe a person who loves to grow plants (e.g. vegetables, flowers) at home or in the garden
titleZh: 喜欢在家花园种菜的人
questions: 【Part 2】
Describe a person who loves to grow plants (e.g. vegetables, flowers) at home or in the garden
You should say: Who this person is / What plants he/she grows / How he/she grows the plants / And explain why he/she loves growing plants
【Part 3】
1. What are the advantages of growing vegetables or flowers at home?
2. Do many people grow vegetables or flowers at home in your country?
3. Is it easy to grow plants at home?
4. Why do some people like to grow plants?
5. Why do some people prefer to grow their own fruits and vegetables instead of buying them from the market?
6. Do you think students should learn to grow plant?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 2 示范答案】
The person I want to talk about is my aunt, who has turned a ten-square-metre balcony into a small farm. She grows tomatoes, chillies, spring onions and mint in old plastic containers, and on the windowsill there are always a few pots of basil that she moves around to catch the sun.

She does everything by hand and by trial and error, which is part of the appeal. She keeps a notebook of what she planted and when, she reuses cooking water, she makes her own fertiliser from kitchen scraps, and she's genuinely offended if you suggest buying vegetables when hers are ready.

Her tomatoes aren't prettier than the ones in the market, but she says the smell is completely different - and she's right.

I think she loves it because it gives her a kind of proof. She spent thirty years in an office where results were measured in documents. And now, in her sixties, she can point at something and say: I grew that. Which sounds like a small thing, but I don't think it is.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 在家种菜花的优点：新鲜、便宜、能减压。Growing your own is as much therapy as food.
2) 你们国家很多人家里种菜吗：老人和郊区家庭很多，年轻人少但增长。
3) 在家种植物容易吗：入门容易，种好难。Anyone can keep a mint plant alive; keeping tomatoes alive takes attention.
4) 为什么有人爱种植物：有耐心的项目，能看见结果。
5) 为什么有人宁愿自己种不买：信任自己和味道。People trust what they have watched grow.
6) 学生该学种植吗：该，能教责任感和食物的来源。It teaches children where food actually comes from.

【Part 3 全文】
1) What are the advantages of growing vegetables or flowers at home?

Freshness first — a tomato picked ten minutes ago tastes nothing like one that has travelled for a week. Then there is the cost, which is small if you grow from seed, and the reliable pleasure of having something to do that is not on a screen. Growing your own is as much therapy as food. On a balcony it also cools the flat and makes the view better.

2) Do many people grow vegetables or flowers at home in your country?

Older people and households in the suburbs do, quite a lot: tomatoes, chillies, spring onions and herbs on balconies and rooftops. Younger city dwellers are starting too, but with a different style — a few pots of mint and a herb box rather than a vegetable patch, partly for the look and partly because it works in a small flat. So the numbers are rising, but the scale is small.

3) Is it easy to grow plants at home?

Getting started is easy and keeping them alive is not. Anyone can keep a mint plant alive; keeping tomatoes alive takes attention — water, sunlight, feeding, and dealing with pests before they win. Most beginners fail because they either drown the plant or leave it in the dark. The trick is to start with things that are hard to kill and take one season to learn.

4) Why do some people like to grow plants?

It is a patient project with visible results, which is rare — you can see the difference your attention made. It is also slow and quiet enough to be genuinely relaxing, and it gives you a reason to go outside twice a day. Some people like the sense of competence, especially after a job where progress is invisible. It is a hobby that rewards waiting.

5) Why do some people prefer to grow their own fruits and vegetables instead of buying them from the market?

Mostly trust and taste: people trust what they have watched grow, and they know exactly what was sprayed on it. There is also the taste difference with things like tomatoes and strawberries, where supermarket varieties are chosen to travel well. And for herbs it is simply cheaper than buying tiny plastic packets every week. Some of it is sentiment rather than economics.

6) Do you think students should learn to grow plants?

Yes, because it teaches something schools are bad at: patience and consequences. If you forget to water it, nothing dramatic happens for two days and then it dies — which is a very clear lesson about responsibility. It also teaches children where food actually comes from, since many assume it comes from a shop. It is cheap, it gets them outside, and it is a subject where nobody gets a bad mark.

title: Describe a new law you would like to introduce in your country
questions: 【Part 2】
Describe a new law you would like to introduce in your country
You should say: What law it is / What changes this law brings / Whether this new law will be popular / How you came up with the new law / And explain how you feel about this new law
【Part 3】
1. What rules should students follow at school?
2. Do people in your country usually obey the law?
3. What kinds of behavior are considered as good behavior?
4. Do you think children can learn about the law outside of school?
5. What are the benefits for people to obey rules?
6. How can parents teach children to obey rules?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 2 示范答案】
The law I'd like to introduce is a limit on how much food supermarkets and restaurants are allowed to throw away - with a requirement to pass the surplus to charities or food banks instead of binning it.

The change would be straightforward but significant: less waste, cheaper food for people who need it, and a legal reason for businesses to plan their stock properly. I think it would be popular with the public, though not with some retailers, who'd complain about storage costs and about liability if someone got ill. France has something similar, which is where I got the idea, and it seems to have worked.

And I came up with it after working a weekend in a bakery where we threw away two bin bags of bread every evening - while a food bank ran out of supplies two streets away.

So it's not a glamorous law, but it fixes something that everybody can see and nobody wants to admit.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 学校该有哪些规矩：安全、尊重和时间的规矩，越少越清楚越好。
2) 你们国家的人守法吗：多数守，小事上常打折扣。People obey the law when it is enforced and visible.
3) 什么样的行为算好行为：有分寸、守承诺、顾他人。Good behaviour is mostly about considering other people.
4) 孩子能在校外学法律吗：能，通过家庭、媒体和社会经验。
5) 守规矩有什么好处：可预期、少冲突、省成本。Rules save you from negotiating everything from scratch.
6) 父母如何教守规矩：先说清原因，再坚持后果。Explain the reason, then keep the consequence consistent.

【Part 3 全文】
1) What rules should students follow at school?

Rules about safety, respect and time — and as few of them as possible, because a long list is the same as no list. Students should understand why each rule exists, which is why the ones about noise and phones are easier to defend than the ones about uniform details. I would also include a rule about taking responsibility for the mess you make. Clear and few beats long and vague.

2) Do people in your country usually obey the law?

Mostly, on the serious things, and with a bit of light bargaining on the small ones. People obey the law when it is enforced and visible — nobody runs a red light when the camera is there. Where enforcement is patchy, people invent their own version of the rule, like parking anywhere at eleven at night. So I would say the level of obedience follows the level of enforcement.

3) What kinds of behavior are considered as good behavior?

Behaving with restraint, keeping your promises, and considering the people around you — in practice, being quiet in a hospital, queueing without being told, and returning things you borrowed. Good behaviour is mostly about considering other people rather than following a long list of manners. It also includes admitting a mistake quickly. The opposite of good behaviour is not rudeness; it is indifference.

4) Do you think children can learn about the law outside of school?

Yes, from three sources: the family, the media, and direct experience with the police, bureaucracy or a rental contract. A child who has watched a parent handle a dispute fairly has learned something no textbook provides. That said, without school the knowledge is patchy and full of rumours, which is how myths about the law survive. I would keep the formal bits in class and the instincts at home.

5) What are the benefits for people to obey rules?

Rules save you from negotiating everything from scratch. If we all agree on how traffic works, you can drive without asking the other driver's opinion; that is a huge saving of time and attention. The second benefit is predictability, which lowers friction: nobody has to be clever about it. And it protects the weaker party, which is exactly why rules about noise and safety matter. Freedom, in practice, is what rules make possible.

6) How can parents teach children to obey rules?

Explain the reason, then keep the consequence consistent — the second half of that sentence is where most parents fail. If bedtime is negotiable whenever a child is charming, they learn the rule is actually about negotiation. Be clear about which few rules are absolute and let the rest go. And follow the rules yourself, because children are very good at detecting exceptions.

title: Describe a friend from your childhood
questions: 【Part 2】
Describe a friend from your childhood
You should say: Who he/she is / Where and how you met each other / What you often did together / And explain what made you like him/her
【Part 3】
1. Do you still keep in touch with your friends from childhood? Why or why not?
2. How important is childhood friendship to children?
3. What do you think of communicating via social media?
4. Do you think online communication through social media will replace face-to-face communication?
5. What's the difference between having younger friends and older friends?
6. Has technology changed people's friendships? How?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 2 示范答案】
The friend I want to describe is someone called Xiao Yu. I met him on my first day of primary school - we were told to sit together because our surnames were next to each other on the register - and we were friends for the next twelve years.

We grew up in the same neighbourhood, so we did everything together: walked to school, played basketball badly on a court behind the shops, swapped comics, and later studied for the same exams. What I remember most fondly is a summer when we built a terrible go-kart out of a wooden crate and two broken skateboards. It survived about fifty metres before it collapsed.

And what made me like him was that he was generous without making a show of it. He shared food, lent me books, and never mentioned it afterwards.

We're less close now, because we live in different cities and lead different lives. But when we do talk, it takes about thirty seconds to get back to normal, which I think is the real test of a childhood friend.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 还和童年朋友联系吗：和少数人，联系不难但要主动。
2) 童年友谊对孩子多重要：非常重要，是社交能力的第一课。Childhood friends teach you how to argue and make up.
3) 怎么看社交媒体交流：方便、低成本，但情绪传递很薄。
4) 线上会取代面对面吗：不会，重要的事仍要见面说。You cannot comfort someone properly through a screen.
5) 年轻朋友和老朋友的差别：老朋友给经验，年轻朋友给新视角。
6) 技术改变友谊了吗：改变了维持方式，淡了也不容易察觉。Technology makes it easy to stay in touch and easy to drift apart.

【Part 3 全文】
1) Do you still keep in touch with your friends from childhood?

With a small number, and keeping in touch is not hard but it does require being the one who sends the message. We do not talk weekly; we exchange a message every few months and then meet once a year and carry on where we left off. The gaps do not damage those friendships, which is the odd advantage of people who knew you before you became careful. I value them more than I did at the time.

2) How important is childhood friendship to children?

Extremely — it is the first lesson in negotiating with an equal, which family life does not provide. Childhood friends teach you how to argue and make up, how to share something you want, and how to keep a secret. Children with a close friend handle school much better, and that effect lasts. It is arguably the most educational thing in a primary school, and it is not on the timetable.

3) What do you think of communicating via social media?

It is convenient and cheap, and it keeps weak ties alive that would otherwise disappear completely — old classmates, distant relatives, people you met once. The weakness is emotional bandwidth: you cannot tell how somebody is really doing from a message about their holiday. Misunderstandings also happen quickly, without a voice to carry the tone. Useful for maintenance, poor for anything delicate.

4) Do you think online communication will replace face-to-face communication?

No, not for anything that matters. You cannot comfort someone properly through a screen, and serious conversations — apologies, break-ups, resignations — still need a room. What I expect is a split: logistics and small talk online, and everything emotional face to face. That is how most people already behave when they have the choice. I would worry more about people who have no choice.

5) What's the difference between having younger friends and older friends?

Older friends give you perspective and short cuts, since they have already made the mistake you are considering. Younger friends give you energy and new references, and they keep you from becoming someone who only talks about the past. In my experience older friends are more useful in a crisis and younger ones are more fun on a Saturday. Ideally you have both, which is what stops you getting stuck.

6) Has technology changed people's friendships? How?

Yes, in a subtle and slightly dangerous way: technology makes it easy to stay in touch and easy to drift apart, and the drift is invisible because there is no signal. Five years can pass with friendly likes and no actual conversation, and neither side noticed it happening. It has also made friendships more numerous and shallower, and reintroduced people from twenty years ago, which is oddly good. You have to be deliberate about depth now.
