title: Describe a person you know who would like to choose a career in the medical field
questions: 【Part 2】
Describe a person you know who would like to choose a career in the medical field
You should say: (e.g. a doctor, a nurse) / When you knew him/her / When he/she started to think about that / What he/she would like to do / And explain why he/she would like to choose this career
【Part 3】
1. Do you think being a doctor is easy or difficult?
2. Do you think learning biology is interesting for children?
3. Why do some children want to become doctors?
4. Do you think governments should put a large amount of money into medical research?
5. Why is some doctors’ pay high and others’ low?
6. Do you think doctors should be paid more?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 2 示范答案】
The person I want to describe is a younger cousin of mine who's decided she wants to work in medicine. I've known her since she was born, but I only realised how serious she was about it two years ago, when she was fifteen.

She started thinking about it after her grandfather spent three weeks in hospital, and she noticed that it was the nurses who explained things properly. Since then she's been pretty single-minded: she reads about anatomy in her spare time, she volunteers at a community clinic on Saturdays, and she's already looked up which universities require which subjects. Her plan is to study clinical medicine and eventually work in paediatrics, because she likes children.

I think she wants this career because it combines the two things she actually cares about - science and being useful to people.

And what strikes me is that she isn't doing it for her parents. She's doing it because of something she saw for herself, which is a much better reason.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 当医生容易还是难：极难，学习长、责任重、情绪消耗大。
2) 孩子学有趣吗生物：有趣，前提是讲人体和实验而不是死记。
3) 为什么有些孩子想当医生：家人影响、经历疾病、想救人。
4) 政府该给医学研究投大钱吗：该，回报周期长但影响大。
5) 为什么医生收入差别大：科室、地区、公立私立差别明显。
6) 医生该拿更高收入吗：该，但要与培训和责任挂钩。Pay should reflect training, risk and hours, not prestige.

【Part 3 全文】
1) Do you think being a doctor is easy or difficult?

Very difficult, and mostly for reasons people do not see. The training is long — six years at university plus years of supervised practice — and after that you carry responsibility for decisions that actually hurt people when they are wrong. It is also emotionally draining, because you meet families on the worst day of their lives. I respect anyone who chooses it.

2) Do you think learning biology is interesting for children?

It can be fascinating if it is taught through the human body, animals and simple experiments instead of lists of terms. Children are naturally curious about how their own heart works and why they get ill. The moment the subject becomes memorising definitions, the curiosity disappears. So I would say the subject is interesting and the traditional method is not.

3) Why do some children want to become doctors?

Family influence is a big one, then a personal experience of illness, either their own or a relative's. Some are drawn to the idea of saving lives, which is genuine, and others simply want a respected job that their parents approve of. I would say the most committed ones usually have a story behind it rather than an ambition.

4) Do you think governments should put a large amount of money into medical research?

Yes, even though the payoff is slow and often invisible. Medical research produced vaccines, insulin and cancer treatments, and no private company would have funded the early uncertain stages. I would fund it alongside basic care, though, because a hospital with no nurses is a strange place to celebrate a breakthrough. Research money is patience money.

5) Why is some doctors' pay high and others' low?

Specialty is the main factor, along with region, whether the hospital is public or private, and how much of the work is procedure-based. A surgeon doing complex operations earns far more than a paediatrician doing the same hours. Rural posts pay less than city ones, which is exactly backwards if you look at need. So pay tracks scarcity and revenue, not importance.

6) Do you think doctors should be paid more?

Yes, up to a point, and the logic should be training, risk and hours rather than prestige. A junior doctor working sixty-hour weeks on the frontline is where the money should go first. What I would avoid is pay that reflects the prestige of a specialty, because that is how you end up with dermatologists out-earning emergency physicians.

【Part 2 示范答案】
The person I want to describe is a family friend who runs a small logistics company. I've known him since I was a child, because he used to deliver furniture for my parents' shop, and he now employs about forty people and has a small fleet of vans.

He started the business after being laid off, which wasn't a bold decision so much as a necessity. He began with one second-hand van and a phone, taking the jobs nobody else wanted - night deliveries, awkward staircases, last-minute moves - and he was reliable when other people weren't.

And that reputation is what grew the company. Customers started asking for him by name, and within five years he had to start hiring drivers.

I'd call his business successful not because of the vans, but because of its stability. He's kept almost all of his staff for years, pays them properly, and never expands faster than he can afford.

1) 为什么有人自己创业：被裁、想自由、看到机会。
2) 政府该给初创企业资金支持吗：该，但要看项目而不是关系。
3) 多数人爱去大店还是小店：日用品去大店，特色和人情味去小店。
4) 什么让生意成功：信任、现金流、稳定的团队。
5) 什么让生意失败：扩张太快、忽视成本、老板不听人劝。
6) 在你们国家创业容易吗：注册容易，活下来难。Registering a company takes a day; surviving three years does not.

【Part 3 全文】
1) Why do some people start their own business?

Three common reasons: being made redundant and having nothing to lose, wanting freedom from a manager, and spotting a gap that nobody has filled properly. Some also do it because they cannot get hired, which is entrepreneurship by necessity. The ones who last usually start because they found a real customer problem, not because they wanted to be the boss.

2) Should governments provide financial support to start-ups?

Yes, but it has to be judged on the project rather than on connections. Tax breaks, cheap loans and small grants work; handing money to whoever is well connected does not. I would also fund the boring parts, like accounting help and cheap workspace, because that is where new businesses actually die. Support should be small, fast and explainable.

3) Do most people prefer shopping at big stores or small stores?

It depends what they are buying. For daily goods and anything where price matters, people go to big stores or online; for fruit, speciality food and personal service they prefer small shops. Small shops win on trust and character and lose on price and choice. So most households use both, and the mix changes with the purchase.

4) What makes a business successful?

Trust, cash flow, and a team that stays for a few years. Trust brings repeat customers, which is cheaper than advertising, and cash flow keeps you alive long enough for the trust to build. I would add a genuine understanding of one customer group rather than a vague attempt to please everyone. Good businesses are usually a bit boring from the inside.

5) What makes a business fail?

Expanding too fast, ignoring costs because revenue looks good, and a founder who stops listening. A lot of failures happen in a good month, when the owner signs a lease or doubles the staff on the strength of one busy season. Others fail because the product is fine but nobody knows it exists. Running out of money is the symptom, not the cause.

6) Is it easy to set up a new business in your country?

Registering a company takes about a day, so formally it is very easy. Surviving three years is the hard part: rent, staffing, tax, and competing with businesses that can undercut you for a year. Access to customers has never been cheaper, but attention has never been more crowded. So: easy to start, hard to last.

title: Describe a plan that you had to change recently

1. Do people often change their plans?
2. Would you tell others if you change your plan?
3. Why do you think parents still make plans for their children nowadays?
4. How does technology help people make plans?
5. What kind of plans do people often make?
6. Do you think people like the process of making plans more, or the moment of carrying them out?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 2 示范答案】
The plan I want to talk about is a trip to the coast that I had to postpone last month. Four of us had booked a guesthouse for a long weekend, and I'd taken two days off work, which is never easy.

What made me change it was the weather, and more importantly a family problem: my father had a minor operation scheduled at short notice and needed somebody to drive him home. So instead of the seaside, I spent the weekend in a hospital car park. We moved the booking to the following month and lost a small deposit in the process.

And here's the strange part - the new plan actually worked out better. The guesthouse was quieter, the weather was better, and one friend who couldn't come on the original dates could join us.

I felt annoyed for about ten minutes, and then oddly relieved. Looking after my father mattered more than a weekend by the sea, and it turned out the sea didn't mind waiting.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 人们经常改计划吗：经常，尤其是朋友聚会。
2) 改计划会告诉别人吗：会，越早说越有礼貌。Telling people early is what makes cancelling acceptable.
3) 为什么父母还替孩子做计划：习惯、担心、以及想省时间。
4) 技术如何帮人做计划：共享日历、提醒、实时改约。
5) 人们常做什么计划：旅行、学习、健身和存钱。
6) 更喜欢制定还是执行计划：多数人享受制定，执行才见真章。Planning feels like progress, but only doing it changes anything.

【Part 3 全文】
1) Do people often change their plans?

Constantly, especially social plans — a dinner slips to next week, a trip moves a month. Weather, money and work all intervene, and most of us overbook slightly in the hope that things will work out. Big life plans change less often but matter far more when they do. I would say flexibility is so normal that rigid plans are the strange case.

2) Would you tell others if you change your plan?

Yes, and the earlier the better, because telling people early is what makes cancelling acceptable. A cancellation two days ahead is fine; two hours ahead wastes someone's evening and their arrangement. If I have to cancel late I usually explain briefly and offer a specific new date. Silence then an apology a week later is the worst version.

3) Why do parents still make plans for their children nowadays?

Partly habit, partly real worry, and partly because the competition for school places and activities genuinely requires planning. Parents also plan to save time: joining a class is easier than waiting for a child to develop the interest. Some of it is simply control, which children detect immediately. The good version is planning opportunities rather than outcomes.

4) How does technology help people make plans?

Shared calendars, reminders, price alerts, group chats where everyone agrees at once, and the ability to change everything instantly. Maps and reviews remove most of the guesswork about where to stay and what to book. That is genuinely a big improvement over phoning round. The downside is that plans are now so easy to make that we overcommit badly.

5) What kind of plans do people often make?

Travel, study, fitness, and saving money — the four seasonal resolutions. Then there are the practical ones: moving house, changing jobs, having a child. Weddings and exams create their own planning industries. What is interesting is how many of these are really about identity, not logistics. We plan the person we intend to become.

6) Do people like the process of making plans more, or the moment of carrying them out?

Honestly, most people enjoy the planning more. Planning feels like progress, but only doing it changes anything, and it costs nothing to imagine a perfect holiday. That is why so many gym memberships and unfinished courses exist. I try to plan in twenty minutes and then start, because the pleasure of the plan can replace the achievement.

title: Describe a time when you worked in a group
questions: 【Part 2】
Describe a time when you worked in a group
You should say: What you did / Who you worked with / What problems you faced / And explain why you worked in the group
【Part 3】
1. Why do some people prefer to work by themselves?
2. What should a leader do to make team members want to follow him or her?
3. Should students learn to do group work?
4. What group tasks are there in schools?
5. What advantages are there for students experiencing teamwork at school?
6. How can you tell if a person is a good leader?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 2 示范答案】
The group project I want to talk about was in my final year at university. Four of us had to design and present a market entry plan for a fictional company, and it counted for half the marks in that module, so the pressure was real.

I worked with three classmates I didn't know particularly well, and our problem wasn't talent, it was coordination. One person wanted to research endlessly, another wanted to finish early whatever the quality was, and our first two drafts were obviously written by different people with different styles.

In the end we fixed the process rather than the people: we divided the work by chapter, set two fixed meetings a week, and gave one person the job of editing everything into a single voice.

And we got a good mark, mainly because we sorted out how we worked, not because anyone was brilliant.

So that's what I took away from it. Group work is mostly a logistics problem, and the cleverest person in the room is useless if nobody agrees on the deadline.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 为什么有人更喜欢自己工作：节奏自由、不用开会解释。
2) 领导者如何让人愿意跟随：定清目标、担责任、给信任。People follow leaders who take the blame and share the credit.
3) 学生该学团队合作吗：该，工作里几乎没人单独完成任务。
4) 学校有哪些团体任务：小组报告、体育、戏剧、实验。
5) 在学校体验团队合作的好处：学会分工、妥协和按时交付。
6) 怎么判断一个人是好领导：看他不在时团队是否照常运转。A good leader is visible in the results, not in the room.

【Part 3 全文】
1) Why do some people prefer to work by themselves?

Because they can set their own pace, skip the meetings, and avoid explaining every decision to five other people. Working alone also means the quality is entirely yours, which some people find more satisfying. For deep, technical work I would choose solitude every time. The cost is that nobody catches your mistakes, which is why I still ask for reviews.

2) What should a leader do to make team members want to follow him or her?

Set a clear goal, take the blame when things go wrong, share the credit when they go right, and then get out of the way. People follow leaders who take the blame and share the credit — it is almost that simple. Add honesty about what is not working, because teams can smell a fake reassurance immediately. Trust is built by consistency, not by speeches.

3) Should students learn to do group work?

Yes, because hardly any job in the real world is done alone, and the skill is learned rather than instinctive — dividing work, agreeing on standards, chasing a slow partner politely. School is a safe place to learn it. The problem is that teachers often grade only the product and never the collaboration, which teaches students to hide rather than contribute.

4) What group tasks are there in schools?

Group presentations, laboratory experiments, sports teams, drama productions, and debates. Also the informal ones: putting on a class event, making a poster, or a shared revision plan. The best tasks have clearly separable parts, so the group has to coordinate rather than sit in a pile. Anything graded as a single mark tends to create a freeloader problem.

5) What advantages are there for students experiencing teamwork at school?

They learn to divide work fairly, to compromise, and to deliver on time for people who are depending on them. They also learn that being right is not enough if you cannot persuade anyone, which is a lesson many clever students need. And they get early experience of the awkward conversation. Those skills show up years later in every job.

6) How can you tell if a person is a good leader?

A good leader is visible in the results, not in the room: the team runs properly when they are away, and people take initiative without asking. You can also tell by what happens after a failure — whether people admit problems early or hide them. If the group only performs in the leader's presence, that is management, not leadership.

title: Describe an important decision that you made
questions: 【Part 2】
Describe an important decision that you made
You should say: What the decision was / How you made your decision / What the results of the decision were / And explain why it was important
【Part 3】
1. Do you think children sometimes have to make important decisions?
2. What important decisions do teenagers need to make after graduation?
3. Who can children turn to for help when making a decision?
4. Do you think advertisements can influence our decisions when shopping?
5. Do you think the influence of advertising is good?
6. How do people usually make important decisions?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 2 示范答案】
The most important decision I've made was choosing which university offer to accept, when I was eighteen. I had two very different options: a prestigious university in another province that I couldn't really afford, and a local one with a solid reputation and a scholarship.

I made the decision slowly, and rather painfully. I wrote a list of what actually mattered to me - money, distance from home, the course itself - and then I talked to a teacher whose judgement I trust. And he asked me one question that settled it: which one would I regret at thirty?

That reframing made the choice much clearer, and I took the scholarship.

And that decision has shaped everything since. No debt, friends I still see, and a course that turned out to suit me.

It was important because it was the first time I had to choose between what looked good and what was actually right for me. Which, I've realised since, is a decision you keep making for the rest of your life.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 孩子有时必须做重要决定吗：有时，比如搬家或转学随父母。
2) 毕业后青少年要做什么决定：专业、城市、是否继续读。
3) 孩子做决定能找谁帮忙：父母、老师、以及了解他的朋友。
4) 广告会影响购物决定吗：会，尤其在冲动消费上。
5) 广告的影响是好事吗：不完全，制造需求也制造攀比。Advertising creates needs you did not have ten minutes ago.
6) 人们通常怎么做重要决定：收集信息、听建议、最后靠直觉。Facts inform a decision, but a gut feeling usually closes it.

【Part 3 全文】
1) Do you think children sometimes have to make important decisions?

Occasionally, and usually not by choice — where to live after a divorce, which school to attend, whether to move cities with a parent. Those decisions are made at an age when the child has the least information and the least power. So I would say they sometimes have to, and adults should be careful not to add to that burden. Consulting them is different from making them choose.

2) What important decisions do teenagers need to make after graduation?

What to study, or whether to study at all; which city to live in; and increasingly whether to take a gap year or go straight into work. These choices feel permanent at eighteen, though most of them are reversible. The pressure comes from the fact that the decision is made with almost no real experience of the options. Good schools teach the decision, not just the exam.

3) Who can children turn to for help when making a decision?

Parents, teachers, and an older friend or cousin who actually knows them. The most useful person is not the one with the strongest opinion but the one who asks questions and makes them say the option out loud. Ideally they get two or three perspectives rather than one authority. What they need is a map of consequences, not a verdict.

4) Do you think advertisements can influence our decisions when shopping?

Definitely, especially for small impulse purchases where there is no real deliberation — a snack, an app, a cheap gadget. Advertising mostly works by making one brand feel familiar, which is enough to break a tie. For expensive considered purchases, reviews and advice matter more than ads. So influence is strongest where decisions are weakest.

5) Do you think the influence of advertising is good?

Partly. It does inform people about new products and keeps prices competitive through competition. But it also manufactures needs and fuels comparison — the feeling that last year's phone is now a problem. And a lot of it targets insecurity, especially in young people. I would regulate advertising aimed at children much more strictly than it is now.

6) How do people usually make important decisions?

They gather information, talk to two or three people they trust, sleep on it, then commit and stop revisiting it. In practice most people decide with their gut and then look for evidence, which is human and not entirely bad. The useful habits are writing the options down and asking what happens if this goes wrong. Regret usually comes from deciding too fast, not from deciding slowly.

title: Describe a live sports event you watched and liked
questions: 【Part 2】
Describe a live sports event you watched and liked

4. What sports matches are suitable for children to attend?
5. Why do some people spend a lot going to other countries to watch sports events?
6. What sports games are popular in your country?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 2 示范答案】
The event I want to talk about is a basketball game I watched live last winter, in my city team's arena. I went with my cousin, who's a season ticket holder, so we had decent seats about ten rows from the court.

It was a league match against the team that had knocked them out of the play-offs the year before, so the atmosphere was tense from the start. There were drums, a whole stand of standing fans, and a referee everybody disagreed with.

And the game itself was close all the way. It went to overtime, and the home team won by two points in the last ten seconds - the kind of thing that happens on television and rarely in front of you.

I liked it far more than I expected, mainly because of the crowd. Watching on a screen, you see the game; in the arena, you feel the collective nervousness, and you can't pause it or check your phone.

So I'd go again. Although next time I'd take a cushion, because those seats are not designed for overtime.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 为什么有人喜欢看比赛：投入感、归属感和不确定性。
2) 人们通常在哪儿看比赛：家里、酒吧、现场或手机上。
3) 在线看的优点：便宜、能回看、多视角。
4) 什么比赛适合孩子看：规则简单、时间不太晚的项目。
5) 为什么有人花大钱出国看比赛：一生一次的体验和仪式感。People pay for the memory, not for the ticket.
6) 你们国家流行什么运动：篮球羽毛球乒乓球最普及，足球最热。Football has the loudest fans, badminton the most players.

【Part 3 全文】
1) Why do some people like to watch sports events?

Because it is a story with an ending you cannot predict, and everyone in the stadium is feeling the same thing at the same moment. There is also loyalty: following a team for a decade gives you a long-running relationship with something outside your own life. And it is genuinely exciting to watch human beings do something at the absolute limit. Sport is drama that nobody scripted.

2) Where do people normally watch sports events?

Mostly at home on television, often with friends and food, because it is cheap and comfortable. Then bars and public screens for the atmosphere, and the stadium itself for the handful who can get tickets. Phones cover the rest — highlights on the way home. So the same event gets watched at four different scales.

3) What are the advantages of watching sports events online?

You can watch any match from anywhere, pause and replay, see camera angles that the stadium cannot offer, and it costs a fraction of a ticket. Statistics and commentary make it easier to understand what actually happened. The obvious downside is the atmosphere and the shared anticipation. I would still take a live match once over fifty streams.

4) What sports matches are suitable for children to attend?

Swimming, athletics, table tennis and volleyball work well, because they are short, loud but not intimidating, and easy to follow. Local or school competitions are ideal first experiences since they are small and friendly. I would hesitate about football derbies with large crowds, mainly for safety and language. Start small and get them hooked.

5) Why do some people spend a lot going to other countries to watch sports events?

For a lot of fans it is a once-in-a-lifetime pilgrimage — the World Cup or the Olympics — and they have been saving for it for years. There is also the feeling of being among supporters from everywhere, which you simply cannot get at home. And for some it is about being present at a historic moment. It is expensive and completely rational in emotional terms.

6) What sports games are popular in your country?

Badminton and table tennis are everywhere, because they are cheap and need very little space. Football has the biggest audience, and basketball is huge among students, with the CBA filling arenas. Swimming and running have grown enormously with the marathon boom. So the sports people play and the ones they watch are not the same list.

title: Describe a food that people eat on special occasions/events
questions: 【Part 2】
Describe a food that people eat on special occasions/events
You should say: What it is / What the special event/occasion is / How it is cooked/made / And explain why people eat it on that special occasion/event
【Part 3】
1. Why are there special foods on special occasions or events?
2. What are the differences between everyday food and festival food?
3. Are there any differences between the food people eat today and the food people ate in the past?
4. Do people today prefer eating at home or in a restaurant?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 2 示范答案】
The food I want to talk about is dumplings, which my family eats on the eve of the spring festival and at almost every family celebration.

The occasion is the New Year reunion dinner, when everyone who possibly can comes home, and the table is full for the only time in the year.

And they're made by hand, which is exactly why they matter. My grandmother makes the dough, my uncle does the filling with pork and cabbage, and everybody else sits around wrapping them - badly, in my case. One dumpling usually has a coin hidden inside, and finding it is supposed to bring you luck for the year, so the children eat far too many trying to win.

People eat them on that occasion because the shape looks like an old gold ingot, and because the process brings the whole family into one room.

So for me, dumplings aren't really about the taste. They're about the two hours of chaos before dinner.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 为什么特殊场合有特殊食物：象征意义和记忆的载体。Food is the fastest way to remember a day.
2) 日常食物和节日食物的差别：节日食物更费工、更有说法。
3) 过去和现在的食物差异：过去少而应季，现在多而全年可得。
4) 现在的人更爱在家吃还是下馆子：平日下馆子，节日回家吃。
5) 传统食物会消失吗：不会完全消失，但会变成节日的仪式。Traditional dishes survive as rituals rather than as daily meals.

【Part 3 全文】
1) Why are there special foods on special occasions or events?

Partly symbolism — dumplings shaped like ingots, noodles for long life — and partly because rare, expensive ingredients used to be the only way to mark a day as different. Sharing a specific dish also creates memory: everyone knows what that evening tasted like. And practically, festivals need a long, slow job that brings the family into one kitchen. The food is the excuse and the event.

2) What are the differences between everyday food and festival food?

Time and effort more than ingredients: festival food is slow, made in quantity, and often involves the whole family for a whole day. It is heavier, sweeter and more expensive, and the portions are unreasonable in a deliberate way. Everyday food is quick, individual and repeatable. So the difference is really about attention rather than nutrition.

3) Are there any differences between the food people eat today and the food people ate in the past?

Enormous ones: far more meat and sugar, far less seasonal, and much more of it bought rather than made. In the past, festival food was genuinely a once-a-year protein hit; today you can eat it any Tuesday. Cooking has moved from a household skill to a service you buy, which saves time and loses something. I would say we eat better and taste less.

4) Do people today prefer eating at home or in a restaurant?

Both, for different occasions. Big traditional festivals are still at home, usually cooked by the eldest woman in the family, because that is where the tradition lives. For birthdays and gatherings with friends, restaurants are far more common because nobody wants to wash up. The trend is clearly towards eating out, except on the two or three days that really matter.

title: Describe a person who is good at learning and speaking new languages
titleZh: 擅长学习和说语言的人
questions: 【Part 2】
Describe a person who is good at learning and speaking new languages
You should say: How you got to know him/her / How he/she learns a new language / What languages he/she can speak / And explain how you feel about him/her
【Part 3】
1. Are there many people who can speak foreign languages in your country?
2. Does speaking other languages help at work?
3. Do people learn any languages other than English?
4. Why is it easier for children to learn new things than for adults?
5. How do people learn new things?
6. What is the most important thing for learning a language well?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 2 示范答案】
The person I want to describe is a friend of mine who collects languages the way other people collect records. We met at university, where we shared a flat for a year, and she now speaks Mandarin, English, Spanish, and enough Japanese to hold a conversation.

Her method is disarmingly simple: she talks to strangers. She practises in shops, on trains, and with delivery drivers, and she doesn't mind sounding ridiculous for months at a time. She also watches television in the target language with subtitles, keeps her vocabulary in a notebook organised by situation rather than alphabetically, and books a cheap flight somewhere every year so she has a deadline.

I admire her, partly for the languages, and mostly for the attitude. She treats mistakes as data rather than as embarrassment, which is why she progresses so fast.

So when people tell me they're bad at languages, I think about her. She isn't especially talented. She's just completely unbothered about getting it wrong in public.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 你们国家会外语的人多吗：一二线城市多，农村很少。
2) 会外语对工作有帮助吗：有帮助，尤其在外贸和科技行业。
3) 除英语外还学什么语言：日语、韩语、法语和德语最常见。
4) 为什么孩子学新东西比大人快：模仿快、不怕丢脸。
5) 人是怎么学新东西的：模仿、练习、被纠正，循环往复。
6) 学好语言最重要的事：持续使用和不怕犯错。Consistency beats talent in language learning.

【Part 3 全文】
1) Are there many people who can speak foreign languages in your country?

A lot of people study English for years, but the number who can hold a comfortable conversation is much smaller. Beyond English, Japanese and Korean are reasonably common, driven by popular culture and business. Truly multilingual people are rare, mostly people who studied abroad or work with international clients. So: a lot of learners, fewer speakers.

2) Does speaking other languages help at work?

Yes, and less obviously than people think. It opens overseas roles and client contact, but it also helps you read the original material in your field rather than waiting for a translation. It signals that you can handle unfamiliar situations, which managers value. Even mediocre language skills are a genuine advantage because so few people have them.

3) Do people learn any languages other than English?

Japanese, Korean, Spanish, French and German mainly. Japanese and Korean are often driven by music, drama and games, which is a very effective motivation. Spanish and French tend to be for travel, study or emigration plans. And a couple of European languages matter for business in specific industries. An interest beats a curriculum almost every time.

4) Why is it easier for children to learn new things than for adults?

Mostly because they are less afraid of looking foolish, and because nobody has told them yet that they are not good at it. They also have far more time and a lot of it is spent copying other children. Children are better mimics, so pronunciation comes more easily. Adults are actually better at grammar and strategy, but they hesitate more.

5) How do people learn new things?

By imitating, practising badly, being corrected, and repeating — a loop that needs feedback to work. Watching alone teaches very little; the learning happens when you try and someone tells you what went wrong. Motivation and a real need accelerate the whole thing. Most people who "cannot learn" have simply never found a use for the skill.

6) What is the most important thing for learning a language well?

Using it every day and being willing to sound silly for a few months. Consistency beats talent in language learning, because languages are a habit rather than a body of knowledge. Speaking with people who will not laugh at you matters just as much. And I would add: learn the phrases you personally need first, not the textbook ones.

title: Describe a challenging technological problem you faced
questions: 【Part 2】
Describe a challenging technological problem you faced
You should say: What the problem was / When and where you faced it / How challenging it was / And explain how you solved it
【Part 3】
1. What are the advantages and disadvantages of AI?
2. Do you think people today should learn about AI technology?
3. Should children learn to use AI?
4. How can AI help in our lives?
5. Do you think students are overly reliant on AI?
6. What can teachers do to stop students from relying too much on AI?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 2 示范答案】
The problem I want to talk about is one I ran into last year - my laptop died two days before a deadline.

It just refused to start, and everything I needed was on it: drafts, references, my whole essay. And my most recent backup was three weeks old.

It was genuinely challenging because I'm not a technical person at all, and the first hour was mostly panic. I tried the obvious things, then took it to a repair shop, where the technician told me the drive was probably fine but the motherboard wasn't. So I ended up buying a cheap enclosure online, pulling the drive out myself with a borrowed screwdriver, and copying everything onto a friend's computer. The whole thing took an evening and a certain amount of swearing.

I did solve it. But what stayed with me was the lesson rather than the fix: I now have automatic backups, and I'll never again trust a three-week-old copy.

So it was an annoying problem that made me slightly better organised, which I suppose is the best you can hope for.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) AI 的优缺点：效率高，但会让人停止思考。AI is excellent at drafts and terrible at judgement.
2) 现在的人该了解 AI 吗：该，至少要懂它的边界。
3) 孩子该学用 AI 吗：该学，但先学会自己写。
4) AI 如何在生活中帮忙：翻译、整理资料、辅助看病。
5) 学生是否过度依赖 AI：相当多的人已经过度依赖。
6) 老师能做什么：要求过程稿和口头答辩。Asking for drafts and spoken explanations is hard to fake.

【Part 3 全文】
1) What are the advantages and disadvantages of AI?

It is excellent at drafts and terrible at judgement — that is the whole thing in one line. It can summarise, translate, code and explain faster than any of us. The risks are real too: confident wrong answers, hidden bias, and a habit of stopping people from thinking for themselves. I would treat it as a very fast assistant, not an authority.

2) Do you think people today should learn about AI technology?

Yes, at least enough to know its boundaries and to check its output. You do not need to understand the mathematics to know that it invents sources and cannot verify facts. Anyone who uses it without knowing that will eventually publish something embarrassing. Basic AI literacy is becoming like knowing how to search properly.

3) Should children learn to use AI?

Yes, but after they can write a paragraph themselves, otherwise they lose the ability to think in sequence. Used well it is a patient tutor that explains the same thing five ways. Used badly it is a machine that does homework. So the order matters: teach the skill, then teach the tool.

4) How can AI help in our lives?

Translation, summarising long documents, planning trips, accessibility tools for blind and deaf users, and triaging medical symptoms before you see a doctor. It also helps with the boring middle of tasks, like reformatting or drafting. The biggest gains go to people who already know their subject and use it to save time.

5) Do you think students are overly reliant on AI?

Quite a lot of them are, in the sense that they cannot explain what they submitted. The warning sign is that the work is fluent and the student is silent when you ask about it. That is a genuine loss, because the struggle is where the learning happens. The students who use it best ask it to explain rather than to produce.

6) What can teachers do to stop students from relying too much on AI?

Ask for drafts, outline plans and spoken explanations — asking for process and spoken defence is hard to fake. In-class writing and oral exams still work well. And the better move is to design tasks AI cannot do alone, like applying the theory to a local case. Prohibition just pushes it underground.

title: Describe an advertisement with a famous person in it
questions: 【Part 2】
Describe an advertisement with a famous person in it
You should say: Who the person is / Where you can see it / What the advertisement is about / And explain how you feel about the advertisement
【Part 3】
1. What are the advantages and disadvantages of advertisements?
2. Why are many advertisements endorsed by celebrities? How useful are they?
3. What is the most important factor in an advertisement?
4. Why are some advertisements boring?
5. Is advertising important for a company? Why?
6. Which is more effective, online advertising or offline advertising?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 2 示范答案】
The advertisement I want to talk about is one for a sports drink, featuring a well-known long-distance runner. It's everywhere in my city at the moment - on the sides of buses, on billboards near the stadium, and in the first five seconds of almost every video I try to watch.

The ad itself isn't clever, honestly. She runs up a hill at dawn, drinks the product, and looks meaningfully at a mountain, while a voice-over says something about pushing limits.

What makes it effective is her credibility. She's famous precisely for doing the thing the drink claims to help with, so you believe her in a way you wouldn't believe an actor.

And how do I feel about it? Mostly irritation, because I see it twenty times a day - mixed with a sort of professional respect. It does exactly what advertising is supposed to do.

So it's a good ad for a product I'll never buy, which is a slightly strange thing to admire.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 广告的优缺点：传递信息，也制造焦虑和浪费。
2) 为什么广告爱用明星：借用信任，效果取决于匹配度。
3) 广告最重要的因素：让人记住并相信。
4) 为什么有些广告无聊：卖点模糊，只会重复口号。
5) 广告对公司重要吗：重要，尤其对新产品。
6) 线上还是线下更有效：线上更精准，线下更有冲击力。Online wins on precision; offline wins on presence.

【Part 3 全文】
1) What are the advantages and disadvantages of advertisements?

They inform people about products they would never discover otherwise and they fund most free content online. The problems are the volume, the way they manufacture wants, and how heavily they target insecurity. I would say they are a genuine service to new businesses and a background tax on everyone's attention.

2) Why are many advertisements endorsed by celebrities? How useful are they?

They borrow trust, and trust is the most expensive thing to build. A familiar face makes a new product feel established. How useful it is depends on the match: a retired athlete promoting a knee supplement works, the same person promoting skincare looks careless. So celebrities buy attention, and relevance still has to be earned.

3) What is the most important factor in an advertisement?

Whether people remember it and believe it. Clever filming is worth nothing if nobody can say what the product is afterwards. The best ads give one clear reason to choose the product, in one sentence, and repeat it. Everything else is decoration.

4) Why are some advertisements boring?

Usually because the selling point is vague, so the ad repeats a slogan instead of saying anything. Boring ads are what happen when a company is afraid of committing to one message. Loud repetition with no information is exhausting rather than memorable, and people skip it instantly. Clarity is more interesting than noise.

5) Is advertising important for a company? Why?

Yes, especially for a new product that nobody knows exists. Word of mouth only works once you have customers, so advertising is how a business buys its first attention and gets to the point where recommendations can start. For established brands, advertising mostly maintains presence and defends the shelf space. Ignoring it is a luxury for monopolies.

6) Which is more effective, online advertising or offline advertising?

Online wins on precision, tracking and cost per contact; offline wins on presence, trust and reaching people who do not live online. A billboard you pass daily builds familiarity in a way a skippable video does not. In practice the strongest campaigns do both: something visible to make the brand real, something targeted to convert. Choose by audience.

title: Describe a place you have travelled to that you would like to recommend to others
questions: 【Part 2】
Describe a place you have travelled to that you would like to recommend to others
You should say: What it is / Where it is / What you saw and did there / And explain why you would like to recommend it to others
【Part 3】
1. Where do people in your country often go for holidays?
2. What is the ideal length for a holiday?
3. How do people usually plan holidays?
4. Is it important to plan a holiday ahead?
5. Why do many countries try to attract people to visit?
6. How do people decide when to travel?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 2 示范答案】
The place I want to talk about is a small coastal town in the south-east where I spent four days two summers ago.

It's not on the standard tourist circuit, which is exactly why I liked it. There's a fishing harbour, a very old temple on a hill, and streets of whitewashed houses so narrow you can touch both sides at once.

And what did I do there? Mostly nothing, in the best sense. I walked to the harbour at six in the morning to watch the boats come in. I ate noodles that cost almost nothing. I took a boat to an island where the only building is a lighthouse, and I spent an afternoon just reading on a wall.

The seafood was caught the same day, and the pace was so slow that I stopped checking my phone within about three hours.

So I'd recommend it because it offers something a famous resort can't: genuine quiet and the feeling that you've found somewhere rather than been sold somewhere.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 人们常去哪里度假：海边、古城和周边国家。
2) 理想的假期长度：一周左右，短了太赶，长了会累。
3) 人们怎么规划假期：看攻略、订票、问朋友。
4) 需要提前规划吗：需要，尤其旺季。
5) 为什么各国都想吸引游客：就业和收入，但也有环境代价。
6) 人们怎么决定出行时间：看假期、天气和价格。Price and public holidays decide most trips.

【Part 3 全文】
1) Where do people in your country often go for holidays?

Seaside cities and old towns domestically, and short-haul countries like Japan, Thailand and Singapore for the ones who travel abroad. Big cities with good food and shopping are always popular. Families tend to choose resorts where children can be entertained, while younger travellers pick places with a reputation for photographs. Visa rules push a lot of decisions.

2) What is the ideal length for a holiday?

About a week for a nearby destination and two weeks for anywhere long-haul. Shorter than that and you spend more time travelling than resting; much longer and people start to miss their own kitchen. I would rather have a week with nothing planned than a month with an itinerary. Rest needs empty space to happen.

3) How do people usually plan holidays?

They read reviews and short videos, ask friends who have been, then book flights and hotels early because of the price. Some plan hour by hour on a spreadsheet and others book a flight and improvise. The most reliable information usually comes from a friend rather than a platform. Half the work is choosing less.

4) Is it important to plan a holiday ahead?

For flights, accommodation and anything in peak season, yes — planning ahead saves real money and avoids sold-out trains. For what you actually do each day, no: the best parts are usually unplanned. So I plan the skeleton and leave the daylight loose. The one thing I book ahead is the first night, so arrival is calm.

5) Why do many countries try to attract people to visit?

Tourism brings jobs and foreign currency and it employs people without requiring a factory. That is why governments build airports and relax visas. There is a cost, of course: crowded old towns, seasonal work and pressure on water and housing. The countries that manage it well tax and limit rather than simply inviting more.

6) How do people decide when to travel?

Public holidays, school terms, price and weather, roughly in that order. Everyone travels at the same three moments, which pushes prices up and makes the sights unbearable. Retired people and freelancers travel in the quiet weeks instead, which is objectively the better choice. If you can move your dates, you have already improved the holiday.

title: Describe a home that you like to visit but do not want to live in

1. Do Chinese people like to visit others’ homes?
2. What do Chinese people do when they visit others?
3. What kind of place do people in your country like to live in?
4. What's the difference between homes in cities and those in the countryside?
5. What kind of gifts do people usually bring when they visit others?
6. How often do you visit your relatives or friends?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 2 示范答案】
The home I want to describe belongs to a friend of my parents - a couple who live in a big old flat near the river. High ceilings, wooden floors, a balcony full of plants, and a kitchen that's permanently warm. I've been going there since I was a child.

I like visiting it for the atmosphere rather than the architecture. The husband cooks enormous meals, the wife plays the piano badly and happily, and there are always three or four people dropping in without an appointment. Being there feels like being in a film about a family that's doing better than mine.

And why wouldn't I want to live there? Well, it's on the fourth floor with no lift, it's cold in winter and impossible to heat properly, and it's full of objects that other people care about - and I'd be responsible for all of them.

So I love it as a guest and would hate it as an owner. Which is probably the healthiest way to love a home that isn't yours.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 中国人喜欢去别人家做客吗：关系近的会去，多数约在餐厅。
2) 去做客时人们做什么：带礼物、换鞋、喝茶、聊天。
3) 人们喜欢住什么样的地方：交通方便、采光好、安静。
4) 城市和乡村住宅的差别：城市小而无电梯，乡村大而空旷。
5) 做客一般带什么礼物：水果、牛奶、茶叶、酒。
6) 你多久去看亲戚朋友：一个月一两次，节日更多。Festivals do more for family contact than good intentions.

【Part 3 全文】
1) Do Chinese people like to visit others' homes?

Close friends and family, yes; everyone else meets in a restaurant. Visiting a home is a fairly intimate act here, so it is reserved for people you have known a long time, and it usually involves being fed more than you can eat. For casual friends, a café is more comfortable for both sides. So the invitation itself signals the level of friendship.

2) What do Chinese people do when they visit others?

Bring something — fruit, milk, tea — take off their shoes, admire the home politely, and then eat whatever is put in front of them. Conversation is often about work, health and children. Hosts compete to feed you, and the guest is supposed to protest politely once before accepting. Refusing the food outright is a small social event.

3) What kind of place do people in your country like to live in?

Somewhere convenient, bright and quiet — a short walk to a metro station, good natural light, and not next to a main road. Newer flats with a lift and decent insulation are prized, and a balcony is a genuine bonus. People also care about the neighbours and the management of the compound more than they admit. Price decides most of it in the end.

4) What's the difference between homes in cities and those in the countryside?

City flats are smaller, expensive and often without a lift in older buildings; country homes are large, cheap and frequently unfinished. The countryside has space, a courtyard and quiet, but fewer services and a long drive to a hospital. City life offers convenience and jobs; rural life offers room and fresh food. Most people choose according to where they can work.

5) What kind of gifts do people usually bring when they visit others?

Fruit, milk, tea, wine, or something for the children, and for a formal visit a boxed gift rather than a bag from the supermarket. Nothing too personal, and nothing that looks like payment. Practical food is safest because it will not be wasted. Flowers are less common than in the West, partly because of associations with funerals.

6) How often do you visit your relatives or friends?

Once or twice a month for close relatives, plus the big festivals when everyone appears at once. Festivals do more for family contact than good intentions, because the date forces it. With friends it is more spontaneous and fewer than I would like. I try to keep one fixed weekly arrangement so it does not depend on finding time.

title: Describe a story/book with animals in it
questions: 【Part 2】
Describe a story/book with animals in it
You should say: What animals are in it / What the story/book is about / Why you read the story/book / And explain what you think of this story/book
【Part 3】
1. Should schools teach children about animals?
2. Some people think pets should not be kept in cities. What do you think?
3. Many people regard pets as members of their family. What do you think?
4. Do many people keep pets in your country?
5. What are the advantages of keeping a pet?
6. Why do people always tell children stories with animals?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 2 示范答案】
The book I want to talk about is a children's novel about a pig and a spider who live in a barn. I read it aloud to my younger cousin last year.

The animals are a pig who's destined for the dinner table, a clever spider, a rat who only works for food, and a goose who repeats everything.

The story is about the spider deciding to save the pig by weaving words into her web so the farmer will spare him - and about what that costs her. It sounds sentimental, but it's beautifully written, and it deals with death and friendship without pretending either of them is simple.

I read it because my cousin needed something long enough to last a week. It ended up lasting a month, because she wouldn't let us skip a night.

And that's why I remember it: it's one of those rare children's books that doesn't talk down to the reader. It's honest about how much a friendship can cost.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 学校该教关于动物的知识吗：该，包括如何善待它们。
2) 城市里该不该养宠物：可以，但要有规矩和空间。
3) 宠物算家庭成员吗：很多人这么认为，也符合情感事实。
4) 你们国家养宠物的人多吗：很多，猫狗最多。
5) 养宠物的好处：陪伴、情绪支持、责任感。
6) 为什么给孩子讲动物的故事：孩子更容易把自己放进动物身上。Children accept lessons from animals that they reject from adults.

【Part 3 全文】
1) Should schools teach children about animals?

Yes — including how to treat them, which is really a lesson about responsibility and empathy. Children who learn where food comes from and what a dog needs become better pet owners and, I suspect, better people. It also connects to science and geography naturally. It should not be a lecture about species; it should be a visit and a conversation.

2) Some people think pets should not be kept in cities. What do you think?

I understand the argument about space and noise, but I think the problem is owners rather than cities. A well-walked dog in a small flat is far better cared for than a bored one in a garden. What cities should do is regulate: registration, vaccination, cleaning up, and size limits in dense buildings. Banning pets is easy and solves nothing.

3) Many people regard pets as members of their family. What do you think?

I think that is emotionally true and, for a lot of people, entirely rational — a pet is a daily companion who never asks anything complicated. Labelling that as silly does not help anybody. At the same time the owner still has a responsibility to other people: a pet's behaviour in public is the owner's behaviour. So: family inside, discipline outside.

4) Do many people keep pets in your country?

A lot, and it has grown fast, with cats and dogs dominating, especially among younger urban households. Small pets are also common: hamsters, birds, fish and turtles. Ownership has become a way of having company in a small flat without the complications of a family. The pet industry here is now enormous.

5) What are the advantages of keeping a pet?

Companionship first, which matters a lot for people living alone, plus the routine of walking and feeding that gets people out of the house. Children learn responsibility when the animal's comfort genuinely depends on them. There is decent evidence that pets lower stress. It is also expensive, and nobody should get one for the photo.

6) Why do people always tell children stories with animals?

Because children accept lessons from animals that they reject from adults — a talking rabbit can be brave, greedy or foolish without anyone feeling accused. Animals also cross cultural boundaries, so the same fox works in any country. And children find them easier to remember and to draw. The animal is a costume for the message.

title: Describe a law on environmental protection
questions: 【Part 2】
Describe a law on environmental protection
You should say: What it is / How you first learned about it / Who benefits from it / And explain how you feel about this law
【Part 3】
1. What kinds of rules do schools in China have?
2. Do you think school rules are important?
3. Are children unhappy with the school rules?
4. How can parents and teachers help children understand and follow rules?
5. What are the rules people should obey at work?
6. What is the purpose of punishment?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 2 示范答案】
The law I want to talk about is the ban on single-use plastic bags, which came in a few years ago.

I first ran into it in a supermarket, when the checkout assistant asked me for a small amount of money for a bag, and I had to buy a reusable one - which I'm still using, actually.

The law is short and practical: large shops can't hand out free thin plastic bags anymore, and customers either bring their own or pay for a reusable one.

And the people who benefit aren't only the environment. The cheap reusable bags are sturdier, and the litter that used to hang in the bushes along the roads has visibly decreased.

So I feel positive about it, mainly because it changed behaviour with a tiny nudge instead of a lecture. It also proved something useful: people will change if the easier option is the better one.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 中国学校有哪些规矩：着装、考勤、手机和卫生要求。
2) 校规重要吗：重要，边界让孩子有安全感。
3) 孩子对校规不满吗：常有，主要是觉得不公平或不解释。
4) 父母老师如何帮孩子理解规矩：讲原因、做示范、后果一致。
5) 工作场所要遵守什么规矩：保密、守时、尊重流程。
6) 惩罚的目的是什么：纠偏与警示，而不是报复。Punishment should correct behaviour, not humiliate the person.

【Part 3 全文】
1) What kinds of rules do schools in China have?

Mostly rules about uniforms, phones, punctuality, homework and behaviour in corridors. They are detailed and mostly about order rather than learning. The ones students actually accept are the ones everyone can see the reason for, like not running in stairwells. Too many rules create selective obedience, which is worse than few rules.

2) Do you think school rules are important?

Yes, but their real function is teaching people to live alongside each other, not controlling them. A school with no rules teaches children that the loudest person wins. What matters is that the rules are consistent and explained, otherwise students learn that rules are arbitrary and get around them.

3) Are children unhappy with the school rules?

Usually unhappy with a minority of them — the ones about hairstyle or phone use, which feel arbitrary and are enforced unevenly. Being annoyed about some rules is normal and arguably healthy. The problem is not unhappiness; it is when students stop believing the rules apply to everyone.

4) How can parents and teachers help children understand and follow rules?

Explain the reason once, keep the consequence consistent, and follow it themselves. Consistency does more than severity — a small penalty applied every time beats a big one applied randomly. And parents should avoid attacking a teacher's rule in front of the child, because that teaches selective obedience.

5) What are the rules people should obey at work?

Punctuality, keeping confidentiality, doing what you promised, and being safe. Then the unwritten ones: do not undermine a colleague publicly, and do not surprise your manager with bad news. Most people are fired for breaking the second category rather than the first. Rules at work are mostly about reliability.

6) What is the purpose of punishment?

In theory: to discourage the behaviour, to protect other people, and to give the offender a reason to change. In practice most punishment is about signalling that the rule is real. What it rarely does is teach the right behaviour, which is why it needs to come with an explanation. Punishment without a lesson just creates resentment.

title: Describe a time when you sent a message or an email to someone but received no reply for a long time

2. In what situations do people not respond to messages at all?

4. Why do some people prefer sending a message instead of making a call?
5. How do you show your respect in your messages?

ninePointAnswer:
【Part 2 示范答案】
I would like to describe an email I sent to a professor about eighteen months ago, asking for a reference for a job application. It was three paragraphs long, polite, specific, and I attached everything he might need, which took me forty minutes to compose.

He did not reply for five weeks. I checked my sent folder twice a day for the first week, assumed it had been ignored, and almost asked a different professor instead. In the end, he replied the night before my deadline with a two-line message and a warm reference attached, explaining that he had been travelling and that my message had been buried under hundreds of others.

Whether I finally got the reply, then, is yes, but the waiting was worse than the answer. What I felt was mostly lesson-learning: I now send a short follow-up after a week, which is normal practice rather than rudeness, and I have stopped reading silence as rejection. It was a small experience that made me much less anxious about professional emails.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 什么情况下回复很慢：工作忙、需要查资料、情绪上不想回。
2) 什么情况下完全不回：信息太多、无关紧要、或刻意回避。
3) 没收到回复你会怎么做：等一周后礼貌跟进一次。
4) 为什么有人宁愿发消息不打电话：不打扰对方，也好组织语言。
5) 消息里怎么表达尊重：称呼、说清目的、别深夜发。
6) 为什么有人因不回消息生气：把回复当成尊重的证据。Silence feels like a judgement even when it is just busyness.

【Part 3 全文】
1) In what situations do people spend a long time responding to others' messages?

When the reply requires a decision, an apology, or an admission — nobody delays a simple 'yes'. Long silence usually means the message has landed in a difficult place. Sometimes it is just overload, and the hardest message keeps being postponed. I have learned to read a slow reply as information rather than rudeness.

2) In what situations do people not respond to messages at all?

Sales messages, group announcements, anything that clearly does not need an answer, and increasingly anything that feels like a demand. People also go quiet when they want to avoid a specific commitment. And sometimes the message simply arrived in a busy week and became embarrassing to answer late. The silence is rarely personal, though it feels that way.

3) What would you do if you did not receive a reply after sending out a message?

I would send one short follow-up after a couple of days, and then let it go — chasing a third time costs more than the answer is worth. If it was important, I would switch channel and call, since a call is harder to ignore. And I try to write the follow-up as if nothing is wrong, because accusation guarantees silence.

4) Why do some people prefer sending a message instead of making a call?

Because a message can be composed, corrected and sent at a convenient moment, whereas a call demands an immediate performance. People who dislike phones find that a call interrupts whatever the other person is doing, which feels rude. Writing also keeps a record of what was agreed. For anything emotional, though, a call is still better.

5) How do you show your respect in your messages?

Answer promptly, address people by name, keep it short, and never send a wall of text with no context. If it is a request, I say why and give them an easy way to decline. And I avoid sending work messages late at night, which is a form of respect that is easy to overlook. Speed and brevity read as respect in most cultures.

6) Why do some people feel angry when others don't reply to their message?

Because silence is ambiguous, and we tend to fill the gap with the least flattering explanation — that we are being ignored or taken for granted. There is also a status element: a slow reply feels like being ranked low. And with messaging, we can see that the person was online, which turns a delay into evidence. Expectations are the real problem.

title: Describe a long-term goal/ambition you would like to achieve
questions: 【Part 2】
Describe a long-term goal/ambition you would like to achieve
You should say: How long you have had this goal/ambition / What it is / How you will achieve it / And explain why you set it
【Part 3】
1. Why should children have ambitions?
2. What do you think of people going after high positions?
3. Why are some young people keen on being fans of superstars?
4. Is it good for a person to be ambitious?
5. Do you think it is necessary to be ambitious when working in a team in a company?
6. Should parents support their children in pursuing their ambitions?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 2 示范答案】
The ambition I would like to describe is to run a small studio of my own within the next ten years - not a big company, just a team of four or five people doing work I am proud of, in a city I actually like living in.

I have had this goal in some form since I was about twenty, when I realised that I enjoyed the design side of my course far more than the theory. To achieve it I am doing unglamorous things: saving a fixed share of my income every month, learning how to price work and deal with clients, taking on freelance projects at weekends, and staying in touch with people who might one day be colleagues.

I set the goal because I want more say over how I spend my days, and because I have watched people older than me wait for permission to start something. I am in no hurry, but I am also aware that ambitions quietly expire if you never set a date, which is why I have written it down.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 孩子为什么要有志向：给努力一个方向。
2) 怎么看追求高位的人：可以理解，但位置不等于价值。
3) 为什么年轻人热衷追星：归属感、榜样、以及可以分享的热爱。
4) 有野心是好事吗：适度是，过度会让人只看结果。
5) 团队里需要野心吗：需要，但要对齐目标。
6) 父母该支持孩子的志向吗：该，即使不认同，也别替他决定。Support does not have to mean agreement.

【Part 3 全文】
1) Why should children have ambitions?

Because an ambition gives effort a direction, and children who can picture a future tend to work harder in the present, even if the ambition changes. It also protects them from defining themselves only by this week's marks. I would be careful not to turn it into a family project — the ambition should belong to the child. Small concrete ones work better than grand ones.

2) What do you think of people going after high positions?

It depends what they want the position for. Someone who wants to run a hospital well is different from someone who wants to be seen running it, and you can usually tell within a year which one you are working for. Ambition for authority is fine as long as the job is actually done. Titles age badly; competence does not.

3) Why are some young people keen on being fans of superstars?

Because a star offers an identity, a community and a story of success that feels available — you are part of something without having to achieve anything yet. Fandom also fills time and gives a social life. There is nothing wrong with it in moderation. It only becomes a problem when it replaces the person's own ambition.

4) Is it good for a person to be ambitious?

Generally yes, if the ambition is for something specific rather than for being admired. Ambition with a direction produces skills and keeps you learning; ambition without one produces restlessness and envy. I would add that it needs to be sustainable, because burning out at thirty-five is not success. The healthy version leaves room for a life.

5) Do you think it is necessary to be ambitious when working in a team in a company?

Useful but not for everyone — a team needs a couple of people who want to push forward, and it also needs people who do the work carefully without wanting to lead. What is genuinely necessary is caring about the outcome. Someone who is ambitious only for themselves usually damages the team in the end.

6) Should parents support their children in pursuing their ambitions?

Support, yes; force, no. That means paying for lessons and driving to competitions, but also not choosing the ambition for them. The hardest part of parenting is supporting something you find a bit pointless — a child who wants to be a sound engineer rather than a doctor. Support is cheap when it agrees with you.

title: Describe a time when you changed an important opinion of yours
questions: 【Part 2】
Describe a time when you changed an important opinion of yours
You should say: When you changed your opinion / What the original opinion was / Why you changed it / And explain how you felt about the experience
【Part 3】
1. When do most children begin to have their own opinions?
2. Whose opinions are more important to children, their parents' or teachers'?
3. Do children communicate more with teachers or with parents?
4. Who do young people like to share opinions with?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 2 示范答案】
I would like to talk about changing my mind about working for a big company. For years I was convinced that large firms were slow, political and dishonest, and I said so often enough that my friends stopped arguing with me.

I changed my opinion during a three-month internship at a large manufacturer. What I saw was the opposite of my expectation: decisions were documented, juniors were trained properly, and the reason things moved slowly was that they had to work for thousands of people rather than ten. I also noticed that most of the small companies I admired survived by cutting corners that large firms could not afford to cut.

I changed it because the evidence simply did not fit my story any more, and I felt slightly embarrassed about how confidently I had held the old view. But I also felt lighter, because I had replaced a slogan with something I had actually observed. I am more careful now about opinions I have held for years without testing them.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 孩子什么时候开始有自己的观点：大约七八岁，先在家事上。
2) 孩子更看重父母还是老师的观点：多数更看重父母，尤其情感问题。
3) 孩子跟谁交流更多：跟父母，尤其是同性别的一方。
4) 年轻人爱跟谁分享观点：同龄朋友和网上的陌生人。Peers matter more than parents once opinions become identity.

【Part 3 全文】
1) When do most children begin to have their own opinions?

Around seven or eight they start disagreeing openly and defending a preference, and by twelve or thirteen they have opinions about music, fairness and style that are genuinely their own. Before that they mostly echo the family. So the interesting shift is not having opinions but admitting them out loud. The teenage years are when the identity gets tested.

2) Whose opinions are more important to children, their parents' or teachers'?

It changes with age. Younger children care most about their parents; teenagers care enormously about their classmates, which is the real third option people forget. Teachers matter mainly through respect — a teacher they respect can change their mind about a subject. Parents stay influential on values, but less so on daily opinions.

3) Do children communicate more with teachers or with parents?

In total time, teachers, since they see them all day. But depth is different: children usually share feelings at home and knowledge with teachers. That said, plenty of teenagers find it easier to talk to a teacher who is not invested in their future, because there is less pressure. The key is having somebody who listens without immediately advising.

4) Who do young people like to share opinions with?

Their closest friend first, then a group they feel safe in, and increasingly a semi-anonymous audience online. They want a reaction rather than advice. That is why families often hear an opinion last — by the time it reaches you it has been tested elsewhere. If you want to be included, the trick is not to argue with the first version.

title: Describe an environmental law you would like your country to introduce
questions: 【Part 2】
Describe an environmental law you would like your country to introduce
You should say: What law it should be / Why people should follow the law / Whether the law will be popular / And explain how you feel about this law
【Part 3】
1. How does technology affect the law?
2. What kinds of rules do schools in China have?
3. Will there be a law that is universally accepted?
4. What environmental laws does your country already have?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 2 示范答案】
The environmental law I'd like my country to introduce is a requirement that every new apartment building includes rainwater collection and a green roof - and that developers can't sell any units until it's certified.

I think people should follow it, or rather developers should, because our cities flood every summer and the technology is neither exotic nor expensive. It would also cut summer temperatures on the top floors, reduce water bills for residents, and give birds somewhere to go - all things residents can actually feel within a year.

I doubt it would be popular with construction companies, who'd complain about costs. But it would be popular with anyone who's ever waded through a flooded underpass.

So I feel hopeful about this one, because it's the kind of change that pays for itself quietly. You don't notice a building that manages rain well; you only notice the ones that don't.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 技术如何影响法律：新技术带来新问题，也带来新的取证手段。
2) 中国学校有哪些规矩：考勤、着装、手机、卫生。
3) 会有所有人都接受的法律吗：不会，只能追求多数人可接受。
4) 你们国家有哪些环保法律：塑料袋禁令、垃圾分类、排放标准。Waste sorting rules are the ones ordinary people notice daily.

【Part 3 全文】
1) How does technology affect the law?

It creates problems faster than legislation can respond: data privacy, deepfakes, what counts as evidence from a phone, where an online business is legally located. Courts end up applying old rules to new situations, sometimes sensibly and sometimes absurdly. Technology also helps enforcement enormously — cameras, tracing and analytics. So it is both the disease and the cure.

2) What kinds of rules do schools in China have?

Uniform, phone restrictions, attendance, homework deadlines and behaviour rules in shared spaces. There is also a strong emphasis on respect for teachers and keeping the classroom tidy. The rules are numerous, though schools have relaxed a lot on appearance in recent years. In practice, students follow the enforced ones and negotiate the rest.

3) Will there be a law that is universally accepted?

No, and I doubt it would be desirable — societies disagree about what is fair, and the disagreement is often the point. Even something as basic as the death penalty or free speech is handled differently everywhere. What we can hope for is agreement on procedures rather than values. Universal participation in trade and climate treaties is probably the realistic version.

4) What environmental laws does your country already have?

There are air and water pollution rules, an emissions trading system, bans on plastic bags in some cities, and a waste-sorting requirement that is enforced unevenly. There are also laws restricting construction dust and industrial discharge. Enforcement varies enormously by region and by how visible the problem is. The framework exists; the consistency is the weak point.

title: Describe a piece of local news that people are interested in
questions: 【Part 2】
Describe a piece of local news that people are interested in
You should say: What it was about / Where you saw/heard it / Who was involved / And explain why people were interested in it
【Part 3】
1. Do people read the newspaper where you live?
2. Do people prefer local or international news?
3. Do you think it's important to have a national identity?
4. How can people develop their national identity?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 2 示范答案】
The piece of local news I want to talk about was the closure of an old market in the centre of my city. It was reported last spring, and people discussed it for weeks afterwards. I read about it first on a local news account, and then it was everywhere in group chats.

The story involved the market traders, a property developer, and the city government. The official reason was safety and renovation. The traders pointed out that the rent in the new building would be four times higher.

And what made it genuinely interesting was a video that circulated of an eighty-year-old woman who'd sold vegetables there for forty years, saying she'd rather retire than move.

So people were interested because it wasn't really about a market. It was about whether the city belongs to the people with money or to the people who live in it.

Which is why I think local news matters more than people admit. It's where these arguments actually happen.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 你们那儿的人看报纸吗：老年人看纸媒，年轻人看手机新闻。
2) 人们更爱本地还是国际新闻：本地更贴近生活，国际更有冲击力。
3) 国家认同重要吗：重要，但要靠共同经历而不是宣传。
4) 如何培养国家认同：语言、节日、教育和共同的历史记忆。Shared rituals build identity faster than slogans.

【Part 3 全文】
1) Do people read the newspaper where you live?

Almost nobody reads a printed newspaper now; most people get news from phone apps and short videos, often in passing. That changes what counts as news, because whatever is alarming and short travels first. Older readers still follow serious outlets in the evening. So the habit of reading news survives; the paper has gone.

2) Do people prefer local or international news?

International news gets the headlines, but local news is what people actually use — school admissions, road closures, a new metro line, a building dispute. It affects their week, so attention follows it. The strange result is that people know more about a foreign election than about the plans for their own district. Local journalism being weaker makes that worse.

3) Do you think it's important to have a national identity?

Some sense of it, yes, because it gives people a shared reference and a reason to cooperate with strangers in their own country. It becomes dangerous when it means superiority rather than belonging. I would say identity is most useful when it is quiet — songs, food, festivals — and least useful when it is loud. Belonging is different from boasting.

4) How can people develop their national identity?

Through language, food, festivals, sport and history learned through stories rather than slogans. Schools matter, but family meals and holidays probably matter more, because that is where the feeling is formed. Supporting local teams and local products is a mild version of it. Identity is absorbed in childhood.

title: Describe a change that you made recently
questions: 【Part 2】
Describe a change that you made recently
You should say: What the change was / What caused the change / What you did for the change / And explain how you feel about the change
【Part 3】
1. Do you think it is good to change one’s daily routine?
2. Do you think it is good to change jobs?
3. Is it good for people to get a job promotion?
4. Do people often make plans around their regular routines?
5. Who tend to change their daily routine more, young people or old people?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 2 示范答案】
The change I want to talk about is moving my bedtime about ninety minutes earlier, which I started doing two months ago.

What caused it was fairly simple: I was permanently tired, my work in the afternoons had become terrible, and a doctor told me that my screen time before bed was doing more damage than coffee.

What I actually did was less dramatic than it sounds. I set an alarm to stop working at ten, I put my phone on a shelf in the hallway instead of next to the bed, and I started reading paper books again. For the first two weeks I lay awake feeling ridiculous. By week three I was asleep before eleven without much effort.

And how do I feel about it? Quietly pleased. Nobody notices, there's no promotion and no applause, but I can concentrate in the mornings again and I've stopped snapping at people in the afternoon.

So it's the most boring change I've ever made, and easily the most effective.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 改变日常作息好吗：好，但要一次改一点。
2) 换工作好吗：不一定，看是逃避问题还是追求成长。
3) 升职好吗：多数是好事，但责任和压力也会涨。
4) 人们会围绕作息做计划吗：会，作息决定了可用的时间。
5) 年轻人和老人谁更常改作息：年轻人更容易改，老人更少变动。Young people change routines faster because their circumstances change faster.

【Part 3 全文】
1) Do you think it is good to change one's daily routine?

Sometimes, yes — a routine keeps you efficient and repeating the same version for five years keeps you stale. Changing one part, like the morning or the commute, is usually enough to refresh the rest. Big overnight changes to everything rarely survive a fortnight. Change one thing, keep the structure.

2) Do you think it is good to change jobs?

Often yes, especially early in a career and especially when the change adds a skill rather than just a salary. Staying too long in one place can quietly limit you. That said, changing every year looks like restlessness and means you never see a project through. The good moment to move is when you stop learning.

3) Is it good for people to get a job promotion?

Usually, though it depends on what the promotion involves — many people are promoted into management and discover that the thing they were good at has disappeared from the job. It brings money, status and more meetings. I would ask whether the new role is work you enjoy, because a promotion into the wrong job is expensive.

4) Do people often make plans around their regular routines?

Yes, most planning quietly assumes the routine: gym before work, calls after dinner, Sunday for family. That is why a change in routine makes everything else collapse for a fortnight. The routine is the scaffolding of the schedule. When it breaks, people discover how much they depended on it.

5) Who tend to change their daily routine more, young people or old people?

Young people do, because their circumstances keep changing — a new job, a move, a child. Older people change less, which is partly wisdom and partly inertia; established health habits make change risky. That said, the older adults I know who stay curious are the ones who pick up a new routine deliberately. Stability is comfortable and slightly dangerous.

title: Lost and found
questions: Have you ever lost your keys?
