Have you ever lost things?
Do you report to the police when finding something lost by others? Why?
What will you do if you find something lost by others?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 1 示范答案】
1) Have you ever lost your keys?
Once, and it was a horrible afternoon. I was locked out of my flat with no wallet and a dead phone, and I ended up borrowing a neighbour phone to call my flatmate.

2) Will you post on social media if you lose your item?
Probably, if it were something valuable like a passport or a laptop. For everyday things, I would rather retrace my steps first, since half of what goes missing turns up in a coat pocket.

3) Have you ever lost things?
Constantly - umbrellas, gloves, a scarf every winter. I have got better since I started keeping everything in the same two pockets, which sounds obsessive but has saved me a fortune.

4) Do you report to the police when finding something lost by others? Why?
For something like a wallet or a phone, yes, because somebody is probably panicking. If it is a small item, I would hand it in to the nearest shop or station office instead of tying up the police.

5) What will you do if you find something lost by others?
I would look for a name or a phone number, and if there is nothing, take it straight to a lost-property desk. I have been on the other end of it, so I know how much it matters.

title: Computers/tablets
questions: Would you like to use a computer or tablet?
In what conditions would you use a computer or tablet?
When was the first time you used a computer or tablet?
What would your life be like without computers or tablets?
In what conditions would it be difficult for you to use a computer or tablet?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 1 示范答案】
1) Would you like to use a computer or tablet?
I would happily use either, though a laptop is my default for anything serious. A tablet is lovely for reading and watching things, but typing a long email on glass still drives me up the wall.

2) In what conditions would you use a computer or tablet?
Mostly for work - spreadsheets, writing, video calls. In the evening it flips around and becomes a film screen or an e-reader, so mine gets more use than my television.

3) When was the first time you used a computer or tablet?
The first was a chunky desktop at primary school, with a monitor the size of a suitcase. My teacher had us play a typing game, and I was hopeless - it took me a whole lesson to find the letters.

4) What would your life be like without computers or tablets?
Quieter and slower, and probably healthier. I would read more paper books and write more by hand, but work would also take twice as long, so it is a trade-off I would not rush into.

5) In what conditions would it be difficult for you to use a computer or tablet?
In bright sunlight, for a start - I can never see the screen. Long journeys without a power socket are another problem, since mine rarely survives a full day.

title: Collecting things

Are there any things you have kept from your childhood?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 1 示范答案】
1) Do you collect things?
Nothing seriously, though I do seem to accumulate train tickets and museum stubs without meaning to. My sister collects fridge magnets from every city she visits, which is a much tidier hobby.

2) Where do you usually keep things you need?
The essentials live in a shallow drawer by the door - keys, wallet, headphones, charger - so that leaving the house is a thirty-second job. Everything else is in labelled boxes, more or less.

3) Would you keep old things for a long time? Why?
Some things, yes, if they mean something: letters, photos, a watch. I am not sentimental about furniture or clothes, but I would regret throwing away anything that reminds me of a particular person.

4) Are there any things you have kept from your childhood?
A tin of stickers, a few school notebooks, and a rather battered teddy bear. They are in a box at my parents house, and every time I go back I open it and lose an hour.

title: Street market
questions: Are there many street markets in China?
When was the last time you went to a street market?
Do you prefer to go shopping in the shopping mall or on the street market?
What do people usually buy on the street market?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 1 示范答案】
1) Are there many street markets in China?
Plenty, though they look different from city to city. In the south you find wet markets selling vegetables and live fish; in touristy areas there are night markets that are mostly food stalls.

2) When was the last time you went to a street market?
Last month, on a Saturday morning. I went for vegetables and came back with two bags of fruit, a bag of dumplings and a pair of slippers I did not need.

3) Do you prefer to go shopping in the shopping mall or on the street market?
For food, the street market every time - it is fresher, cheaper and far more interesting. For anything electrical or branded, I head to a mall because I want a receipt and a guarantee.

4) What do people usually buy on the street market?
Vegetables, fruit, meat and fish, obviously, but also cheap kitchen tools, socks, phone cases and snacks. Half the pleasure is the browsing rather than the buying.

half the pleasure is（一半的乐趣在于）

title: Feeling bored
questions: Do you think childhood is boring or adulthood is boring?
What do you do when you feel bored?
When would you feel bored?
Do you often feel bored?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 1 示范答案】
1) Do you think childhood is boring or adulthood is boring?
Adulthood, without question - there is far more waiting around in it. Childhood felt long, but the days were full; now I spend a shocking amount of time in queues and traffic.

2) What do you do when you feel bored?
I reach for my phone, which is not a great habit. If I catch myself doing it, I would sooner go for a walk or call someone, because boredom usually means I need to move rather than to be entertained.

3) When would you feel bored?
In waiting rooms, on long drives, and in meetings that could have been an email. Rainy weekends at home are another one - an afternoon with nothing planned can turn into an itch.

4) Do you often feel bored?
Not very often, honestly. My days are fairly full, and when I do have a blank hour I tend to enjoy it, so boredom is more of an occasional visitor than a permanent state.

title: Friends

ninePointAnswer:
【Part 1 示范答案】
1) Would you invite friends to your home?
I would, and I do, though my flat is small so it is usually three or four people at most. Hosting is more relaxed than meeting in a noisy restaurant, and nobody has to queue for the toilet.

2) Do you prefer to spend time with one friend or with a group of friends?
It depends on my mood. One-to-one is better for proper conversations, whereas a group is more about laughing and eating, and I need both on a regular basis.

3) Do you have a friend you have known for a long time?
I do - we met on the first day of secondary school and have stayed close ever since. We can go months without talking and pick up exactly where we left off, which is the mark of a real friendship.

4) What do you usually do with your friends?
Nothing dramatic: eat, walk, watch something, complain about work. Occasionally we go hiking, and once a year we try to travel somewhere together.

5) Where do you often meet each other?
Usually at a cheap restaurant near the metro station, or at someones flat for a film. In summer we default to the park with a picnic blanket.

6) Do you often go out with your friends?
Once or twice a week on average, more at the weekend. It has got harder as we have taken on more work, so we have started putting dinners in the calendar, which sounds dull but works.

7) How important are friends to you?
Extremely - they are the people I call when something goes right or wrong. Family gives you roots, but friends are the ones who choose you, and that matters.

8) Why are some places suitable for meeting while others are not?
It comes down to noise, seating and how easy it is to get to. A place where you are shouting over music and leaving after an hour kills conversation, whereas a quiet corner with big tables and a late closing time keeps everyone there.

9) Is there a difference between where you meet friends now and where you used to meet them in the past?
Yes - at school it was the canteen and the basketball court, and now it is restaurants and living rooms. The places are grander, but the point has not changed: somewhere you can sit for three hours without being asked to leave.

title: Describe a course that impressed you a lot
questions: 【Part 2】
Describe a course that impressed you a lot
You should say: What the course was about / Where you took the course / What you did during the course / And explain why it impressed you a lot
【Part 3】
1. What can we learn from history?
2. What do people need to remember in their daily lives?
3. Can technology help people remember things better? How?
4. Which can help people remember things better, words or photos?
5. Do people like things of memorial significance?
6. Why do some people have a better memory than others?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 2 示范答案】
The course I want to talk about was a two-week summer course on documentary film-making at a university in another province, two years ago. It wasn't part of my degree - I applied because a friend sent me the advertisement and I had nothing planned for August.

And what impressed me was that we did very little listening. We were sent out in pairs with borrowed cameras and told to film a five-minute portrait of somebody we'd never met. Then we spent the afternoons watching each other's rushes and being criticised - politely, but precisely.

The tutor had worked in television for twenty years, and she had one rule that's stayed with me: if a shot doesn't tell us something new, cut it.

So it impressed me because it was the first course where the feedback was specific enough to actually act on. Not "good work" or "needs improvement", but exactly which shot was redundant and why.

I've used that rule on presentations ever since.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 我们能从历史学到什么：模式的重复与人性的局限。
2) 日常生活需要记住什么：约定、纪念日、以及别人的底线。
3) 技术能帮人记东西吗：能，提醒、拍照、搜索。
4) 文字还是照片更帮记忆：照片触发情绪，文字保留细节。
5) 人们喜欢有纪念意义的东西吗：喜欢，那是记忆的凭证。Objects carry memories that descriptions lose.
6) 为什么有人记性更好：方法、注意力、以及是否真的在意。Memory follows interest more than intelligence.

【Part 3 全文】
1) What can we learn from history?

Patterns, mostly: how people respond to scarcity, why institutions decay, how quickly normality can collapse. The specific facts matter less than the sense that the present is not permanent. History also teaches humility about predictions. Anyone who reads it carefully becomes harder to frighten with a single story.

2) What do people need to remember in their daily lives?

Passwords, appointments and what they promised someone — the practical things. Beyond that, most people need to remember the dates that matter to the people they love, which is a form of care. I would add that forgetting is not always a failure; a lot of it is just having too much to hold. Systems help people more than memory training.

3) Can technology help people remember things better? How?

Yes, enormously, but it does so by removing the need to remember — calendars, reminders, photos, search. That is a genuine improvement in reliability and a quiet loss of ability. The useful version is offloading the trivial and deliberately remembering what matters. My phone remembers everything and I remember less.

4) Which can help people remember things better, words or photos?

Photos are stronger for events, because they bring back the whole sensory scene at once, and words are stronger for facts and reasoning. Combining them works best: a photo plus a short caption anchors the memory. The odd thing is that taking a photo can worsen memory if you never look at it again. Reviewing beats capturing.

5) Do people like things of memorial significance?

A lot of people do — souvenirs, tickets, a piece of a journey, a photo on the wall. They are less about nostalgia than about proof that a period of your life happened. For families they carry stories that words lose. Some people find them sentimental clutter, which is fair, but that is a minority opinion.

6) Why do some people have a better memory than others?

Attention is the main difference — people with good memories usually encode the moment carefully rather than storing more. Then there is practice with a method, like linking facts to places or stories. Sleep and stress matter enormously and are ignored. So it is mostly technique and attention rather than natural hardware.

title: Describe a city that you have been to and would like to visit again
questions: 【Part 2】
Describe a city that you have been to and would like to visit again
You should say: When you visited it / What you did there / What it was like / And explain why you would like to visit it again
【Part 3】
1. What should the government do to improve citizens' safety?
2. Are there any changes in your city?
3. Do you think people in the countryside are friendlier than people in the city?
4. Do you think it is possible that all of the population move to cities?
5. Some people say large cities are suitable for old people. What do you think?
6. What's the difference between the city and the countryside?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 2 示范答案】
The city I would like to return to is a port city in the south that I visited for four days three years ago, mostly because a friend was studying there. I arrived expecting somewhere industrial and found wide avenues, crumbling colonial buildings next to glass towers, and a very slow pace.

While I was there I did ordinary things rather than sightseeing: I went to a market at dawn, took a ferry across the bay, ate a bowl of noodles at a stall with plastic stools, and spent a whole afternoon in a park watching old men play chess. What I liked most was that the city did not seem to be performing for visitors - people were living their lives and you were simply allowed to watch.

I would like to go back because four days was not enough, and because it is changing quickly. Friends tell me the old market has already gone, and I would rather see what is left now than read about it later. I also owe my friend a dinner there.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 政府如何提升市民安全：照明、警务可见度、公共交通。
2) 你的城市有变化吗：有，地铁扩建和旧区改造最快。
3) 乡下人更友好吗：更开放，但城市人更守分寸。
4) 所有人都搬进城市可能吗：不可能，也不必要。
5) 大城市适合老人吗：医疗方便，但噪音和台阶是障碍。
6) 城市和乡村的差别：密度、节奏、以及人情距离。Cities offer anonymity; villages offer recognition.

【Part 3 全文】
1) What should the government do to improve citizens' safety?

Make the basic environment safe: lighting, pavements, traffic enforcement, functioning street cameras where they help, and reliable emergency response times. Most safety is engineering rather than policing. Also visible rules with consistent enforcement, because unpredictability frightens people more than strictness. And decent mental-health services reduce more violence than cameras do.

2) Are there any changes in your city?

Quite a few: new metro lines, a lot of buildings, more electric cars and scooters, and more delivery traffic on the pavements. Old markets have been replaced by shopping centres, which people over fifty still complain about. The pace of physical change is high; the social change is slower. My own street looks nothing like it did a decade ago.

3) Do you think people in the countryside are friendlier than people in the city?

They appear friendlier, and partly they are, because they meet the same people every day and there is less to gain from being distant. City people are not unfriendly, they are just processing far more people and protecting their attention. So I would call it a difference in pace rather than warmth. The countryside is also less forgiving of strangers who stay.

4) Do you think it is possible that all of the population move to cities?

No, and it would be a disaster — food production needs rural land, and cities could not absorb everyone. What is happening is that young people move and older people stay, which creates empty villages and overstretched cities. The realistic goal is fewer, better-served regional towns. Concentration has limits.

5) Some people say large cities are suitable for old people. What do you think?

I disagree with the strong version. Big cities have excellent hospitals, transport and social activities, but they are expensive, noisy and often lonely for people whose families have moved away. The best place for an older person is wherever they have neighbours and a doctor, which is not necessarily a metropolis. Safety and familiarity matter more than glamour.

6) What's the difference between the city and the countryside?

The main ones are density, pace and access: the city has jobs, transport and choice; the countryside has space, quiet and fresh food. City life shortens distances and lengthens working hours. The countryside gives you a courtyard and takes away convenience — no late-night pharmacy. Most people end up wanting a bit of both.

title: Describe a person you only met once recently and want to know more about
titleZh: 一见且想继续了解的人
questions: 【Part 2】
Describe a person you only met once recently and want to know more about
You should say: Who he/she is / When you met him/her / Why you want to know more about him/her / And explain how you feel about him/her
【Part 3】
1. What should we not talk about when we meet a person for the first time?
2. What can we do to leave a good impression on people we meet for the first time?
3. What qualities make true friends?
4. Is it important to have the same hobbies and interests when making friends?
5. On what occasions do people like to make friends?
6. How do people make friends in China?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 2 示范答案】
I would like to describe a woman I met at a friend dinner about a month ago and have thought about several times since. She is a landscape architect in her late thirties, and we ended up sitting next to each other because we were both late.

Why I want to know more about her is that she asked better questions than anyone I have met this year. She asked about my work, then about what I would change about my city, and she listened to the answer properly rather than waiting to speak. She also told me that she had moved countries at thirty-one to retrain, which I found quietly impressive.

How I feel about her is a mixture of curiosity and slight regret that we only had an hour. I have her contact details and I have been meaning to send a message, though I am aware that these impulses often fade within a fortnight. I am fairly confident she would be a good person to know.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 初次见面不该聊什么：收入、年龄、婚姻和私人健康问题。
2) 如何留下好印象：准时、记住名字、问开放的问题。Good listeners are remembered as charming people.
3) 真正朋友的品质：可靠、诚实、能保守秘密。
4) 爱好相同重要吗：不必相同，但要有共同的时间。
5) 什么场合容易交朋友：上学、工作、兴趣小组和旅行。
6) 中国人怎么交朋友：同事、同学介绍，以及餐桌。Most friendships here start around a meal.

【Part 3 全文】
1) What should we not talk about when we meet a person for the first time?

Money, salary, marital status, age, health problems and politics — anything that requires the other person to disclose something personal before they trust you. Questioning people is the fastest way to make a first meeting uncomfortable. Safe ground is work, travel, food, a shared event or the city you are both in. Curiosity should be general rather than personal.

2) What can we do to leave a good impression on people we meet for the first time?

Remember their name, listen more than you talk, and ask one follow-up question about what they said — which shows you were listening. Arrive on time, be specific rather than flattering, and follow up later with a short message. Warmth plus competence is the impression most people want to give. Sincerity is remembered longer than charm.

3) What qualities make true friends?

Reliability, honesty and a willingness to be uncomfortable for you — they tell you what you need to hear, and they show up when it is inconvenient. Shared history matters more than shared hobbies. And there is a genuine quality of ease: you can sit in silence. Anyone who is only pleasant when things are going well is an acquaintance.

4) Is it important to have the same hobbies and interests when making friends?

Not necessary, though a shared activity is a good excuse to meet weekly. Some of the strongest friendships pair people with almost different interests, bonded by humour or values. What matters is a compatible pace: how often you want to see each other and how much space you need. Hobbies start friendships; character keeps them.

5) On what occasions do people like to make friends?

Transitions, mostly: starting university, a new job, moving city, having a baby, a regular class or sports club. Shared difficulty makes bonding faster than shared pleasure. Adult friendship depends on repeated contact, which is why work and clubs do so much of the work. Without a routine, friendship quietly fades.

6) How do people make friends in China?

Often through school and university, then through work, and increasingly through shared hobbies such as sport, gaming or fan communities. Introductions by mutual friends still carry a lot of weight, and group meals do much of the formal work. People are friendly quickly but take time to include you in the real circle. Consistency and being useful both help.

title: Describe a gift you would like to buy for your friend
questions: 【Part 2】

You should say: How you knew your friend / How long you have known him/her / How you would choose a gift for him/her / And explain why you would choose that gift for him/her
【Part 3】
1. Are there any unlucky things that people should not buy as gifts in your country?
2. What do people usually consider when buying gifts?
3. Which do people give on traditional festivals, red envelopes or other kinds of gifts?
4. Will people feel happy when receiving an expensive gift?
5. Is it hard to choose a gift?
6. When do people normally send gifts to others?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 2 示范答案】
The gift I would like to buy is a good pair of walking shoes for a friend of mine who has recently started hiking. I met him at university about eight years ago, and in the last year he has become one of those people who texts you photographs of mountains on Sunday evenings.

I would choose the gift by watching him rather than asking him, because he is the sort of person who says he needs nothing. He currently walks in old trainers that are falling apart, and I have heard him complain about wet feet twice. My plan is to take him to a shop, let him try on four or five pairs, and pay for the one he would never buy for himself.

I would choose this gift because it is genuinely useful and slightly indulgent, which is the combination I like in a present. He also helped me move flats twice without being asked, so I am quietly in his debt, and shoes feel like a fair settlement.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 送礼有什么忌讳：钟表、伞和鞋在部分语境里不吉利。
2) 买礼物时考虑什么：对方的实际需要和心意。
3) 节日送红包还是礼物：长辈给红包，朋友之间送礼。
4) 收到贵礼物会开心吗：会，但也可能感到压力。
5) 挑礼物难吗：难，越了解对方越难挑。
6) 人们一般什么时候送礼：生日、节日、婚礼和探病。Gifts mark the moments that matter rather than the price.

【Part 3 全文】
1) Are there any unlucky things that people should not buy as gifts in your country?

Yes: clocks are strongly avoided because the word sounds like attending a funeral, and sharp objects like knives suggest severing a relationship. Pears have associations with separation, and anything in sets of four is avoided because of the number. Wrapping choices matter too. Most younger people say they do not care, but older relatives genuinely do.

2) What do people usually consider when buying gifts?

Whether it is useful, whether it fits the relationship, and the budget so it does not create an obligation. People also consider whether the gift is personal enough to show attention. Food is the safest category, and something for the recipient's child is a reliable move. Above a certain price the gift becomes a statement, which can backfire.

3) Which do people give on traditional festivals, red envelopes or other kinds of gifts?

Red envelopes to children, parents and sometimes employees, and boxed goods — tea, wine, fruit, health products — to everyone else. Red envelopes are the more honest gift, because the recipient can buy what they need. Physical gifts are more thoughtful but often end up stored. At weddings and New Year the envelope is standard.

4) Will people feel happy when receiving an expensive gift?

Not always — an expensive gift can create discomfort, because the recipient feels they must match it eventually or that a favour is now expected. The happiest reactions usually go to something well-chosen and moderately priced that shows the giver knows them. Expensive gifts work between close family. Between friends, they can shift the balance.

5) Is it hard to choose a gift?

Yes, for people who already have everything, which is most adults. The trick is to think about a small friction in their week and solve it — a better cable, a good thermos, a nice notebook. Consumables are safer than objects, since they do not need shelf space. Choosing well is mostly listening beforehand.

6) When do people normally send gifts to others?

Spring Festival, weddings, the birth of a child, graduations, birthdays, and visits to someone's home. Work occasions include starting a job and leaving one. The rhythm is mostly about marking a change in someone's life rather than the calendar. Arriving with something is almost always better than arriving empty-handed.

title: Describe an occasion that you lost something in public
questions: 【Part 2】
Describe an occasion that you lost something in public
You should say: What you lost / When and where you lost it / What you did to find it / And explain how you felt about it
【Part 3】
1. What do people often feel after losing things?
2. What can we do to reduce the possibility of losing things?
3. What kinds of people may lose things often?
4. Is it effective to offer rewards to find lost things?
5. What will people do when losing things?
6. What kinds of things do people usually lose?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 2 示范答案】
I would like to describe losing my wallet on a crowded bus two winters ago. It was a Friday evening, the bus was packed, and I only realised the wallet was gone when I tried to pay for a coffee about twenty minutes later.

What I did first was stupid: I ran back along the route checking the pavement, which achieved nothing except getting cold. Then I did the sensible things - I froze my bank card through the app, went to the bus company lost-property office the next morning, and left my phone number with two shopkeepers near the stop. Three days later a woman called to say she had found it under a seat with my student card inside, and I collected it with everything except the cash.

How I felt was a strange mixture of panic and, in the end, surprise at other people kindness. The money was gone but nothing else, and the whole episode cost me about thirty pounds and a weekend of standing in queues, which I now think was cheap.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 丢东西后人们常有什么感受：先是慌乱，然后自责。
2) 如何减少丢东西的可能：固定位置、少带现金、检查口袋。
3) 哪种人常丢东西：忙、累、注意力分散的人。
4) 悬赏找回失物有效吗：有效，但也要靠制度和信用。
5) 人们丢东西后会做什么：原路找、报警、求助网络。
6) 人们常丢什么：手机、钥匙、伞、耳机。Umbrellas and earphones are the great annual casualties.

【Part 3 全文】
1) What do people often feel after losing things?

A short burst of panic, then self-blame, then a phase where the loss feels bigger than it is — especially for a phone or a wallet. There is a strange grief to losing something irreplaceable, like photos or a key. Most people also feel embarrassed in public. Then it passes quickly once the practical steps are taken.

2) What can we do to reduce the possibility of losing things?

Fewer items, and always the same place for each one — keys in one pocket, phone in another. A lanyard or a card holder helps enormously, and so does a wallet that stays closed. Taking a photo of where you put something in a hotel room feels silly and works. Routine beats vigilance for most people.

3) What kinds of people may lose things often?

People who handle many items at once — commuters, delivery riders, parents — and anyone who is sleep-deprived or stressed, since attention is the actual mechanism. Creative, fast-moving people lose more than methodical ones. Children lose things constantly, which is normal. I would say circumstances explain more than personality.

4) Is it effective to offer rewards to find lost things?

Sometimes it works for documents or a pet, where a stranger benefits from helping you quickly. For a phone or a wallet, the reward sometimes creates a strange negotiation rather than a return. Most honest people hand things in without expecting money. A clear contact number is more useful than a reward.

5) What will people do when losing things?

They retrace their steps, call the place, check the last three transactions, and either freeze the cards and lock the phone or ask someone to help. Then they post in local groups, which occasionally works. Documentation matters — you often need an ID to collect an ID. The first hour is the productive one.

6) What kinds of things do people usually lose?

Umbrellas, bank cards, phones, keys, headphones and wallets, along with the occasional passport, which is the worst because it has no substitute. Umbrellas are the classic, because nobody values one until it is raining. In practice people lose small reusable objects with no strong emotional attachment. Things you care about rarely get lost.

title: Describe a way/change that helps you save a lot of time
questions: 【Part 2】
Describe a way/change that helps you save a lot of time
You should say: What it is / How you implement it / How difficult it is / And explain how you feel about the way/change
【Part 3】
1. What can people do to save time?
2. Does technology help people save time? How and why?
3. Do you think parents should be responsible for teaching children to save time?
4. Do people who can manage time well become successful more easily?
5. Is it necessary for children to learn time management?
6. What can schools do to help students learn time management?
ninePointAnswer:
【Part 2 示范答案】
The change that saves me the most time is doing my food shopping once a week online instead of dropping into shops three or four times. I introduced it about a year ago, mostly out of frustration at losing an hour every other evening to a supermarket queue.

It was easy to implement, which is why it stuck. I keep a running list on my phone during the week, order on Saturday morning and have it delivered the same afternoon, so I only spend about twenty minutes a week on the whole process. The one adjustment was meal planning: I had to start deciding what I would cook, otherwise I still ended up in the shop midweek buying onions.

How I feel about it is disproportionately pleased for such a boring change. It gives me back about three hours a week and, more importantly, stops the small daily decisions about food from crowding out things I actually want to think about.

【Part 3 观点与表达】
1) 人们怎么省时间：批量处理、提前计划、减少来回。
2) 技术帮忙省时间吗：帮，但也会吃掉时间。Technology saves minutes and steals hours.
3) 父母该教孩子省时间吗：该，先教守时和优先级。
4) 会管理时间的人更容易成功吗：更容易，因为承诺更可靠。
5) 孩子需要学时间管理吗：需要，越早越自然。
6) 学校能做什么：明确截止时间、教做计划和复盘。Teaching children to plan is more useful than teaching them to hurry.

【Part 3 全文】
1) What can people do to save time?

Group similar tasks, decide small things in advance, and say no earlier. A lot of time is lost in transitions between tasks rather than in the tasks themselves. Batch the shopping and the messages, and stop opening your phone for anything that is not a decision. Preparation buys more time than rushing ever does.

2) Does technology help people save time? How and why?

It saves time on tasks — navigation, payments, comparison, translation, reminders — and takes it back with notifications, scrolling and the endless availability it creates. So the net effect depends entirely on whether you control it. The honest version is that I save an hour a day and lose ninety minutes. Boundaries matter more than apps.

3) Do you think parents should be responsible for teaching children to save time?

Partly, mainly by modelling it: if parents are perpetually late, children learn that time is flexible. But schools and the child's own experience do as much — missing a bus teaches punctuality quickly. I would teach planning, not rushing, because rushing is what people do when they have not planned. Small habits matter more than talks.

4) Do people who can manage time well become successful more easily?

Usually, yes, because reliability compounds: you get trusted with bigger things, and you avoid the emergencies that come from being late. But time management alone is not a talent; it just stops you wasting the talent you have. The people I know who are genuinely good are organised in a relaxed way rather than rigid.

5) Is it necessary for children to learn time management?

Yes, and starting with simple, visible things: how long does homework really take, what comes first, what needs to move. Children learn it faster when they have some control over their own schedule. Without it they carry an anxious feeling of being always behind. School deadlines give it a natural context.
